metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the evaluation, risk stratification, surveillance, treatment, and follow-up of adults with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction. It covers urinary symptoms and complications, including incontinence, retention, urinary tract infection, and autonomic dysreflexia, across a range of neurologic conditions. It also discusses how neurologic status, functional abilities, and available support affect shared treatment decisions.

target_population: Adults with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction
Adults with neurologic conditions affecting lower urinary tract function

toxicities.event: Autonomic dysreflexia during urodynamic testing or cystoscopy
recognition: The principal at-risk group has SCI at T6 or above, although some patients with injuries at T7 or T8 may also be susceptible.

Possible manifestations include hypertension, headache, visual disturbance, flushing, sweating, nasal congestion and reflex bradycardia. Bladder distension is the most frequent trigger; bowel distension can also provoke an episode.

management.actions: Stop the examination immediately, empty the bladder and continue hemodynamic monitoring. Position the patient upright, loosen restrictive clothing or devices, and check blood pressure at least every five minutes until baseline vital signs return.

Start pharmacologic treatment and/or escalate care. The guideline describes applying 1 to 2 inches of 2% nitroglycerine paste above the neurological lesion; it also describes immediate-release sublingual nifedipine (10 mg capsules), while cautioning that its blood-pressure effect may be abrupt and difficult to reverse. If antihypertensive treatment fails, a more intensively monitored setting and intravenous sodium nitroprusside may be appropriate.

prevention: Continuously monitor hemodynamics during urodynamic testing or cystoscopy in patients at risk.
Use staff trained to recognize and manage autonomic dysreflexia, and ensure pharmacologic treatment is readily available before the procedure.
Educate patients, caregivers, family members and clinicians about triggers and warning signs.

toxicities.incidence: In a meta-analysis, dry mouth with antimuscarinics versus placebo had Relative Risk (RR) = 4.23; 95% CI: 1.85-9.67, p<0.05. In a comparison involving combination treatment, 30 of the 97 patients receiving two medications reported dry mouth. In an intravesical-versus-oral oxybutynin study, adverse events occurred in 55.6% and 82.4%, respectively.
recognition: Dry mouth is the most frequently reported adverse effect. Reported effects also include constipation, nausea and blurred vision.

Long-term anticholinergic treatment raises a potential concern about cognitive impairment or dementia, but the guideline characterizes the evidence on this association as conflicting and of low certainty.
Antimuscarinics may increase PVR in patients with SCI.
prevention: Discuss potential cognitive risks and therapeutic benefits through shared decision-making; for selected patients, an alternative agent less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier may be appropriate.

toxicities.incidence: In the cited phenoxybenzamine study, one-quarter of patients discontinued because of adverse effects; the guideline also reports a 25% discontinuation rate. In the cited randomized tamsulosin phase, adverse-effect discontinuation was 4.4% with placebo and 2.3 and 2.5% in the two active-drug groups, respectively; during the open-label extension it was 9.6%.
recognition: Reported tamsulosin effects include dizziness, abnormal ejaculation and fatigue; doxazosin ER was associated with transient, mild dizziness.
The terazosin studies reported syncope, lethargy, rash and peripheral edema.
Phenoxybenzamine was associated with severe orthostatic hypotension, severe tachycardia, incontinence and ejaculatory failure.

toxicities.event: Urethral and bladder-outlet injury associated with an indwelling urethral catheter
toxicities.incidence: Urethral erosion affects up to 23% of men with NLUTD and a urethral catheter.
recognition: Men may develop catheter-associated hypospadias or urethral erosion. Women may develop progressive urethral and bladder-neck dilation, urethral tissue loss and leakage around the catheter.
Prolonged pressure may cause necrosis of urethral tissue or even the pubic bone. Reduced perineal sensation, impaired cognition, larger catheters and prolonged sitting increase concern.

management.actions: Investigate its cause rather than enlarging the catheter or its balloon, since either enlargement can worsen the problem.

Urethroplasty may be possible when tissue permits. In a woman with limited dilation and little tissue loss, an autologous sling may suffice if drainage is changed to a suprapubic tube; severe urethral loss may require bladder neck closure with suprapubic drainage or urinary diversion.

prevention: Examine the catheter and its urethral entry site periodically so injury can be detected early.
Secure the catheter appropriately, recognizing that this does not eliminate erosion risk.
Consider conversion to suprapubic drainage when urethral damage develops.

toxicities.event: Suprapubic catheter placement and site complications
toxicities.incidence: In a cited series of 219 patients, intraoperative complications occurred in 10%, 30-day complications in 19%, and 43.5% required intervention for an adverse event during follow-up. The reported 30-day events included UTI with sepsis (4.6%), surgical site infection (3.65%), bleeding (1.82%) and SPC malfunction (2.28%).
recognition: An inadequately secured suprapubic catheter may erode through the abdominal wall.
Granulation tissue around its site can bleed or impede catheter exchange.

management.severity: Granulation tissue at the suprapubic catheter site
management.actions: The guideline describes office treatment with topical silver nitrate.

prevention: Periodically examine the catheter and suprapubic insertion site.

toxicities.event: Urinary tract calculi associated with indwelling catheter management
toxicities.incidence: Reported bladder-stone prevalence among patients with indwelling catheters ranges from 8% to 41%; upper-tract stones occur in 6-32% of this population.
recognition: Calculi can remain clinically silent, particularly when patients do not void or have altered sensation.
The catheter can provide a surface for biofilm and crystal formation; material remaining after balloon deflation may seed bladder stones.

management.actions: The guideline notes that very small stones may be irrigated in clinic and slightly larger ones managed by cystolithalopaxy.

prevention: For patients with indwelling catheters at risk of upper- or lower-tract calculi, perform urinary tract imaging every 1-2 years.
Continue surveillance according to the patient's moderate- or high-risk NLUTD category.

toxicities.event: Urinary retention or incomplete emptying after botulinum toxin treatment
toxicities.incidence: Across single-injection RCTs, urinary retention ranged from 2.6 – 54% in onabotulinumtoxinA groups and 1.9 – 5.0% in placebo groups. In non-catheterizing MS patients in the DIGNITY analysis, initiation of CIC for retention was 31.4% with onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U, 47.1% with 300 U and 4.5% with placebo. In the cited 100 U trial, CIC was needed by 15.2% of the onabotulinumtoxinA group and 2.6% of the placebo group, for median durations of 64.0 and 2.0 days, respectively.
recognition: Incomplete bladder emptying, a rising PVR or urinary retention may necessitate catheterization after injection.
The need to initiate CIC in initially non-catheterizing MS patients increased with dose.

management.actions: CIC may be required for weeks to months; an indwelling catheter may be necessary if CIC cannot be performed. A trained caregiver may be needed when physical or cognitive limitations prevent self-catheterization.

prevention: Before selecting botulinum toxin therapy for a spontaneously voiding patient with NLUTD, discuss the specific retention risk and possible need for intermittent catheterization.
Consider the patient's capacity, caregiver availability, training and supplies through shared decision-making.

toxicities.event: Urinary tract infection after botulinum toxin treatment
toxicities.incidence: The cited meta-analysis reported OR = 1.68; 95% CI 1.20 to 2.35; p<0.05 for UTI with botulinum toxin A. Across the RCTs, reported UTI rates ranged from 21 – 70%, although definitions and bladder-management methods differed. In a cited trial of non-catheterizing MS patients, UTI occurred in 25.8% of onabotulinumtoxinA-treated patients and 6.4% of placebo-treated patients; symptomatic UTI occurred in 13.6% and 1.3%, respectively.
recognition: UTI is among the most frequently reported adverse events following onabotulinumtoxinA injections.

toxicities.event: Muscular weakness after botulinum toxin treatment
toxicities.incidence: In cited RCTs, muscular weakness after onabotulinumtoxinA ranged from 0 – 13.4%, compared with 0 – 14.29% with placebo. In a cited adult spinal-dyraphism series, muscular weakness occurred in 0.5% of injection cases.
recognition: Distant toxin spread has been reported to cause weakness. The few weakness events described in the cited RCTs were transient and resolved without further treatment.

toxicities.incidence: In a cited study of 84 men with spinal injury, the procedure failed in 57 patients (68%, median time to failure 36 months); 30 underwent a second procedure.
recognition: Failure or recurrence can involve impaired emptying, elevated intravesical pressures, recurrent UTI or autonomic dysreflexia.
Long-term problems include skin breakdown from a condom catheter and difficulty maintaining the catheter in position. Postoperative bleeding may require transfusion.

management.actions: Continue follow-up for recurrent UTI, autonomic dysreflexia, elevated DLPP and residual urine. Urodynamics may be performed after sphincterotomy to evaluate its result; further treatment or surgery may be necessary.

prevention: Before sphincterotomy, counsel patients about its substantial failure risk and the possibility of additional procedures.

toxicities.event: Complications of artificial urinary sphincter implantation
toxicities.incidence: In one cited study, reoperation occurred in 28% of patients and 78% needed intermittent catheterization. In a cited series of women undergoing AUS, reported non-mechanical complications across all women included infection (4.8%), vaginal erosion (3.2%), urethral erosion (1.9%), labia-major erosion (1.9%) and bladder erosion (1.1%); these rates were not reported separately for women with NLUTD.
recognition: Potential problems include postoperative voiding dysfunction, device erosion or infection, mechanical failure and a need for CIC or further surgery.
An outlet procedure can aggravate impaired bladder compliance and threaten the upper urinary tract.
prevention: Assess relevant bladder storage parameters with UDS before implantation and confirm that the patient can manipulate the device.
Counsel about possible CIC, increased erosion or infection risk, revision and explantation.

toxicities.incidence: The guideline reports continence rates of 75 – 100% and fistulization with recurrent incontinence in up to 25% of cases. In a cited series, a fistula occurred in 6 (15%) patients.
recognition: A fistula may cause recurrent leakage after closure.
Without safe postoperative bladder storage pressures, the upper urinary tract may be at risk.

management.actions: In the cited series, some fistulas required repeat surgery; one closed after prolonged drainage.

prevention: Plan a method of bladder drainage and evaluate storage pressures with UDS when the outlet procedure could worsen compliance.
Discuss the irreversible nature of closure and its risks, benefits and alternatives.

toxicities.incidence: In a cited systematic review, risks of stones, bowel dysfunction and mucus-related complications exceeded 10%. In a cited comparison of two surgical series, early (< 3 months) and late (> 3 months) postoperative complication rates were 15% and 17%, respectively.
recognition: Potential complications include stones, bladder perforation, bowel dysfunction and mucus production.
Patients who undergo reconstruction using bowel may develop metabolic or acid-base disturbances and upper-tract obstruction.
prevention: Before surgery, discuss long-term risks, the need for lifelong follow-up and whether the patient or a caregiver can perform regular CIC.
After reconstruction incorporating bowel, assess history, examination, symptoms, a basic metabolic panel and urinary tract imaging annually.
If terminal ileum was used, monitor B12 over time and supplement it when appropriate.
Do not perform routine surveillance cystoscopy without an indication; perform cystoscopy if gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI develops.

toxicities.incidence: In the cited systematic review, re-operations were required in 40% of patients, and CCC stenosis occurred in 4-32% (median 14%).
recognition: Channel stenosis can impede catheterization. Other reported reasons for further surgery include neovesicocutaneous fistulae, bladder stones and bladder perforation.

management.actions: Revision or another operation may be required.

prevention: Counsel patients before surgery about expected outcomes, complications and the possibility of channel revision.

toxicities.incidence: Across cited retrospective studies, subsequent procedures were required in 33 to 75%. In a cited comparison of patients with severe urethral destruction, urosepsis occurred in 82% after BNC with ileovesicostomy, 60% after an ileal conduit and 29% after BNC with SPC; subsequent surgical intervention was required in 88%, 50% and 52%, respectively.
recognition: Stomal problems, inadequate drainage, urinary stones, fistulae and persistent incontinence may necessitate further treatment.

management.actions: The cited studies report stomal revision as the most common reoperation, followed by removal of bladder or kidney stones.

prevention: Counsel patients about risks, benefits, alternatives and the high likelihood of additional treatment or surgery.
Provide regular long-term follow-up to assess drainage and detect stones.

toxicities.event: Metabolic and late complications after urinary reconstruction using bowel
toxicities.incidence: For supravesical diversion, the guideline reports a delayed complication rate of 21-50%. In a cited series of 53 patients with MS after ileal conduit construction, 11 required surgery for a late complication; another cited study reported upper-tract changes in 34% after conduit construction.
recognition: Electrolyte or acid-base abnormalities may occur after bowel-based reconstruction; risk depends in part on pre-existing renal dysfunction, comorbidities, the bowel segment and diversion type.
Late concerns include upper-tract obstruction, recurrent bladder infection and pyocystis.
prevention: Continue lifelong surveillance after bowel-based lower urinary tract reconstruction, with annual focused clinical assessment, basic metabolic panel and urinary tract imaging.
Monitor B12 over time if terminal ileum was used and supplement when appropriate.

Consider cystectomy when constructing a supravesical diversion; the guideline says concurrent supratrigonal cystectomy or cystoprostatectomy should be strongly considered for male patients with NLUTD.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use daily antibiotics to prevent UTI in patients with NLUTD who manage their bladder with an indwelling catheter.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD using an indwelling catheter

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use daily antibiotics in patients using clean intermittent catheterization who do not have recurrent UTI.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD using clean intermittent catheterization without recurrent UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Clinicians may offer prophylaxis to reduce recurrent UTI after shared decision-making that includes the increased risk of antibiotic resistance.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD using clean intermittent catheterization who have recurrent UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Clinicians may offer bladder instillations to reduce recurrent UTI; evidence is insufficient to favor any single instillation strategy. The guideline encourages an individual discussion of risks and benefits for gentamicin instillation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD using clean intermittent catheterization who have recurrent UTI

prophylaxis.recommendation: Clinicians may explain that cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to lower UTI rates; the guideline does not recommend it as an effective preventive intervention.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD and recurrent UTI using various catheter-management methods

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline identifies treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria before urologic procedures expected to disrupt the urothelium or manipulate the upper tract as an exception to its general advice against treatment. It describes perioperative antimicrobial treatment or prophylaxis for contaminated or clean-contaminated procedures as best practice.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD and bacteriuria undergoing the specified urologic procedures

prophylaxis.recommendation: The guideline cites the SUFU Best Practice Policy Statement's recommendation of a single oral dose of trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with NLUTD undergoing urodynamic testing

infection_management.prevention: Do not routinely screen asymptomatic patients with urine testing or culture. Avoid unnecessary antibiotic exposure and its contribution to resistance.
infection_management.management: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, except in pregnancy or before urologic procedures expected to disrupt the urothelium or manipulate the upper tract. For an endoscopic urologic procedure, the guideline cites obtaining a preprocedural culture and giving a targeted short antimicrobial course rather than empiric therapy.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Suspected symptomatic urinary tract infection in NLUTD
infection_management.management: Obtain urinalysis and urine culture when signs or symptoms suggest UTI. Symptoms alone cannot reliably establish the diagnosis across patients with NLUTD; use culture results to guide antibiotic selection. When suspicion is high, empiric antibiotics may be started and changed if the culture result warrants it; a recent prior culture may help select the initial drug.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Febrile urinary tract infection in NLUTD
infection_management.management: Obtain urinalysis and culture and administer appropriate culture-specific antibiotics. Order upper-tract imaging if the patient does not respond appropriately to antibiotic therapy. Also order imaging for a moderate- or high-risk patient whose routine upper-tract imaging is overdue, regardless of treatment response.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Suspected urinary tract infection with an indwelling catheter
infection_management.prevention: Do not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis solely to prevent UTI in patients managing their bladder with an indwelling catheter.
infection_management.management: Replace the catheter, allow urine to accumulate while the catheter is plugged, and then collect the culture specimen. Do not obtain urine from extension tubing or the collection bag.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Recurrent urinary tract infection in NLUTD
infection_management.prevention: For patients using clean intermittent catheterization, clinicians may offer oral antimicrobial prophylaxis after discussion of resistance risk, or may offer bladder instillations. Cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to reduce UTI rates.
infection_management.management: Evaluate both upper and lower urinary tracts using imaging and cystoscopy. If that evaluation is unremarkable, clinicians may perform urodynamic assessment. The guideline does not establish a fixed definition of recurrent UTI specifically for NLUTD.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent urinary tract infection after lower urinary tract reconstruction using bowel
infection_management.management: Perform cystoscopy. The guideline also describes a full assessment including urine cytology and computerized tomography of the abdomen and pelvis when concerning symptoms arise; do not presume that bleeding or unexplained recurrent infection is caused by catheter trauma, cystitis or pouchitis without evaluation.

conditions.name: neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction
conditions.description: Neurological disease can disrupt urine storage, bladder emptying, sphincter relaxation during voiding, or continence during filling. Dysfunction may involve the bladder, bladder neck, or sphincters, and storage and emptying problems may coexist. Non-neurogenic urinary conditions can also contribute to symptoms.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline reports that 28-79% of people have UI after CVA; studies suggest LUTS in up to 50-90% of patients with MS; over 80% of patients with SCI require a catheter after injury; and up to 80% of people with diabetes experience a lower urinary tract complication during their lifetime. These figures concern specific neurological populations, not NLUTD overall.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Manifestations include urgency, frequency, UI, urinary retention, incomplete emptying, recurrent UTI, and AD. Symptoms can change over time; in diabetes, an initially asymptomatic patient may develop OAB-type symptoms and later incomplete emptying with possible overflow incontinence.

subtypes.name: low-risk NLUTD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Low likelihood of upper urinary tract damage, generally with stable renal function and imaging, low PVR, and synergistic voiding when assessed.

subtypes.name: unknown-risk NLUTD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Initial findings do not permit complete risk classification; upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, and multichannel UDS are needed.

subtypes.name: moderate-risk NLUTD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes patients requiring bladder drainage by catheter or having elevated PVR, without the dangerous findings that define high risk.

subtypes.name: high-risk NLUTD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Characterized by concerning UDS findings, significant upper tract disease, or abnormal or unstable renal function.

subtypes.name: NLUTD secondary to SCI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Suprasacral lesions can produce DO and DSD; cervical and high thoracic injuries can place patients at particular risk of elevated storage pressures and AD.

subtypes.name: NLUTD secondary to MS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Symptoms may involve storage, emptying, or both, and neurological progression can alter lower urinary tract function.

subtypes.name: NLUTD secondary to PD
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A suprapontine cause commonly associated with DO and balanced voiding; coexisting BOO can complicate assessment.

subtypes.name: NLUTD secondary to CVA
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A suprapontine cause that often produces DO and synergistic voiding, although elevated PVR can occur.

subtypes.name: NLUTD secondary to SB
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A congenital cause with variable neurological involvement and possible high-risk storage findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize neurological disease, urinary symptoms, bladder management, complications, prior treatment, functional ability, cognition, bowel function, and available support.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For every patient at initial evaluation; focused reassessment according to risk during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: New symptoms or complications may require reassessment of risk and further investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess cognition, mobility, upper extremity function, abdomen, flanks, genital or pelvic findings, skin integrity, and relevant neurological and reflex findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For every patient at initial evaluation and during risk-appropriate follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify findings including hematuria, pyuria, glucosuria, and proteinuria.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For every patient at initial evaluation; also when UTI is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Results require consideration of symptoms, underlying disease, and catheter use; an abnormal dipstick may warrant microscopic examination.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urine remaining after voiding and detect impaired emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation for patients who void spontaneously; a suspected abnormal elevation should be checked again at another visit, and measurement may be repeated to assess changes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An elevated value can reflect DU, BOO, or both and may prompt multichannel UDS and indicated treatment. No definitive NLUTD-specific normal or abnormal cutoff is established. A low value does not rule out dangerous storage dysfunction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record voiding or catheterization timing and volumes, leakage, and potentially intake and urgency; inform assessment, treatment, and response monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Optional at initial evaluation when additional information could guide care, particularly if recall is unreliable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Recorded volumes can help assess functional bladder volume and guide interpretation of UDS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Objectively establish leakage or quantify its severity and assess outcomes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Optional in selected patients.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess flow during spontaneous voiding.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Optional for patients who void spontaneously.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal result indicates voiding-phase dysfunction but does not distinguish BOO from DU; a normal result does not exclude significant coexisting disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect hydronephrosis, renal scarring or parenchymal loss, and calculi.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation for unknown-risk NLUTD and subsequently according to risk or new clinical findings; not routinely at initial evaluation or surveillance in stable low-risk NLUTD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Significant upper tract abnormalities can establish high-risk status.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify renal impairment and support risk classification and surveillance.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation for unknown-risk NLUTD and during indicated moderate- or high-risk surveillance; not routinely in stable low-risk NLUTD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In SCI, low muscle mass can limit serum creatinine interpretation; a significant rise from baseline warrants assessment even if the result remains within the normal range.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess storage pressure, compliance, DO, emptying, and DLPP when relevant.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation for unknown-risk NLUTD; subsequently when indicated by risk, changed findings, or treatment response. Not routinely for stable low-risk NLUTD.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Poor compliance, high storage pressures, or DSD may identify risk to the upper urinary tract. The precise pressure threshold for injury is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urodynamic function together with findings such as VUR.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used in high-risk surveillance when clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: VUR contributes to high-risk classification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate hematuria, recurrent UTI, or suspected anatomical abnormalities such as strictures or false passages.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a specific clinical indication exists; not routinely for initial evaluation or screening surveillance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Capture patient-reported symptoms or quality of life and assess change over time.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used when applicable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Collect baseline symptom information and assess subsequent change or response.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be administered when applicable.

prognostic_tools.name: NLUTD Risk Stratification

risk_groups.criteria: Normal/stable renal function; low PVR; normal/stable urinary tract imaging if assessed; synergetic voiding if assessed.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Low likelihood of upper urinary tract deterioration attributable to NLUTD.

risk_groups.criteria: Normal/stable renal function; elevated PVR; normal urinary tract imaging; neurogenic retention or DO with incomplete emptying on UDS.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Ongoing risk of urinary complications, lower than in High-Risk NLUTD.

risk_groups.criteria: Abnormal/unstable renal function; imaging showing hydronephrosis, new renal scaring, loss of renal parenchyma, or staghorn/ large stone burden; or UDS showing poor compliance, VUR if fluoroscopy is performed, or high storage pressures with DO and DSD.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: Substantial risk of renal deterioration, worsening bladder function, and urinary infection.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Assign the highest risk category whose criteria the patient meets in any component. Patients whose risk cannot be determined initially require further evaluation.

follow_up.schedule: Surveillance depends on risk category. Patients should be told which new or worsening findings require additional assessment; risk classification should be revisited when symptoms, complications, upper tract findings, or renal function change.
recommended_tests: Risk-appropriate focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
Risk-appropriate renal function assessment
Risk-appropriate upper tract imaging
Multichannel UDS when indicated by risk, changing findings, or response assessment
Cystoscopy for specified clinical indications rather than routine screening
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Management and surveillance should account for the neurological disease, physical and cognitive ability, caregiver support, and patient preferences.

conditions.name: low-risk NLUTD
conditions.description: A risk category generally associated with a neurological condition unlikely to damage the upper urinary tract, satisfactory emptying, and no recurrent urinary complications.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may have stable urinary symptoms or no symptoms. A new complication or change in symptoms can alter their risk classification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish clinical findings and assess risk.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Stable symptoms, no recurrent UTI or complications, and a compatible neurological diagnosis support low-risk classification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation if the patient voids spontaneously.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A low PVR supports low-risk classification; an elevated PVR warrants further investigation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, and multichannel UDS
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Reassess risk when clinically indicated.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not routinely at initial evaluation or during surveillance while urinary signs and symptoms remain stable; new findings or complications can prompt investigation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Normal upper tracts and renal function with synergistic voiding can establish low risk in a patient initially classified as unknown-risk.

follow_up.schedule: No routine upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, or multichannel UDS while urinary findings remain stable. Re-evaluate and repeat risk stratification if new symptoms, complications, or upper tract or renal deterioration occur.
recommended_tests: Clinical reassessment when new urinary findings occur
Further testing as indicated by reassessed risk
long_term_effects: Possible later urinary retention, UTI, stones, or deterioration despite initially low risk
follow_up.survivorship_notes: When further urological management is unnecessary, follow-up may occur in primary care with education about findings that warrant reassessment.

conditions.name: unknown-risk NLUTD
conditions.description: Initial clinical assessment is insufficient to determine the patient's risk of urinary tract complications.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential reasons for uncertain risk include suprasacral spinal disease, stones, elevated PVR, recurrent UTI, or new or fluctuating urinary findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify renal and upper tract abnormalities needed for risk classification.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Hydronephrosis, renal scarring, parenchymal loss, or substantial stone burden can indicate high risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify functional deterioration and complete risk classification.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal or unstable function indicates high risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess storage and emptying characteristics that cannot reliably be predicted from clinical findings alone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Concerning findings include poor compliance, high storage pressures, DO, and DSD. Values less than 12.5 ml/cmH2O have been suggested as abnormal compliance; sustained intravesical pressures in excess of 40 ml/cmH2O are associated with increased upper tract deterioration risk, although precise thresholds remain uncertain.

follow_up.schedule: After the additional initial assessments, surveillance follows the resulting risk category.
recommended_tests: Risk-appropriate surveillance after classification

conditions.name: moderate-risk NLUTD
conditions.description: A classified group commonly requiring catheter drainage or having elevated PVR after spontaneous voiding, without high-risk UDS or upper tract findings.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Impaired emptying and reduced mobility can contribute to complications; renal stones may be asymptomatic or present atypically because of altered sensation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect new complications, catheterization difficulties, and changes requiring management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually while urinary findings remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A change in symptoms or new complications can prompt further evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor for renal deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually while urinary findings remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A significant rise in serum creatinine from baseline merits careful assessment, including when still within the normal range.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify stones and other upper tract abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Every 1-2 years while urinary findings remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Renal US can assess kidneys and bladder; an equivalent interval upper tract study may also be reviewed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible changes in bladder function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be performed if symptoms change, complications develop, or upper tract or renal function deteriorates.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: High-risk findings can change risk classification.

follow_up.schedule: Annual focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, and renal function assessment; upper tract imaging every 1-2 years.
recommended_tests: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
Renal function assessment
Upper tract imaging
Multichannel UDS if clinically indicated
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Stone surveillance may be needed throughout life. Imaging frequency can be adjusted for a patient who has remained stable and reliably seeks care for new symptoms.

conditions.name: high-risk NLUTD
conditions.description: A risk category defined by dangerous bladder storage findings, significant upper tract abnormalities, or abnormal or unstable renal function.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Deteriorating compliance, elevated storage pressures, and VUR may progress without noticeable symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess clinical status and complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At least annually while urinary findings remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Clinical findings help determine whether additional UDS is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor renal deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually while urinary findings remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Unstable or abnormal function remains a high-risk feature.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor calculi, parenchymal loss, and other upper tract abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually while urinary findings remain stable.

diagnostic_workup.test: Multichannel UDS, with or without fluoroscopy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess storage pressure, compliance, and potential VUR or other deterioration.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be repeated when clinically indicated, including in some patients whose symptoms remain stable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Results and prior findings inform ongoing risk classification and treatment.

follow_up.schedule: At least annual focused clinical and symptom assessment, renal function assessment, and upper tract imaging; repeat multichannel UDS when clinically indicated. Additional visits may be needed for treatment or complications.
recommended_tests: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
Renal function assessment
Upper tract imaging
Multichannel UDS, with or without fluoroscopy, when clinically indicated
follow_up.survivorship_notes: If treatment and subsequent assessment establish a lower risk category, later surveillance follows that new category.

conditions.name: autonomic dysreflexia
conditions.description: An acute medical emergency involving an abnormal spinal reflex in susceptible patients with SCI. Bladder distension or a lower urinary tract procedure can trigger sympathetic activity and hypertension.
conditions.epidemiology: Bladder distension related to retention, catheter blockage, or lower urinary tract procedures accounts for up to 85% of AD cases.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible findings include hypertension, headache, visual disturbance, flushing, sweating, nasal congestion, and reflex bradycardia. Bowel distension is another potential trigger.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize and follow an episode during a provoking procedure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Continuously during UDS or cystoscopy in NLUTD patients at risk; after an episode begins, monitor blood pressure at least every five minutes until baseline vital signs return.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Persistent symptoms with systolic blood pressure greater than 150 mm Hg and/or 20 mm Hg above baseline following bladder drainage indicate that initial measures have not adequately controlled the episode.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a removable trigger such as bladder distension or catheter blockage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When AD develops.

follow_up.schedule: Continue hemodynamic observation during an acute episode until vital signs stabilize; educate patients about new or worsening AD between visits.
recommended_tests: Blood pressure and other vital sign monitoring during an episode
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Risk is greatest with SCI at T6 or above, although some patients with injuries at T7 or T8 may also be susceptible.

conditions.name: urinary tract infection
conditions.description: Infection in a patient with NLUTD can be difficult to recognize because neurological deficits and bladder management methods can change usual symptoms.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline cites an estimated 2.5 episodes of infection per patient per year in NLUTD. In a review of 48,327 patients with >1 neurogenic bladder-specific diagnosis, 38.6% had a UTI over a one-year period, comprising 36.4% lower and 2.2% upper UTI.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible findings include fever, new leakage or incontinence, leakage around a catheter, increased spasticity, malaise, lethargy, cloudy or malodorous urine, back or bladder pain, dysuria, and AD. No individual symptom pattern reliably diagnoses UTI across all NLUTD patients.

subtypes.name: febrile urinary tract infection
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Fever can signal a potentially serious complication, particularly when the infection does not respond appropriately to antibiotics.

subtypes.name: recurrent urinary tract infections
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Repeated infections warrant upper and lower urinary tract evaluation; the guideline does not set a definitive recurrence threshold specifically for NLUTD.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support assessment of suspected infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When signs or symptoms suggest UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Symptoms and urine findings must be interpreted together; symptoms alone are insufficiently reliable.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnosis and selection of culture-specific antibiotics.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When signs or symptoms suggest UTI.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For a suspected UTI with an indwelling catheter, collect urine after catheter replacement and accumulation with the catheter plugged, not from extension tubing or the collection bag. The guideline cites IDSA catheter-associated UTI criteria of compatible symptoms, no other identifiable infection source, and >103 CFU/mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate findings such as stones or hydronephrosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For febrile UTI that does not respond appropriately to antibiotics; also if a moderate- or high-risk patient is overdue for routine imaging, regardless of treatment response.

diagnostic_workup.test: Upper and lower urinary tract imaging
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible sources of recurrent UTI.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For recurrent UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess lower tract causes of recurrent infection, including anatomical abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For recurrent UTI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate functional contributors to recurrent infection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be performed if recurrent UTI persists despite an unremarkable upper and lower tract evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Findings such as elevated PVR, VUR, DO, or poor compliance may inform management.

follow_up.schedule: New, more frequent, or febrile infections should be reported and evaluated; further assessment depends on response to treatment and NLUTD risk category.
recommended_tests: UA and urine culture for suggestive symptoms
Upper tract imaging under the specified febrile UTI circumstances
Imaging and cystoscopy for recurrent UTI
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Avoid interpreting nonspecific symptoms alone as proof of infection; culture results can guide antibiotic selection.

conditions.name: asymptomatic bacteriuria
conditions.description: Urinary bacterial growth without symptoms of UTI. Colonization is common in NLUTD, but most patients with bacterial growth do not subsequently develop symptomatic infection.
conditions.epidemiology: In the cited Tornic et al. cohort of 317 asymptomatic NLUTD patients cultured before UDS, 61% had bacterial growth, while 18% developed symptomatic UTI during one year of follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify bacteriuria when a specific clinical circumstance warrants assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not recommended as routine screening or surveillance in asymptomatic NLUTD. The guideline describes exceptions relevant to pregnancy and procedures anticipated to disrupt the urothelium or manipulate the upper tract.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result without symptoms does not by itself justify antibiotic treatment in the usual NLUTD setting.

follow_up.schedule: No routine urine-test surveillance solely to identify asymptomatic bacteriuria.
long_term_effects: Antibiotic resistance associated with unnecessary treatment
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline identifies pregnancy and specified urologic procedures as exceptions to the general recommendation not to treat.

conditions.name: neurogenic detrusor overactivity
conditions.description: A neurogenic bladder storage abnormality addressed in the guideline through assessment of storage function and treatment of associated incontinence or unsafe pressures.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May be associated with urgency, UI, reduced functional storage, or elevated detrusor storage pressure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess DO, MCC, detrusor pressures, compliance, and related storage parameters.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As determined by NLUTD risk or a clinical change, and to assess response when unsafe storage findings threaten the upper tracts.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: High storage pressures with DO and DSD are high-risk findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document functional volumes, leakage, and treatment response.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used when it informs evaluation or management.

diagnostic_workup.test: Upper tract imaging and renal function assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess potential consequences of unsafe storage function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: According to NLUTD risk and clinical findings.

follow_up.schedule: Repeat UDS at an appropriate interval after treatment if storage findings place the upper tracts at risk; the guideline describes two years or less as reasonable once pressures have normalized in patients at risk, with less frequent testing possible if clinically stable.
recommended_tests: Multichannel UDS to assess treatment effect when indicated
Risk-appropriate upper tract imaging and renal function assessment
long_term_effects: Upper urinary tract deterioration if unsafe storage pressures persist
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Additional treatment should be offered if high-risk storage findings remain refractory to therapy.

conditions.name: stress urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Stress-related urinary leakage can coexist with NLUTD and requires assessment of bladder storage safety before an outlet procedure is selected.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urinary leakage can reflect sphincteric dysfunction or severe urethral damage, including damage associated with a chronic urethral catheter.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess leakage severity, neurological impairment, prior interventions, urethral condition, and ability to manage the proposed treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before selecting treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether storage pressures and compliance are acceptable before an outlet procedure.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before relevant SUI procedures when NLUTD-related compliance could worsen after increasing outlet resistance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Unsafe storage pressures may threaten the upper urinary tracts; marked sphincteric dysfunction may require temporary bladder neck or urethral occlusion to assess filling adequately.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm ability to operate an AUS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before AUS implantation.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up depends on the chosen procedure and the patient's NLUTD risk; monitor for impaired voiding and changes in storage safety.
recommended_tests: Assessment for postoperative voiding dysfunction
Risk-appropriate UDS and upper tract surveillance
long_term_effects: Possible need for CIC after an outlet procedure
Potential upper tract risk if bladder compliance worsens
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Counseling should account for progression of neurological disease and the possibility of later difficulty emptying.

conditions.name: NLUTD patients who have undergone lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating a bowel segment(s)
conditions.description: Patients with NLUTD after reconstruction using bowel require ongoing assessment for urinary tract and metabolic complications.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential later findings include incontinence, infection, hematuria, metabolic disturbance, or upper tract obstruction. Gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI warrants investigation rather than automatic attribution to catheter trauma or inflammation.

subtypes.name: augmentation cystoplasty
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Bowel-based bladder augmentation entails lifelong surveillance for complications including stones, bowel dysfunction, mucus-related problems, and perforation.

subtypes.name: continent urinary diversion
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Metabolic risk depends in part on the type of reconstruction and may be higher with a continent diversion.

subtypes.name: incontinent urinary diversion
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Continued assessment is needed for late complications and upper tract changes.

diagnostic_workup.test: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify symptoms and complications related to reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually after lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating bowel.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline states that yearly assessment without this panel suffices after construction of only a continent urinary stoma without AC.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify upper tract findings, including possible obstruction associated with reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Annually.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a deficiency that may require supplementation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Monitor over time if terminal ileum was used in the reconstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI, including possible malignancy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI develops; not as routine surveillance solely because reconstruction was performed.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urine cytology and computerized tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to evaluation of concerning symptoms after bowel-based reconstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The guideline describes these as part of a full assessment when concerning signs or symptoms occur.

follow_up.schedule: Lifelong surveillance, with annual focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging after reconstruction incorporating bowel.
recommended_tests: Focused history, physical examination, and symptom assessment
Basic metabolic panel when indicated by the reconstruction
Urinary tract imaging
B12 monitoring over time if terminal ileum was used
Cystoscopy for gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Metabolic risk varies with pre-existing renal function, comorbidities, bowel segment, and diversion type. Routine cystoscopy in otherwise asymptomatic, stable patients is not supported.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle training
approved_indications: Improvement of urinary symptoms and quality-of-life measures in appropriately selected patients with NLUTD, particularly those with MS or CVA.
monitoring: Assess urinary symptoms and quality-of-life measures.

therapies_index.name: antimuscarinics
approved_indications: Improvement of bladder storage parameters in NLUTD.
key_toxicities: Potential cognitive impairment or dementia with long-term anticholinergic treatment; the evidence on this association is conflicting and of low certainty.
Possible increase in PVR in patients with SCI.
monitoring: Discuss potential cognitive effects when weighing treatment benefits and risks.

therapies_index.name: beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists
approved_indications: Improvement of bladder storage parameters in NLUTD.

therapies_index.name: antimuscarinics or beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, or a combination of both
approved_indications: Improvement of bladder storage parameters in NLUTD.
monitoring: Discuss the risks and benefits of concomitant treatment with the patient.

therapies_index.name: alpha-blockers
approved_indications: Improvement of voiding parameters in patients with NLUTD who void spontaneously.

therapies_index.name: alpha-blockers combined with antimuscarinics
approved_indications: Amelioration of symptoms across several NLUTD etiologies.
key_toxicities: Adverse events described as relatively minor.

therapies_index.name: tamsulosin
approved_indications: Improvement of bladder storage and emptying in patients with SCI, as described by the cited trial.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited trial, 0.4 mg or 0.8 mg for one month, followed by a one-year open-label extension.
monitoring: Assess voiding and bladder storage outcomes.

therapies_index.name: terazosin
approved_indications: Improvement of voiding or bladder compliance in patients with SCI in cited studies.
Management of elevated blood pressure associated with refractory AD is discussed as a potential use of alpha-adrenergic receptor blockers.
therapies_index.administration: Cited SCI studies used up to 5 mg daily for approximately 10 days or 5 mg for one month.

therapies_index.name: prazosin
approved_indications: Reduction of AD episode severity and duration in individuals with cervical or high thoracic SCI, as reported in cited evidence.
therapies_index.administration: 3 mg twice a day, given for 2 weeks in the cited report.

therapies_index.name: trospium
approved_indications: Treatment of DO in patients with SCI in cited studies.
therapies_index.administration: A cited trial used 20 mg twice daily for three weeks.
monitoring: Assess bladder capacity, detrusor pressure and compliance.

therapies_index.name: solifenacin
approved_indications: Treatment of urinary storage symptoms in patients with SCI, MS or PD in cited studies.
therapies_index.administration: Cited studies used 10 mg for 13 months in SCI, 5 – 10 mg daily for two months in MS, and 5-10 mg daily for three months in PD.
monitoring: Assess bladder storage outcomes and tolerability.

therapies_index.name: oxybutynin
approved_indications: Treatment of NDO and urinary storage symptoms in NLUTD, including SCI and MS, as evaluated in cited studies.
therapies_index.administration: Cited oral schedules include controlled-release 10 mg to 30 mg daily and 15 mg daily; cited intravesical schedules include 15 mg three times daily, 0.1% solution three times daily and 5 mg three times daily.
key_toxicities: Visual, gastrointestinal, nervous system and skin adverse events were reported more often with oral than intravesical administration in a cited comparison.
monitoring: Assess bladder storage parameters, incontinence and PVR.

therapies_index.name: intravesical oxybutynin
approved_indications: An option advocated by the Panel for selected patients with NLUTD who perform CIC, to improve storage parameters and reduce incontinence.
therapies_index.administration: Cited studies administered 15 mg three times daily, 0.1% solution three times daily or 5 mg three times daily.
monitoring: Assess bladder capacity, detrusor pressure, compliance and incontinence.

therapies_index.name: propantheline
approved_indications: Treatment of urinary symptoms in MS in a cited comparative trial.
Investigated as a bladder instillation in SCI.
therapies_index.administration: The cited MS trial used 45 mg daily for seven weeks.
key_toxicities: Severe adverse events prompted withdrawal in approximately one-quarter of patients in the cited MS trial; their types were not specified.

therapies_index.name: tolterodine
approved_indications: Treatment of bladder storage symptoms and incontinence in NLUTD in cited studies.
therapies_index.administration: Cited schedules included 4 mg daily, patient-selected 4-12 mg, and extended-release 4 mg daily.
monitoring: Assess catheterized or voided volumes, incontinence and bladder storage parameters.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron
approved_indications: Improvement of bladder storage measures and urinary symptoms in patients with SCI and NDO in a cited observational study.
therapies_index.administration: The cited study started at 25 mg daily and increased to 50 mg after two weeks.
monitoring: Assess urinary frequency, incontinence, bladder capacity, compliance and storage pressure.

therapies_index.name: doxazosin
approved_indications: Improvement of urinary flow and symptoms in PD in a cited study.
therapies_index.administration: The cited study used doxazosin ER 4 mg daily for three months.
monitoring: Assess urinary flow and symptoms.

therapies_index.name: phenoxybenzamine
approved_indications: Reduction of PVR in some patients with NLUTD who continued treatment in a cited study.
therapies_index.administration: The cited study used 15 to 30 mg daily.
monitoring: Assess PVR and adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: oxybutynin + trospium
approved_indications: Investigated for NLUTD after failure of single-medication treatment in a cited combination trial.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated over six months in the cited trial.

therapies_index.name: oxybutynin + tolterodine
approved_indications: Investigated for NLUTD after failure of single-medication treatment in a cited combination trial.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated over six months in the cited trial.

therapies_index.name: tolterodine + trospium
approved_indications: Investigated for NLUTD after failure of single-medication treatment in a cited combination trial.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated over six months in the cited trial.

therapies_index.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
approved_indications: Recommended after failure of oral medication for patients with NLUTD due to SCI or MS, to improve bladder storage, incontinence and quality of life.
May be offered after failure of oral medication for NLUTD from other causes for the same outcomes.
Investigated as an external sphincter injection for DSD; routine chemical sphincterotomy is not recommended.
therapies_index.administration: Intradetrusor injections of 200 U and 300 U were evaluated in SCI and MS; a cited trial evaluated 100 U in non-catheterized patients with MS. Repeat intradetrusor injections were also studied.
monitoring: Before treatment in patients who void spontaneously, discuss retention and the possible need for intermittent catheterization.
Assess bladder storage parameters, incontinence and adverse events; assess the effect of repeated treatment when indicated.

therapies_index.name: abobotulinumtoxinA
approved_indications: Investigated for refractory urinary incontinence in patients with NLUTD; evidence is insufficient to establish the same recommendation made for onabotulinumtoxinA in SCI or MS.
therapies_index.administration: Cited studies evaluated intradetrusor injections of 500 U or 750 U; repeat-injection studies included doses ranging from 500 U – 1000 U.
monitoring: Assess urinary symptoms, bladder storage measures and adverse events.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin A
approved_indications: Treatment investigated for NDO and persistent symptoms after augmentation enterocystoplasty.
Chemical sphincterotomy for DSD has limited durability and is not recommended for routine management.
therapies_index.administration: The document discusses intradetrusor injections and transperineal injection into the striated sphincter.
monitoring: Discuss retention and catheterization needs before treatment in patients who void spontaneously.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
approved_indications: Used as a comparator for external sphincter injection in a cited DSD study.
therapies_index.administration: A single transperineal external sphincter injection was used in the cited study.

therapies_index.name: capsaicin
approved_indications: Investigated as a bladder instillation in a cited SCI study.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation was investigated.

therapies_index.name: 2% nitroglycerine paste
therapies_index.mechanism: Nitrates relax vascular smooth muscle, dilating coronary vessels and peripheral veins.
approved_indications: Pharmacologic management of persistent AD-associated blood pressure elevation.
therapies_index.administration: Apply 1 to 2 inches of 2% nitroglycerine paste to skin above the spinal cord lesion; it can be removed after the hypertensive episode subsides.
key_toxicities: Hypotension after resolution of the hypertensive episode
monitoring: Continue hemodynamic monitoring during AD management.

therapies_index.name: nifedipine
therapies_index.mechanism: A voltage-sensitive calcium channel blocker with coronary and peripheral vasodilator effects.
approved_indications: An alternative medication discussed for AD-associated blood pressure elevation.
therapies_index.administration: The cited form is immediate-release sublingual 10 mg capsules.
key_toxicities: Rapid, marked reduction of blood pressure below baseline that may not be readily reversed in the clinic
monitoring: Monitor blood pressure closely when used for AD.

therapies_index.name: sodium nitroprusside
approved_indications: May be indicated for rapid blood pressure titration if other antihypertensive treatment does not relieve AD symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: Intravenous administration in an intensively monitored setting.
monitoring: Intensive blood pressure monitoring.

therapies_index.name: daily antibiotic prophylaxis
approved_indications: May be offered as oral antimicrobial prophylaxis to patients with NLUTD who perform CIC and have recurrent UTI, after shared decision-making.
Not recommended for patients with NLUTD using an indwelling catheter or for CIC users without recurrent UTI.
therapies_index.administration: Daily administration; the cited CIC trial used 50 mg nitrofurantoin, 100 mg trimethoprim or 250 mg cephalexin over 12 months.
monitoring: Discuss the increased risk of antibiotic resistance before offering prophylaxis.

therapies_index.name: weekly oral cycling antibiotic (WOCA)
approved_indications: Investigated for recurrent UTI prevention in patients with NLUTD performing CIC in cited observational studies.
therapies_index.administration: Alternate two antibiotics selected from prior cultures, administering one antibiotic once in week A and a different antibiotic once in week B. Antibiotics reported were amoxicillin (3000 mg), cefixime (400 mg), fosfomycin-trometamol (6000 mg), nitrofurantoin (300 mg), and trimethoprim/ sulfamethoxazole (320–1600 mg).
monitoring: Selection in the cited protocols was based on prior cultures.

approved_indications: Used in cited WOCA protocols for recurrent UTI prevention.
therapies_index.administration: 400 mg in the cited WOCA protocols.

approved_indications: Used in cited WOCA protocols for recurrent UTI prevention.

approved_indications: Used in cited WOCA protocols for recurrent UTI prevention.
therapies_index.administration: 320–1600 mg in the cited WOCA protocols.

approved_indications: Investigated for daily UTI prophylaxis in CIC users in a cited trial.

monitoring: Consider antibiotic resistance when deciding on prophylaxis.

approved_indications: Investigated for daily UTI prophylaxis in CIC users in a cited trial.
therapies_index.administration: 250 mg daily in the cited trial.

monitoring: Consider antibiotic resistance when deciding on prophylaxis.

therapies_index.administration: A single oral dose according to the cited policy.

therapies_index.name: gentamicin

approved_indications: A component of neomycin-polymyxin GU irrigant investigated in a cited study.
therapies_index.administration: 200,000 units/mL in the cited irrigant.

approved_indications: Investigated as bladder irrigation for asymptomatic bacteriuria in chronically catheterized patients with NLUTD; the cited trial found no statistically significant difference among irrigation groups in bacterial load, pyuria or inflammation.

therapies_index.name: normal saline
approved_indications: Used as a comparator bladder irrigant in a cited study of chronically catheterized patients with NLUTD.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited trial, 30 mL was retained for 20 minutes, twice daily for 8 weeks.

approved_indications: Investigated for UTI prevention in a cited SCI trial; no statistically significant difference in six-month UTI-free survival was reported among its groups.

approved_indications: Office treatment of granulation tissue around a suprapubic catheter site.
therapies_index.administration: Topical application.

therapies_index.name: polydimethylsiloxane (PDS)

therapies_index.administration: Submucosal injection.

approved_indications: Preferred over indwelling catheters to facilitate bladder emptying in NLUTD.
