monitoring: Assess catheter passage, adherence to the schedule, volumes, complications and ability to perform catheterization.

therapies_index.name: clean intermittent catheterization
approved_indications: Bladder emptying in NLUTD; preferred over indwelling catheterization when feasible.
therapies_index.administration: Performed intermittently by the patient or a caregiver.
monitoring: Assess catheterization difficulties, urinary symptoms and the need to adjust catheter type or frequency.

therapies_index.name: hydrophilic catheters
approved_indications: An intermittent-catheter option that may be associated with less UTI and urethral trauma, particularly in SCI; cited studies yielded mixed findings.
therapies_index.administration: Used for intermittent catheterization.
key_toxicities: UTI and urethral trauma remain possible.

therapies_index.name: indwelling urethral catheter
approved_indications: Chronic bladder drainage when used as a bladder-management method; the guideline prefers intermittent catheterization when feasible and suprapubic catheterization when a chronic indwelling catheter is required in appropriately selected patients.
therapies_index.administration: Indwelling urethral placement.
monitoring: Examine the catheter and urethral site at intervals.
Perform urinary tract imaging every 1-2 years when stone risk is present.

therapies_index.name: suprapubic catheterization
approved_indications: Preferred over an indwelling urethral catheter for appropriately selected patients with NLUTD requiring chronic indwelling drainage.
therapies_index.administration: A catheter is placed suprapubically for bladder drainage.
key_toxicities: Granulation tissue at the catheter site
monitoring: Examine the catheter and entry site at intervals.
Assess for stones with imaging every 1-2 years in patients at risk.

therapies_index.name: oral antimicrobial prophylaxis
approved_indications: May be offered to patients with NLUTD who perform CIC and have recurrent UTI to reduce UTI frequency, after shared decision-making and discussion of resistance risk.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration; the document describes both daily and weekly cycling approaches in cited studies.
monitoring: Discuss antibiotic resistance and individual treatment risks.

therapies_index.name: bladder instillations
approved_indications: May be offered to patients with NLUTD performing CIC who have recurrent UTI to reduce UTI frequency; evidence for any single strategy is inadequate.
therapies_index.administration: Instillation into the bladder; agents and schedules varied across cited studies.
monitoring: Assess individual benefits and risks, including the time and effort required.

therapies_index.name: sphincterotomy
approved_indications: May be offered to appropriately selected male patients with NLUTD to facilitate emptying, with counseling about the high risk of failure and further treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic external urethral sphincter incision or resection at the 12 o’clock position using electrocautery or laser.
key_toxicities: Failure or need for another procedure
Skin breakdown related to condom-catheter use
Persistent or recurrent impaired emptying and elevated pressures
monitoring: Maintain regular follow-up for recurrent UTI, AD, elevated DLPP and residual urine.
Urodynamics may be performed after surgery to assess the result.

therapies_index.name: urethral bulking agents
approved_indications: May be offered for SUI in NLUTD, with counseling that benefit is modest and cure uncommon.
therapies_index.administration: Urethral injection.
monitoring: Assess continence and potential need for further treatment.

therapies_index.name: slings
approved_indications: Should be offered to selected patients with NLUTD, SUI and acceptable bladder storage parameters.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical sling placement; the Panel advises against synthetic material for an occlusive sling and advises avoiding synthetic slings if future CIC may be necessary.
key_toxicities: Potential worsening of bladder compliance and storage pressure after an outlet procedure
De novo OAB symptoms reported in a cited study
monitoring: Assess bladder storage with UDS before an SUI procedure when NLUTD may put the upper tracts at risk.
Discuss possible future voiding difficulty and CIC.

therapies_index.name: artificial urinary sphincter
approved_indications: May be offered to selected patients with NLUTD, SUI and acceptable bladder storage parameters.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical implantation; adequate hand function to operate the device must be established.
key_toxicities: Possible need for revision or explantation
monitoring: Confirm acceptable storage pressures with UDS before implantation when NLUTD is relevant.
Assess hand dexterity and discuss possible future CIC and additional surgery.

therapies_index.name: bladder neck closure
approved_indications: May be offered with a bladder drainage method to selected patients with NLUTD and refractory SUI after discussion of risks, benefits and alternatives.
therapies_index.administration: An irreversible surgical closure accompanied by urinary drainage; a retropubic approach is used in men, while retropubic or transvaginal approaches are described in women.
key_toxicities: Risk to the upper urinary tract if storage pressures are unsafe
monitoring: Assess bladder storage parameters with UDS when outlet closure could raise storage pressures.
Plan and assess the accompanying drainage method.

therapies_index.name: posterior tibial nerve stimulation
approved_indications: May be offered to selected patients with NLUTD who void spontaneously and have urgency, frequency or urgency incontinence; the document separately notes approval for non-neurogenic OAB.
therapies_index.administration: Schedules in cited studies included weekly 30 minutes sessions for twelve weeks or daily 20minute sessions for 12 weeks; maintenance schedules varied.
monitoring: Assess urinary symptom response and whether continued maintenance visits are feasible.

therapies_index.name: transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (TTNS)
approved_indications: Investigated for urinary symptoms in patients with PD or CVA in cited studies.
therapies_index.administration: A cited PD trial used 30-minutes twice a week for five weeks.

therapies_index.name: sacral neuromodulation
approved_indications: May be offered to selected patients with NLUTD and urgency, frequency or urgency incontinence.
Should not be offered for NLUTD in patients with SCI or SB; early use after SCI to modify disease progression remains investigational.
therapies_index.administration: Implanted neuromodulation device.
monitoring: Consider possible loss of efficacy as progressive neurologic disease worsens.
Consider MRI compatibility when applicable.

therapies_index.name: augmentation cystoplasty
approved_indications: May be offered to selected patients with NLUTD who are refractory to, or intolerant of, less invasive treatment for DO or poor bladder compliance.
therapies_index.administration: Bladder reconstruction; the document discusses augmentation using bowel.
monitoring: Arrange lifelong follow-up.
Assess the ability of the patient or caregiver to perform regular CIC before surgery.
For reconstruction incorporating bowel, assess symptoms, perform a basic metabolic panel and obtain urinary tract imaging annually.

therapies_index.name: continent catheterizable channels
approved_indications: May be offered, with or without augmentation, to selected patients with NLUTD to facilitate catheterization.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical creation of a catheterizable channel.
monitoring: Counsel before surgery about catheterization ability, complications and potential revision.
Consider cognitive function, hand function and caregiver support.

therapies_index.name: ileovesicostomy
approved_indications: May be offered to selected patients with NLUTD, with counseling about benefits, alternatives and the high risk of further treatment or surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical construction of an ileal urostomy for bladder drainage.
monitoring: Continue regular long-term follow-up for drainage, emptying and stones.
Consider body habitus and ostomy placement before surgery.

therapies_index.name: urinary diversion
approved_indications: Should be offered to patients with NLUTD when other options have failed or are unsuitable, to improve long-term quality of life.
therapies_index.administration: The document discusses continent and incontinent surgical diversion.
key_toxicities: Metabolic disturbances when bowel is incorporated
monitoring: Continue long-term follow-up.
Consider hand function and the patient's social and home support before surgery.

therapies_index.name: ileal conduit
approved_indications: An incontinent urinary-diversion option discussed for patients with NLUTD refractory to other management.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical ileal conduit construction, sometimes with cystectomy.
monitoring: Continue regular long-term follow-up after conduit construction.
Consider concomitant cystectomy when planning diversion, particularly in male patients.

therapies_index.name: cystectomy
approved_indications: Considered at urinary diversion because a retained, defunctionalized bladder can develop delayed complications; concurrent supratrigonal cystectomy or cystoprostatectomy should be strongly considered in male patients with NLUTD undergoing diversion.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical bladder removal, discussed alongside ileal conduit or other diversion.

therapies_index.name: Spence procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Creates a vesicovaginal fistula to drain a defunctionalized bladder.
approved_indications: Described as a potential drainage option for women who develop pyocystis after supravesical diversion, possibly avoiding cystectomy.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical creation of a vesicovaginal fistula.

therapies_index.name: adjustable continence mechanism
approved_indications: Investigational treatment studied for SUI in NLUTD; the guideline does not support widespread use on the available evidence.
therapies_index.administration: Implanted device.

therapies_index.name: Xiao procedure
therapies_index.mechanism: Reroutes nerves to establish a somatic-to-autonomic reflex arc intended to restore voluntary bladder and bowel control.
approved_indications: Investigational procedure for NLUTD associated with SCI or SB; the guideline calls for appropriate counseling and limits consideration to investigational settings.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical nerve rerouting.
key_toxicities: Transient leg weakness reported in a cited pilot study

therapies_index.name: Brindley sacral anterior root stimulator (SARS)
approved_indications: An investigational or specialty-center option discussed for bladder management after SCI.
therapies_index.administration: Electrodes are placed on bilateral S2-S4 nerves and connected to a subcutaneous abdominal receiver; implantation is usually combined with posterior sacral rhizotomy from S2 to S5.
key_toxicities: Potential loss of function associated with irreversible sacral rhizotomy
monitoring: Use is limited to investigational settings or specialty centers familiar with the operation and device.

therapies_index.name: tissue engineering
approved_indications: Investigational approach to bladder reconstruction or replacement in NLUTD.
therapies_index.administration: The document discusses scaffolds, cells and regenerative factors; it does not establish a treatment protocol.
key_toxicities: Significant postoperative morbidity was reported for one cited scaffold-based augmentation approach.

therapies_index.name: stem cells
approved_indications: Investigational treatment of neurologic injury or urinary dysfunction; the document states that further high-quality studies are needed before establishing a role in NLUTD.

therapies_index.name: deep brain stimulation
approved_indications: Used for motor symptoms of PD and other neurologic disorders; possible lower urinary tract benefit is discussed from a cited review.
therapies_index.administration: A cited review examined stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus.

therapies_index.name: bladder allograft transplantation
approved_indications: An investigational possibility discussed after feasibility reports in cadaveric models; clinical utility for NLUTD has not been established.
therapies_index.administration: The cited models involved vascular anastomoses.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected adults, particularly those with MS or CVA.
decision_rules: Pelvic floor muscle training may be offered to improve urinary symptoms and quality-of-life measures.

recommended_regimens.name: pelvic floor muscle training
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer to suitable patients as a non-invasive approach to urinary symptoms.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a study of MS patients, urinary frequency, incontinence, the 24-hour pad test and pelvic floor endurance improved after a 9-week intervention; improvements persisted at 24 weeks.

response_assessment.method: Assess urinary symptoms and quality-of-life measures.
response_assessment.interpretation: Improvement may accompany increased pelvic floor muscle strength and endurance.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence is concentrated in MS and CVA; the reviewed interventions and patient groups varied.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults needing improved bladder storage parameters.
decision_rules: Clinicians may use an antimuscarinic, a beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonist, or both.
Discuss potential cognitive effects of anticholinergic treatment through shared decision-making.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinics
recommended_regimens.summary: May be used to improve bladder storage; no individual medication is established as superior.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis versus placebo reported MCC WMD = 49.49 ml; 95% CI: 15.38-84.2; p<0.05, and MDP WMD = 38.30; 95% CI -53.17 to -23.43; p<0.05.

recommended_regimens.name: beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: May be used to improve bladder storage parameters.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinics and beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Concomitant treatment is a reasonable option after discussion of benefits and risks, although substantial condition-specific safety and efficacy data for this combination were not identified.

alternative_regimens.name: alpha-blockers combined with antimuscarinics
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline describes evidence of symptom improvement with this combination across several NLUTD etiologies.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in light of the patient's storage and voiding symptoms; this combination is discussed as evidence rather than assigned a separate formal recommendation.

response_assessment.method: Assess storage symptoms, incontinence and, when indicated, urodynamic storage parameters.
response_assessment.interpretation: Antimuscarinics can increase MCC and voided or catheterized volumes and decrease detrusor pressure.

supportive_care: Discuss possible cognitive impairment and dementia associated with long-term anticholinergic exposure; the evidence about the association is conflicting and of low certainty.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Dry mouth is frequently reported with antimuscarinics. For selected patients, an alternative agent less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier may be appropriate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults who void spontaneously and need improved voiding parameters.
decision_rules: Clinicians may recommend alpha-blockers to improve voiding parameters.

recommended_regimens.name: alpha-blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: May improve voiding in patients who retain spontaneous voiding.

response_assessment.method: Assess voiding symptoms and relevant flow or residual-volume parameters.
response_assessment.interpretation: The reviewed studies reported improvements in some voiding measures, with differences across neurologic conditions.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for particular medications over clinically relevant durations is insufficient.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with SCI and impaired bladder storage or spontaneous voiding.
decision_rules: Choose storage-directed medication for storage dysfunction; alpha-blockers may be used for voiding parameters in those who void spontaneously.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinics
recommended_regimens.summary: Storage-directed options studied in SCI include trospium, solifenacin and oxybutynin.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a placebo-controlled trospium study, MCC increased by 138.1 mL, MDP decreased by 37.8 cm H2O and compliance increased by 12.2 mL/cm H2O. In an oxybutynin study, MCC increased from 274 to 380 mL, while PVR increased from 26 to 51 mL.

recommended_regimens.name: beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: mirabegron is described as a studied storage-directed option in SCI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In an observational study of mirabegron, MCC changed from 365 to 419 mL, compliance from 28 to 54 mL/cm H2O, and storage detrusor pressure from 45.8 to 30 cm H2O.

recommended_regimens.name: alpha-blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: For spontaneous voiding, studied options include tamsulosin and terazosin.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a tamsulosin trial, the randomized-phase MUP changes were -12.2 and – 9.6 cm H20 with 0.4 and 0.8 mg, respectively, versus -6.5 cm H2O with placebo; these between-group differences were not statistically significant.

response_assessment.method: Assess continence, bladder capacity, detrusor pressure, PVR and voiding where relevant.
response_assessment.interpretation: Antimuscarinics may increase PVR in SCI.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The reported effects and adverse events belong to individual studies and do not establish superiority among the named drugs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with MS who have bladder storage symptoms.
decision_rules: Antimuscarinics may be recommended to improve storage parameters.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinics
recommended_regimens.summary: oxybutynin, propantheline and solifenacin are among the agents studied in MS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a comparative study, MCC improved by 144 mL with oxybutynin and by 35 mL with propantheline; subjective improvement was reported by 67% and 36%, respectively.

response_assessment.method: Assess frequency, nocturia, urgency, incontinence and voided volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: The reviewed MS studies reported improvement in these measures with antimuscarinic treatment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the cited oxybutynin-versus-propantheline study, approximately one-quarter of each group withdrew because of severe adverse events.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with PD and urinary storage symptoms or spontaneous voiding with voiding symptoms.
decision_rules: Select treatment according to whether storage or voiding parameters need improvement.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinics
recommended_regimens.summary: solifenacin was studied for frequency, nocturia and incontinence in PD.

recommended_regimens.name: alpha-blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: doxazosin ER was studied for urinary symptoms and flow in spontaneously voiding patients with PD.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In an observational study, maximum flow rate changed from 9.3 to 11.2 mL/sec with doxazosin ER.

response_assessment.method: Assess urinary symptoms, frequency, incontinence or flow according to the treatment objective.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: These disease-specific findings come from the cited studies; the formal medication recommendations apply to NLUTD more broadly.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults already performing CIC who need better bladder storage control or less incontinence.
decision_rules: Intravesical oxybutynin is advocated for selected patients performing CIC when its potential storage benefit and tolerability make it appropriate.

recommended_regimens.name: intravesical oxybutynin
recommended_regimens.summary: The Panel advocates this option in selected CIC users; it is not assigned a separate graded guideline statement.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a randomized comparison, MCC increased by 116.6 mL with intravesical oxybutynin versus 18.1 mL with oral oxybutynin; adverse events occurred in 55.6% versus 82.4%, respectively.

response_assessment.method: Assess storage parameters, incontinence and adverse effects.
response_assessment.interpretation: Available studies suggest improved storage measures and possibly fewer adverse effects than with oral administration.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited studies used differing intravesical schedules; the guideline does not establish one preferred schedule.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults requiring assistance with bladder emptying who can perform intermittent catheterization themselves or with help.
decision_rules: Recommend intermittent catheterization in preference to an indwelling catheter when feasible.

recommended_regimens.name: intermittent catheterization
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred catheter-based means of facilitating bladder emptying.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited randomized comparison, pyelonephritis, epididymo-orchitis and urosepsis occurred in 5%, 2.5% and 0% of the CIC group versus 25%, 7% and 5% of the indwelling urethral catheter group, respectively.

alternative_regimens.name: indwelling catheter
alternative_regimens.summary: An option when intermittent catheterization is not feasible.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Assess hand function, cognition, mobility and availability of caregiver assistance.

response_assessment.method: Review emptying, catheter-related difficulties, urinary infections, stones and quality of life.
response_assessment.interpretation: Studies generally favor intermittent over indwelling catheterization, although outcomes vary across studies.

supportive_care: Assess whether the patient can self-catheterize or requires caregiver assistance.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Hydrophilic catheters may be associated with fewer UTIs and less urethral trauma, particularly in SCI, but the reviewed findings are mixed. Dependence on a caregiver for intermittent catheterization may adversely affect quality of life.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected adults who require a chronic indwelling catheter.
decision_rules: Recommend suprapubic rather than indwelling urethral catheterization.

recommended_regimens.name: suprapubic catheterization
recommended_regimens.summary: Preferred chronic indwelling route for appropriately selected patients.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited follow-up study after suprapubic catheter insertion, 72% reported satisfaction and 89% preferred it to their previous urethral catheter.

response_assessment.method: Examine the catheter and its insertion site.
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify catheter-site injury, erosion, granulation tissue or other complications.

supportive_care: Secure the catheter appropriately and inspect the site regularly.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Suprapubic placement has procedural risks and may require later intervention. It avoids urethral complications but can cause abdominal-wall erosion or granulation tissue.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults managing the bladder with an indwelling catheter.
decision_rules: Do not use daily antibiotics solely to prevent UTI.

not_recommended.name: daily antibiotic prophylaxis
not_recommended.reason: The cited systematic review did not find a significant reduction in symptomatic infections in spinal cord dysfunction and reported approximately a two-fold increase in antimicrobial-resistant bacteria.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation against daily prophylaxis is a Strong Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade B.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults using clean intermittent catheterization without recurrent UTI.
decision_rules: Do not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis in the absence of recurrent UTI.

not_recommended.name: daily antibiotic prophylaxis
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support its routine use in this population; the cited reviews did not establish a significant reduction in symptomatic UTI and identified increased bacterial resistance.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation against daily prophylaxis is a Moderate Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade B. Patients with recurrent UTI follow a different decision pathway.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults using clean intermittent catheterization who have recurrent UTI.
decision_rules: After shared decision-making and discussion of antibiotic resistance, clinicians may offer oral antimicrobial prophylaxis to reduce UTI frequency.
Clinicians may also offer bladder instillations.

recommended_regimens.name: oral antimicrobial prophylaxis
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for recurrent UTI during clean intermittent catheterization, contingent on discussion of resistance.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited trial of CIC users, 39% of whom had NLUTD, symptomatic antibiotic-treated UTI incidence over 12 months was 1.3 cases per person-year (95% CI 1.1–1.6) with prophylaxis versus 2.6 cases per person-year (2.3–2.9) without it; IRR=0.52; 95% CI 0.44–0.61; p<0.0001.

alternative_regimens.name: bladder instillations
alternative_regimens.summary: May be offered to reduce recurrent UTI; this is an Expert Opinion, and evidence is insufficient to establish a single instillation strategy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the patient's ability and willingness to perform the procedure and its uncertain longer-term risks.

response_assessment.method: Review symptomatic UTI frequency, adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance.
response_assessment.interpretation: Balance any reduction in infections against increased resistance.

supportive_care: Use shared decision-making about antibiotic resistance and potential medication harms.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The WOCA protocols and daily nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim or cephalexin schedules are described as study interventions, not as a uniquely preferred guideline regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with recurrent UTI using various catheter-management methods.
decision_rules: Clinicians may explain that cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to lower UTI frequency.

not_recommended.name: cranberry extract
not_recommended.reason: A consistent reduction in UTI frequency has not been demonstrated across the reviewed evidence; one study reported favorable findings but had stated design limitations.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The counseling statement is a Conditional Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade B; it states lack of demonstrated benefit, not proof that benefit is impossible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with symptomatic UTI.
decision_rules: Obtain UA and urine culture when symptoms suggest UTI, then use culture-specific antibiotic treatment when appropriate.
If suspicion is high, empiric antibiotics may be started and changed if the culture result warrants it.

For febrile UTI without an appropriate antibiotic response, obtain upper tract imaging; also image moderate- or high-risk patients who are overdue for routine upper tract imaging regardless of treatment response.

recommended_regimens.name: culture-specific antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat symptomatic infection according to the urine culture when indicated.

alternative_regimens.name: empiric antibiotics
alternative_regimens.summary: May be started while culture results are pending when suspicion of UTI is high; revise treatment if needed after results become available.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A recent prior culture may help guide initial selection.

response_assessment.method: Assess the clinical response and review the urine culture.
response_assessment.interpretation: In febrile UTI, inadequate response prompts upper tract imaging to investigate problems such as stones or hydronephrosis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: UTI manifestations can be atypical with altered sensation; symptoms alone do not reliably establish infection in every patient with NLUTD. If an indwelling catheter is present, collect culture urine after replacing the catheter and allowing urine to accumulate with the catheter plugged, not from extension tubing or the collection bag.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with asymptomatic bacteriuria.
decision_rules: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria routinely.

alternative_regimens.name: antimicrobial treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Treatment is an exception to the general rule rather than routine management.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Pregnancy or an anticipated urologic procedure involving urothelial disruption or upper tract manipulation.

not_recommended.name: antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria
not_recommended.reason: Unnecessary exposure contributes to antibiotic resistance; in cited SCI studies, treatment did not improve subsequent bacteriuria or UTI rates in intermittent-catheter users, and bacteriuria recurred with more resistant strains in catheter-free patients.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation against treatment is a Moderate Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade C. The guideline also advises against surveillance urine testing, including culture, in asymptomatic patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with SCI or MS whose bladder symptoms are refractory to oral medication.
decision_rules: Recommend onabotulinumtoxinA to improve bladder storage, decrease incontinence and improve quality of life.
Discuss retention and the possible need for CIC before treatment, particularly with patients who void spontaneously.

recommended_regimens.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
recommended_regimens.summary: Intradetrusor treatment is recommended after inadequate response to oral medication in SCI or MS; repeated injections can restore initial improvements.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The cited Yuan et al. meta-analysis reported a reduction in UI episodes of -1.41 episodes (95% CI -1.70 to -1.12, p<0.05) and an MCC increase of 135.5 mL (95% CI: 118.2 to 152.8 mL; p<0.05) versus placebo. The guideline reports no efficacy difference between 200 U and 300 U.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Repeated treatment may be used when clinically appropriate; no single treatment interval is specified for this pathway.

response_assessment.timepoint: After injection and on repeat treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess incontinence, MCC, detrusor pressure, quality of life, urinary retention and need for CIC.
response_assessment.interpretation: Most patients retained efficacy with repeated injections in the reviewed evidence.

supportive_care: Discuss and plan for intermittent catheterization if post-injection urinary retention develops.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: UTI and urinary retention are frequently reported adverse events. In non-catheterizing MS patients in the DIGNITY pooled analysis, initiation of CIC for retention occurred in 31.4% and 47.1% with 200 U and 300 U, respectively, versus 4.5% with placebo.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults other than those with SCI or MS whose symptoms are refractory to oral medication.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer onabotulinumtoxinA for storage dysfunction, incontinence and quality-of-life improvement.
Before treating patients who void spontaneously, discuss retention and the potential need for CIC.

recommended_regimens.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
recommended_regimens.summary: An option after failure of oral medication in other NLUTD etiologies.

response_assessment.method: Review storage symptoms, incontinence, bladder emptying, PVR and possible need for catheterization.
response_assessment.interpretation: Underlying CNS disorders or pre-existing emptying dysfunction may complicate post-treatment bladder management.

supportive_care: Before treatment, establish whether the patient or a trained caregiver could perform CIC if required.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For etiologies other than SCI or MS, adequately powered high-quality evidence is insufficient and the balance of benefit and risk is unclear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Appropriately selected men needing improved emptying, particularly those with DSD who cannot or will not perform CIC and can manage reflex voiding with a condom catheter.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer sphincterotomy, but must explain the substantial failure risk and possible need for further treatment or surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: sphincterotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: An irreversible outlet procedure to facilitate emptying in selected men.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited study of 84 men with spinal injury, 57 patients (68%, median time to failure 36 months) experienced procedural failure; definitive DSD control after a single procedure occurred in 32%.

alternative_regimens.name: oral anticholinergic treatment in combination with intermittent catheterization
alternative_regimens.summary: Described as the primary treatment approach for DSD due to SCI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use when intermittent catheterization is feasible.

not_recommended.name: chemical sphincterotomy
not_recommended.reason: Botulinum toxin injection into the sphincter is not recommended for routine DSD management because its efficacy over time is limited.

response_assessment.timepoint: After sphincterotomy and during ongoing follow-up
response_assessment.method: Clinicians may perform UDS to assess outcome; monitor emptying, storage pressures, residual urine, recurrent UTI and AD.
response_assessment.interpretation: Impaired emptying or elevated pressures can recur, including without obvious symptoms.

supportive_care: Counsel about condom-catheter management, skin injury, bleeding and possible repeat procedures.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Post-sphincterotomy UDS to assess outcome has a separate Conditional Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade C.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with SUI and acceptable bladder storage parameters.
decision_rules: Clinicians should offer slings to selected patients.
Assess storage parameters before an outlet procedure when NLUTD could make reduced compliance and elevated storage pressure a concern.

recommended_regimens.name: slings
recommended_regimens.summary: An outlet procedure for selected patients with SUI and safe bladder storage.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited meta-analysis of sling studies, success and failure rates were 58% and 22%, respectively; definitions of success differed or were not reported for every study.

not_recommended.name: synthetic slings
not_recommended.reason: The Panel recommends avoiding them when future CIC is a concern and not using synthetic material for an occlusive sling.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before surgery and during subsequent follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess bladder storage with UDS when relevant; afterward, assess continence and ability to void.
response_assessment.interpretation: An outlet procedure could worsen compliance and endanger the upper urinary tracts.

supportive_care: Discuss possible future voiding dysfunction and need for CIC.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For an occlusive sling, the Panel advises considering autologous fascia or another biologic graft rather than synthetic material.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with SUI considering a minimally invasive outlet intervention.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer urethral bulking agents only after explaining that benefit is modest and cure is uncommon.

recommended_regimens.name: urethral bulking agents
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for SUI with limited expected efficacy, especially over the longer term.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited study of collagen injections with outcomes available for nine men, two patients (22.2%) had near-complete symptom resolution; another cited study of PDS injections reported 37.5% completely dry after a mean follow-up of 37.5 months.

response_assessment.method: Assess continence, pad use and patient-reported improvement.
response_assessment.interpretation: Repeat injection does not have established superior outcomes in the cited evidence.

supportive_care: Counsel about modest efficacy, uncommon cure and limited long-term evidence.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The effect of regular CIC or the choice of bulking agent on outcomes in NLUTD remains unclear.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with SUI, acceptable storage parameters and sufficient hand function to operate a device.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer an artificial urinary sphincter after assessing storage safety and the patient's ability to manipulate it.

recommended_regimens.name: artificial urinary sphincter
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for selected patients with SUI after counseling about voiding dysfunction and device-related risks.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited retrospective study of 51 adult men with SB or SCI, 60% were completely continent and 22% moderately continent after seven years.

not_recommended.name: transvaginal cuff
not_recommended.reason: The Panel considers this a poor placement option in women with NLUTD.

response_assessment.method: Confirm acceptable storage pressures with UDS when relevant; assess continence, device function, erosion, infection and ability to empty.
response_assessment.interpretation: An outlet procedure can exacerbate impaired compliance and place the upper tracts at risk.

supportive_care: Discuss possible CIC, device revision, explantation and additional surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline considers use in adult women uncommon and appropriate only in limited circumstances.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with refractory SUI or severe outlet or urethral damage.
decision_rules: After thorough discussion of risks, benefits and alternatives, clinicians may offer bladder neck closure together with a method of bladder drainage.
Plan for safe bladder storage, particularly when using a continent catheterizable stoma rather than continuous suprapubic drainage.

recommended_regimens.name: bladder neck closure and concomitant bladder drainage methods
recommended_regimens.summary: An irreversible option for selected patients with refractory outlet incontinence.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports continence rates of 75 – 100% after BNC, with fistulization and recurrent incontinence in up to 25% of cases.

alternative_regimens.name: tight fascial sling
alternative_regimens.summary: May preserve emergency urethral access and facilitate access to an upper tract stone.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Requires sufficient remaining urethral tissue; it is not suitable for many patients with severe urethral loss.

response_assessment.method: Assess storage pressures with UDS when relevant, then monitor continence, drainage and fistula formation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Outlet closure without adequately safe storage could threaten the upper urinary tracts.

supportive_care: Discuss potential loss of male fertility and the possible need for assisted reproduction before surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Drainage approaches described include a suprapubic catheter, continent catheterizable stoma or ileovesicostomy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults who void spontaneously and have urgency, frequency and/or urgency incontinence.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer posterior tibial nerve stimulation.

recommended_regimens.name: posterior tibial nerve stimulation
recommended_regimens.summary: A possible treatment for storage symptoms in selected spontaneous voiders, with the most directly described evidence in MS, PD and CVA.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited MS study using daily treatment, 83.3% of patients reported improvement in warning time, urgency and voids per day at study end, with p<0.001, p=0.023 and p<0.01, respectively.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Study schedules varied; no single schedule is specified as the guideline regimen.

response_assessment.timepoint: After initial treatment and during any maintenance treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess urgency, frequency, urgency incontinence and continued benefit.
response_assessment.interpretation: Some patients in the cited MS studies required frequent maintenance sessions to preserve improvement.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence is limited; overlap between systematic reviews of MS studies may overestimate the effect.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with urgency, frequency and/or urgency incontinence, excluding patients with SCI or SB.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer sacral neuromodulation to selected patients.
Do not offer it to patients with SCI or SB.

recommended_regimens.name: sacral neuromodulation
recommended_regimens.summary: An option for selected NLUTD populations; the guideline discusses MS, CVA and PD among potentially responsive etiologies.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited mixed-NLUTD study, 107/182 (58.8%) proceeded to generator placement; outcomes were reported for the pooled population rather than individual neurologic conditions.

not_recommended.name: sacral neuromodulation in SCI or SB
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against offering it because bladder dysfunction and disease courses are highly variable and the reviewed clinical situations were heterogeneous.

response_assessment.method: Review urinary symptoms, retention where relevant, device function and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Efficacy can diminish as progressive neurologic disease worsens.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The exclusion for SCI or SB is a separate Moderate Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade C. MRI compatibility is relevant for MS; the guideline notes that newer devices are MRI conditional.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults with DO and/or poor bladder compliance who are refractory to, or cannot tolerate, less invasive therapy.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer augmentation cystoplasty after discussing its long-term risks and the need for lifelong follow-up.
Confirm that the patient or a caregiver can perform the regular CIC that may be necessary.

recommended_regimens.name: augmentation cystoplasty
recommended_regimens.summary: A reconstructive option for inadequate capacity, compliance or DO despite less invasive management.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited review found resolution of VUR in 108 of 150 renal units and reported that risks of stones, bowel dysfunction and mucus-related complications exceeded 10%.

response_assessment.method: Assess continence, renal function, upper urinary tract findings and reconstruction-related complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Long-term complications can require further treatment.

supportive_care: Counsel about stones, perforation, bowel dysfunction, mucus production and regular CIC.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The reviewed studies associate surgery with high continence and upper-tract protection rates, but the quality and quantity of evidence are limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults who need easier catheterization, including patients with an unusable urethra or difficulty catheterizing through the urethra.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer a continent catheterizable channel with or without augmentation.
Consider cognitive function, dexterity, caregiver support and the likelihood of later revision before surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: continent catheterizable channels
recommended_regimens.summary: A reconstructive route intended to facilitate catheterization.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited review involving 213 patients, the channel could be catheterized in 84%, stomal continence was >75%, and re-operations were required in 40%.

response_assessment.timepoint: After reconstruction and during long-term follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess the ability to catheterize, stomal continence, stenosis and need for revision.
response_assessment.interpretation: Channel stenosis and re-operation are important longer-term considerations.

supportive_care: Provide preoperative counseling about outcomes, complications and possible repeat procedures.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Multidisciplinary preoperative assessment may help when cognition or upper-extremity function is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected adults unable to self-catheterize because of factors such as poor hand function, immobility, difficult body habitus or skin damage associated with a condom catheter.
decision_rules: Clinicians may offer ileovesicostomy but must explain its risks, benefits, alternatives and substantial likelihood of additional treatment or surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: ileovesicostomy
recommended_regimens.summary: An option intended to provide low-pressure drainage through a urostomy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across cited studies, subsequent procedures were required in 33 to 75%. In one cited study, urethral continence was 72% (n=36) at a mean follow-up of 26 months (range 1-79 months).

response_assessment.timepoint: After surgery and during long-term follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess drainage, continence, stomal problems and urinary stones.
response_assessment.interpretation: Revision or an alternative operation may be needed.

supportive_care: Discuss ostomy placement and appliance management.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline raises concern that ileovesicostomy may drain poorly in patients with obesity and may not be an optimal choice for them.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults for whom other bladder-management options have failed or are inappropriate.
decision_rules: Clinicians should offer urinary diversion to improve long-term quality of life when other options have failed or are unsuitable.

recommended_regimens.name: urinary diversion
recommended_regimens.summary: A final reconstructive option for severe bladder or urethral dysfunction, persistent fistula or a non-healing pressure ulcer when adequate, safe storage cannot otherwise be achieved.

alternative_regimens.name: ileal conduit
alternative_regimens.summary: An incontinent diversion approach described in the reviewed studies.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choice of diversion depends on the patient's condition, functional ability and support.

alternative_regimens.name: continent urinary diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: A continent approach described in a smaller body of evidence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider catheterization ability and the requirements of the reconstruction.

response_assessment.method: Monitor quality of life, upper urinary tract changes, infection and late reconstruction-related complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Complications can develop long after the original surgery.

supportive_care: Counsel about diversion options and assess hand function, upper-extremity function, and home or social support.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Because complications may arise in a retained bladder after supravesical diversion, the guideline advises considering concomitant cystectomy; it advises strongly considering concurrent supratrigonal cystectomy or cystoprostatectomy in male patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults whose impaired storage parameters continue to place the upper urinary tracts at risk despite treatment.
decision_rules: Repeat UDS at an appropriate interval after treatment when storage or voiding dysfunction threatens the upper tracts.
Offer additional treatment if unsafe storage persists.
A stepwise increase in treatment invasiveness is reasonable if repeated UDS confirms effectiveness; strongly consider continuous drainage when all therapies fail.

recommended_regimens.name: additional treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Escalate therapy when initial treatment has not adequately improved high-risk bladder storage.

alternative_regimens.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
alternative_regimens.summary: A more advanced option when symptoms or elevated storage pressures persist despite oral storage-directed treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select according to clinical circumstances and the applicable onabotulinumtoxinA recommendation for the neurologic condition.

alternative_regimens.name: augmentation cystoplasty
alternative_regimens.summary: A more invasive option for persistent unsafe storage despite less invasive treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when less invasive therapies fail or cannot be tolerated.

alternative_regimens.name: SPC or supravesical urinary diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: Continuous drainage should be strongly considered when other therapies have failed.

response_assessment.timepoint: At an appropriate interval after treatment
response_assessment.method: Repeat multichannel UDS to assess storage pressures and compliance.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistently unsafe findings warrant further treatment.

supportive_care: Continue upper urinary tract surveillance when renal damage remains a risk.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes an interval of two years or less as reasonable once pressures normalize in at-risk patients, while noting that the optimal UDS interval is poorly studied and may be extended in clinically stable patients.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults who have undergone lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating bowel.
decision_rules: Assess patients annually with focused history, examination and symptom review, a basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging.

response_assessment.method: Focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, basic metabolic panel and urinary tract imaging.
response_assessment.interpretation: Look for metabolic disturbance and upper urinary tract obstruction or other reconstruction-related complications.

response_assessment.timepoint: If gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI develops
response_assessment.method: Perform cystoscopy.
response_assessment.interpretation: Investigate symptoms rather than assuming they arise from catheter trauma, cystitis or pouchitis.

supportive_care: If terminal ileum was used, monitor B12 over time and supplement when appropriate.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Annual surveillance after bowel-based reconstruction is an Expert Opinion. Cystoscopy for gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI is a Moderate Recommendation with Evidence Level: Grade C. For a continent urinary stoma constructed without AC, the guideline states that annual assessment without a basic metabolic panel is sufficient.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults considering additional approaches outside established NLUTD treatments.
decision_rules: Treat other potential NLUTD interventions as investigational and counsel patients accordingly.
Limit non-standardized treatments to a well-designed clinical trial.

not_recommended.name: non-standardized NLUTD treatments outside a well-designed clinical trial
not_recommended.reason: The guideline considers these approaches investigational because development or outcome evidence is insufficient.

supportive_care: Explain the investigational status and uncertainties to patients.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The discussion includes an adjustable continence mechanism, early SNM after SCI as a disease-modifying intervention, the Xiao procedure and tissue engineering. Sacral anterior root neurostimulator implantation is described as limited to investigational settings or specialist centers familiar with the procedure.

special_populations.considerations: SCI can place patients at risk of unsafe bladder storage pressures, urinary tract complications and AD. Upper tract risk depends on the individual findings rather than the neurologic diagnosis alone.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For NLUTD refractory to oral medication, clinicians should recommend onabotulinumtoxinA; 200 U and 300 U did not differ in efficacy, although retention and the need for CIC increased with dose. Clinicians should not offer SNM to patients with SCI.

special_populations.considerations: Symptoms can involve storage, emptying or both. Progressive neurologic disease can change lower urinary tract function, and patients who void without catheterization may require CIC after botulinum toxin treatment. MRI compatibility is relevant when considering an implanted neuromodulation device.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For NLUTD refractory to oral medication, clinicians should recommend onabotulinumtoxinA. The 200 U and 300 U doses did not differ in efficacy, but retention and initiation of CIC increased with dose. Before botulinum toxin treatment in a patient who voids spontaneously, clinicians must discuss retention and possible CIC.

special_populations.considerations: Bladder dysfunction may coexist with BOO. Evidence for botulinum toxin treatment is limited, and post-injection urinary retention is a particular concern when outlet obstruction coexists.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Clinicians may offer onabotulinumtoxinA when oral medication has failed, but this population is covered by a Conditional Recommendation supported by Grade C evidence rather than the recommendation for SCI or MS. Retention and a possible need for catheterization must be discussed before botulinum toxin treatment in patients who void spontaneously.

special_populations.considerations: Cognitive or physical limitations can prevent independent CIC. Advanced lesions with poor sensory awareness may increase the risk of impaired bladder sensation, retention and UTI after botulinum toxin treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Patient selection for botulinum toxin treatment should account for the ability to manage subsequent retention; a caregiver or temporary catheter may be needed.

special_populations.considerations: Lesions are often incomplete and clinical manifestations vary. Reports on botulinum toxin treatment in adults are sparse, and poor bladder compliance was associated with lower global success in a cited retrospective study.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Clinicians may offer onabotulinumtoxinA after failure of oral medication under the Conditional Recommendation for NLUTD other than SCI or MS; the evidence level is Grade C.

special_populations.population: Patients following an acute brain or spinal cord injury
special_populations.considerations: Early neurologic and urodynamic findings can change and do not reliably predict long-term lower urinary tract function. Spinal shock may last several days or months, usually resolving in approximately 3-6 months, but it can persist for 1-2 years.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Risk stratification should be deferred until the neurologic condition has stabilized; UDS during spinal shock may also be delayed.

special_populations.population: Patients with SCI at T6 or above
special_populations.considerations: AD is a medical emergency associated with injury at this level; a few patients with injuries at T7 or T8 may also be at risk. Bladder distension and urinary procedures can trigger an episode.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: During UDS or cystoscopy, clinicians must monitor at-risk patients hemodynamically. If AD occurs, they must stop the procedure, drain the bladder immediately and continue monitoring; persistent AD after drainage calls for pharmacologic management and/or escalation of care.

special_populations.population: Patients with NLUTD who are pregnant
special_populations.considerations: Pregnancy is an exception to the recommendation against treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in NLUTD.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The recommendation not to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria does not apply during pregnancy.

special_populations.population: Patients who perform CIC and have recurrent UTI
special_populations.considerations: Evidence for oral antimicrobial prophylaxis is limited, and reducing infections must be weighed against increased antibiotic resistance. Evidence for any single bladder-instillation strategy is also insufficient.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Following shared decision-making about resistance, clinicians may offer oral antimicrobial prophylaxis to reduce UTI frequency. They may also offer bladder instillations.

special_populations.population: Patients who perform CIC without recurrent UTI
special_populations.considerations: The recommendation on daily antibiotic prophylaxis distinguishes these patients from those with recurrent infections.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Clinicians should not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis.

special_populations.population: Patients with a chronic indwelling catheter
special_populations.considerations: Catheter-related urethral or suprapubic-site injury and urinary calculi require attention. Catheter-associated bacterial growth complicates interpretation of urine specimens.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Clinicians should not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis or screening cystoscopy solely because of the catheter. They should periodically examine the catheter and its entry site. For patients at risk of calculi, urinary tract imaging should be performed every 1-2 years. If UTI is suspected, the culture specimen should be collected after catheter replacement and urine accumulation, not from the tubing or collection bag.

special_populations.considerations: PVR measurement informs assessment of emptying. Botulinum toxin treatment can cause retention that requires intermittent catheterization.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: PVR should be measured at initial evaluation. Alpha-blockers may be recommended to improve voiding parameters. Before choosing botulinum toxin treatment, clinicians must discuss retention and the possible need for intermittent catheterization.

special_populations.population: Patients with impaired hand function, mobility or cognition
special_populations.considerations: These limitations may make CIC or manipulation of an AUS difficult. Caregiver availability and the patient's home circumstances affect the feasibility of bladder management and reconstruction.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Intermittent catheterization remains preferred when feasible. For appropriately selected patients requiring a chronic indwelling catheter, suprapubic catheterization should be recommended over a urethral catheter. Ability to perform regular CIC, independently or with a caregiver, should be assessed before AC or CCC; adequate hand dexterity should be confirmed before AUS implantation.

special_populations.population: Patients after lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating bowel
special_populations.considerations: Complications can arise long after reconstruction, including metabolic disturbances and upper tract obstruction. Terminal ileum use may affect B12 levels.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Annual assessment should include a focused history, examination and symptom review, a basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging. B12 should be monitored over time and supplemented when appropriate if terminal ileum was used. Gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI warrants cystoscopy.

special_populations.population: Patients with a continent urinary stoma without AC
special_populations.considerations: They do not have the electrolyte or acid-base risk described for bowel-based bladder augmentation solely because of the stoma.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Annual evaluation without a basic metabolic panel is sufficient for this circumstance.

recommendations.statement: At the initial assessment, clinicians should classify patients as low-risk or unknown-risk; those in the unknown-risk group require further assessment before risk stratification is complete.
recommendations.rationale: Risk classification guides evaluation and surveillance aimed at limiting upper urinary tract damage.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: At initial evaluation, every patient should receive a detailed history, physical examination, and urinalysis.
recommendations.rationale: These findings guide subsequent investigation and management.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Measure post-void residual at initial evaluation in patients who void spontaneously.
recommendations.rationale: Post-void residual helps assess bladder emptying.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: A voiding or catheterization diary, pad test, and non-invasive uroflow may be used selectively during initial evaluation.
recommendations.rationale: These tests can add diagnostic or prognostic information or help direct care in selected patients.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely obtain upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, or multichannel urodynamics at initial evaluation in low-risk patients.
recommendations.rationale: Without other concerning factors, these studies are unlikely to provide clinically useful findings.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: At initial evaluation of unknown-risk patients, obtain upper tract imaging, assess renal function, and perform multichannel urodynamics.
recommendations.rationale: Additional assessment is needed to establish risk when the initial findings do not establish a low-risk category.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: After an acute neurological event causes NLUTD, defer risk stratification until the neurological condition has stabilized.
recommendations.rationale: Early clinical and urodynamic findings may change and may not predict long-term function.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Do not perform cystoscopy routinely as part of the initial evaluation.
recommendations.rationale: NLUTD alone is not an indication for this invasive test.
recommendations.source_heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: During urodynamic testing or cystoscopy, hemodynamically monitor patients at risk of autonomic dysreflexia.
recommendations.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia is a medical emergency that can be triggered by these procedures.

recommendations.statement: If autonomic dysreflexia develops during urodynamic testing or cystoscopy, terminate the procedure, drain the bladder immediately, and continue hemodynamic monitoring.
recommendations.rationale: Stopping the provoking stimulus and emptying the bladder are first-line measures.

recommendations.statement: If autonomic dysreflexia persists after bladder drainage, initiate pharmacologic treatment and/or escalate care.
recommendations.rationale: Persistent symptoms and blood pressure elevation require further intervention.

recommendations.statement: Educate patients about signs and symptoms that should prompt further assessment.
recommendations.rationale: Urological complications may arise between visits and may present atypically.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: In low-risk patients whose urinary signs and symptoms remain stable, do not obtain surveillance upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, or multichannel urodynamics.
recommendations.rationale: Routine advanced testing has little utility in this group while findings remain stable.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: For moderate-risk patients with stable urinary findings, perform a focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, and renal function assessment annually; obtain upper tract imaging every 1-2 years.
recommendations.rationale: These patients remain at risk of complications despite lacking dangerous urodynamic findings.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: For high-risk patients with stable urinary findings, perform a focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, renal function assessment, and upper tract imaging annually; perform multichannel urodynamics with or without fluoroscopy, repeating it when clinically indicated.
recommendations.rationale: Upper tract deterioration or worsening bladder storage parameters can occur without new symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Re-evaluate and repeat risk stratification in low-risk patients who develop new signs or symptoms, new complications such as autonomic dysreflexia, urinary tract infections or stones, or deterioration of the upper tract or renal function.
recommendations.rationale: A change in urinary tract status may warrant follow-up under a different risk category.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Multichannel urodynamics may be performed in moderate- or high-risk patients when signs or symptoms change, complications arise, or upper tract findings or renal function deteriorate.
recommendations.context: Change in moderate- or high-risk status
recommendations.rationale: Testing prompted by a clinical change can identify bladder dysfunction that alters management.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Perform cystoscopy when a patient has hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, or a suspected anatomical abnormality such as a stricture or false passage.
recommendations.rationale: Cystoscopy can identify sources of bleeding, recurrent infection, or difficult catheter passage.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Do not perform cystoscopy solely for screening or surveillance in patients with NLUTD.
recommendations.rationale: Routine cystoscopy has not been proven to reduce morbidity or mortality and can prompt investigation of benign lesions.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Do not perform screening or surveillance cystoscopy in patients with NLUTD who have a chronic indwelling catheter.
recommendations.rationale: Routine cystoscopy has not been established as a useful bladder cancer screening test in this population.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Periodically examine the indwelling catheter and its suprapubic or urethral insertion site.
recommendations.rationale: Examination can detect catheter-related tissue injury or site complications.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Obtain urinary tract imaging every 1-2 years in patients with indwelling catheters who are at risk of upper or lower urinary tract calculi, including those with spinal cord injury, recurrent urinary tract infection, immobilization, or hypercalcuria.
recommendations.context: Stone-risk surveillance with an indwelling catheter
recommendations.rationale: Calculi may become large before they are otherwise detected.
recommendations.source_heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD

recommendations.statement: Do not perform surveillance or screening urine tests, including urine cultures, in asymptomatic patients.
recommendations.rationale: Avoiding screening reduces the likelihood of unnecessary antibiotic treatment of bacterial colonization.

recommendations.statement: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in patients with NLUTD.
recommendations.rationale: Unnecessary antibiotic exposure contributes to resistance; the guideline identifies pregnancy and certain urologic procedures as exceptions.

recommendations.statement: Obtain urinalysis and urine culture when signs or symptoms suggest a urinary tract infection.
recommendations.rationale: Symptoms alone do not reliably identify infection across all patients with NLUTD.

recommendations.statement: In febrile urinary tract infection, obtain upper tract imaging if antibiotic treatment does not produce an appropriate response, or if a moderate- or high-risk patient is overdue for routine upper tract imaging regardless of treatment response.
recommendations.rationale: Persistent fever may indicate upper tract complications, and risk-based imaging remains necessary even after a response to antibiotics.

recommendations.statement: When urinary tract infection is suspected in a patient with an indwelling catheter, change the catheter, allow urine to collect while it is plugged, and then obtain the culture specimen; do not collect urine from extension tubing or the collection bag.
recommendations.context: Urine culture collection with an indwelling catheter
recommendations.rationale: A newly placed catheter may provide a more suitable culture specimen than a chronically placed catheter.

recommendations.statement: Evaluate both the upper and lower urinary tracts with imaging and cystoscopy when urinary tract infections recur.
recommendations.rationale: These investigations assess for urinary tract sources of recurrent infection.

recommendations.statement: Urodynamic evaluation may be performed for recurrent urinary tract infections when upper and lower urinary tract assessments are unremarkable.
recommendations.context: Recurrent infection after an unremarkable anatomical evaluation
recommendations.rationale: Urodynamics may identify functional abnormalities contributing to infection risk.

recommendations.statement: Do not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent urinary tract infection in patients managing their bladder with an indwelling catheter.
recommendations.rationale: The cited review did not find a significant reduction in symptomatic infections and reported increased antimicrobial resistance.

recommendations.statement: Do not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis in patients using clean intermittent catheterization who do not have recurrent urinary tract infections.
recommendations.context: Clean intermittent catheterization without recurrent infection
recommendations.rationale: The cited evidence did not establish a reduction in symptomatic infection for this group and raised concern about resistance.

recommendations.statement: Pelvic floor muscle training may be recommended to appropriately selected patients, particularly those with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular accident, to improve urinary symptoms and quality-of-life measures.
recommendations.rationale: Selected patients may benefit, although evidence varies across interventions and populations.

recommendations.statement: Antimuscarinics, beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, or their combination may be recommended to improve bladder storage parameters.
recommendations.context: Pharmacologic treatment of bladder storage dysfunction
recommendations.rationale: Evidence supports improved storage measures, while evidence for particular medications and patient groups remains limited.

recommendations.statement: Alpha-blockers may be recommended to improve voiding parameters in patients who void spontaneously.
recommendations.rationale: The cited studies reported improvements in voiding parameters, with limited precision of evidence.

recommendations.statement: Recommend intermittent catheterization instead of an indwelling catheter to assist bladder emptying.
recommendations.rationale: The panel judged the risk and complication profile of indwelling catheters to favor intermittent catheterization when feasible.

recommendations.statement: For appropriately selected patients who need a chronic indwelling catheter, recommend suprapubic catheterization rather than an indwelling urethral catheter.
recommendations.rationale: The panel favored the suprapubic route while acknowledging limitations and conflicting complication rates in the evidence.

recommendations.statement: For patients using clean intermittent catheterization who have recurrent urinary tract infection, oral antimicrobial prophylaxis may be offered to lower infection frequency after shared decision-making and discussion of the increased risk of antibiotic resistance.
recommendations.context: Recurrent infection during clean intermittent catheterization
recommendations.rationale: Potential reductions in infection must be balanced against increased antimicrobial resistance.

recommendations.statement: Bladder instillations may be offered to patients using clean intermittent catheterization who have recurrent urinary tract infection to reduce infection frequency.
recommendations.context: Recurrent infection during clean intermittent catheterization
recommendations.rationale: Evidence for individual instillation approaches is insufficient and heterogeneous.

recommendations.statement: Patients with recurrent urinary tract infection who use various catheter-management methods may be counseled that cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to reduce infection frequency.
recommendations.rationale: The cited studies do not provide consistent evidence supporting a reduction in urinary tract infections.

recommendations.statement: Recommend onabotulinumtoxinA for patients with spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis whose condition is refractory to oral medication, to improve bladder storage parameters and quality-of-life measures and reduce incontinence episodes.
recommendations.context: Refractory symptoms in spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis
recommendations.rationale: The cited controlled trials and systematic reviews support improvements in continence, storage measures, and quality of life.

recommendations.statement: OnabotulinumtoxinA may be offered to patients other than those with spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis whose condition is refractory to oral medication, to improve bladder storage parameters and quality-of-life measures and reduce incontinence episodes.
recommendations.context: Refractory symptoms with other neurological causes
recommendations.rationale: Evidence outside spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis is limited by small studies and uncertain benefit–risk balance.

recommendations.statement: Before selecting botulinum toxin treatment for a patient who voids spontaneously, discuss the specific risk of urinary retention and the possible need for intermittent catheterization.
recommendations.rationale: Incomplete bladder emptying or retention after treatment may necessitate catheterization.

recommendations.statement: Sphincterotomy may be offered to appropriately selected male patients to aid bladder emptying, but they must be counseled about the high risk of failure and the possible need for further treatment or surgery.
recommendations.rationale: The procedure may improve emptying, but failure and repeat intervention are common.

recommendations.statement: Urethral bulking agents may be offered for stress urinary incontinence, provided patients are counseled that effectiveness is modest and cure is uncommon.
recommendations.rationale: The available studies report limited success and poor long-term outcomes.

recommendations.statement: Offer slings to selected patients with stress urinary incontinence and acceptable bladder storage parameters.
recommendations.context: Stress urinary incontinence with acceptable storage parameters
recommendations.rationale: Outlet surgery can worsen storage pressures, making assessment of bladder storage important.

recommendations.statement: An artificial urinary sphincter may be offered to selected patients with stress urinary incontinence and acceptable bladder storage parameters.
recommendations.context: Stress urinary incontinence with acceptable storage parameters
recommendations.rationale: Potential improvement in continence must be weighed against voiding dysfunction and device-related risks.

recommendations.statement: After thoroughly discussing risks, benefits, and alternatives, bladder neck closure with a concurrent bladder drainage method may be offered to selected patients with refractory stress urinary incontinence.
recommendations.rationale: Closure is irreversible and requires a plan for urinary drainage and safe bladder storage.

recommendations.statement: Posterior tibial nerve stimulation may be offered to selected patients who void spontaneously and have urgency, frequency, and/or urgency incontinence.
recommendations.rationale: Selected patients may benefit, although the supporting evidence is limited.

recommendations.statement: Sacral neuromodulation may be offered to selected patients with urgency, frequency, and/or urgency incontinence.
recommendations.rationale: Observational evidence suggests benefit in selected neurological populations but is limited and inconsistent.

recommendations.statement: Do not offer sacral neuromodulation to patients with spinal cord injury or spina bifida.
recommendations.context: Spinal cord injury or spina bifida
recommendations.rationale: Bladder dysfunction and clinical circumstances in these populations are highly variable, and further procedures may be needed.

recommendations.statement: Augmentation cystoplasty may be offered to selected patients with detrusor overactivity and/or poor bladder compliance who are refractory to, or cannot tolerate, less invasive treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Potential continence and upper tract benefits must be weighed against complications and lifelong follow-up.

recommendations.statement: Continent catheterizable channels, with or without augmentation, may be offered to selected patients to make catheterization possible or easier.
recommendations.rationale: Channels may provide catheter access, although complications and revision procedures are common.

recommendations.statement: Ileovesicostomy may be offered to selected patients, who must be counseled about its risks, benefits, alternatives, and high risk of needing further treatment or surgery.
recommendations.rationale: The cited studies report a substantial need for subsequent procedures.
