recommendations.statement: Offer urinary diversion to improve long-term quality of life when other treatment options have failed or are unsuitable.
recommendations.context: Failure or unsuitability of other treatments
recommendations.rationale: Diversion is a last-resort option when other approaches cannot provide safe, adequate urinary storage.

recommendations.statement: Regard other potential NLUTD treatments as investigational and counsel patients accordingly.
recommendations.rationale: These approaches are insufficiently developed or lack adequate supporting outcomes data.

recommendations.statement: After treatment, repeat urodynamic studies at an appropriate interval when impaired storage and/or voiding parameters place the upper urinary tracts at risk.
recommendations.context: Post-treatment assessment of upper tract risk
recommendations.rationale: Repeat testing assesses whether treatment has adequately improved concerning bladder pressures or function.

recommendations.statement: Offer additional treatment when storage parameters continue to threaten the upper urinary tracts despite therapy.
recommendations.rationale: Persistently elevated storage pressures threaten renal function and may contribute to symptomatic infections.

recommendations.statement: After lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating bowel segment(s), assess the patient annually with a focused history, physical examination, symptom assessment, basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging.
recommendations.context: Follow-up after bowel-based lower urinary tract reconstruction
recommendations.rationale: Lifelong follow-up can identify metabolic abnormalities and urinary tract complications.

recommendations.statement: Urodynamics may be performed after sphincterotomy to evaluate its outcome.
recommendations.rationale: Testing can document changes in bladder pressures and emptying after the procedure.

recommendations.statement: Perform cystoscopy when a patient who has undergone bowel-based lower urinary tract reconstruction develops gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent urinary tract infection.
recommendations.rationale: These symptoms warrant evaluation rather than being presumed to result from catheter trauma or inflammation.

document_sections.heading: Executive Summary
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses evaluation, surveillance, treatment, and follow-up of adults with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD). Its recommendations combine evidence-based statements with Clinical Principles and Expert Opinions.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: NLUTD describes dysfunction of the bladder, bladder neck, or sphincters associated with a neurological disorder; the older term “neurogenic bladder” does not encompass all affected structures. Treatment decisions should consider urinary symptoms and, when available, urodynamic findings alongside cognition, hand function, mobility, bowel management, neurological disease course, and caregiver or social support. The guideline aims to support individualized, shared decisions that improve quality of life related to bladder management.

document_sections.heading: Methodology
document_sections.content: The evidence search covered studies published from January 2001 through October 2017 and was updated in February 2021. It identified 20,496 distinct citations; 3,036 articles underwent full-text assessment, and 184 primary studies met inclusion criteria. Failure to meet PICO criteria was the principal reason for exclusion at full-text review.

document_sections.heading: Guideline Statements
document_sections.content: The executive summary presents 60 clinical statements covering initial assessment, autonomic dysreflexia, surveillance, urinary tract infection, nonsurgical and surgical treatment, and post-treatment follow-up. Their individual qualifications and evidence grades are specified below.

document_sections.heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD
document_sections.content: Initially, patients should be classified as low-risk or unknown-risk; the latter need further assessment for definitive stratification (Clinical Principle). Every patient should have a detailed history, examination, and urinalysis; spontaneous voiders should also have post-void residual measured (Clinical Principle). A voiding or catheterization diary, pad test, and non-invasive uroflow are optional (Expert Opinion). Routine upper tract imaging, renal function testing, and multichannel urodynamics should not be obtained initially for low-risk patients, but should be obtained for unknown-risk patients (both Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). After an acute neurological event, risk should be stratified once the neurological condition stabilizes; routine initial cystoscopy should not be performed (both Clinical Principle).

document_sections.heading: Autonomic Dysreflexia
document_sections.content: Patients at risk of autonomic dysreflexia must undergo hemodynamic monitoring during urodynamics or cystoscopy. If dysreflexia develops, clinicians must stop the procedure, immediately empty the bladder, and continue monitoring. Persistent dysreflexia after drainage calls for pharmacological treatment and/or escalation of care (all Clinical Principle).

document_sections.heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD
document_sections.content: Clinicians must teach patients which new signs or symptoms require assessment (Clinical Principle). Stable low-risk patients should not receive routine upper tract imaging, renal function testing, or multichannel urodynamics (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Stable moderate-risk patients should have an annual focused history, examination, symptom review, and renal function assessment, plus upper tract imaging every 1-2 years; stable high-risk patients should have the same annual clinical and renal assessments, annual upper tract imaging, and multichannel urodynamics, with or without fluoroscopy, repeated when clinically indicated (both Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). New symptoms, complications, or upper tract or renal deterioration warrant reassessment and renewed risk stratification in low-risk patients; multichannel urodynamics may be performed in moderate- or high-risk patients with these changes (Clinical Principle). Hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, or suspected anatomical abnormalities warrant cystoscopy (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). Screening or surveillance cystoscopy should not be performed in NLUTD, including in patients with chronic indwelling catheters (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). Indwelling catheters and their entry sites should be examined periodically, and catheter users at risk of calculi should have urinary tract imaging every 1-2 years (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C).

document_sections.heading: Urinary Tract Infection
document_sections.content: Asymptomatic patients should not receive screening urine tests or cultures, and asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Suspected infection warrants urinalysis and culture (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). For febrile infection, obtain upper tract imaging if antibiotic response is inadequate or if a moderate- or high-risk patient is overdue for routine imaging, regardless of response (Clinical Principle). With a suspected infection and indwelling catheter, replace the catheter, allow urine to collect while it is plugged, and obtain the culture from that urine rather than extension tubing or the bag (Clinical Principle). Recurrent infections warrant upper and lower tract imaging and cystoscopy; if those assessments are unrevealing, urodynamics may be performed (respectively Clinical Principle and Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Daily antibiotic prophylaxis should not be used for patients with indwelling catheters (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B), or for clean intermittent catheterization users without recurrent infections (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B).

document_sections.heading: Non-Surgical Treatment
document_sections.content: Pelvic floor muscle training may be recommended for selected patients, especially with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular accident, to improve urinary symptoms and quality of life. Antimuscarinics, beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, or their combination may be recommended for bladder storage; alpha-blockers may be recommended for spontaneous voiders to improve voiding (each Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Intermittent catheterization should be preferred to indwelling catheterization for emptying, and appropriately selected patients requiring a chronic indwelling catheter should be offered suprapubic rather than urethral catheterization (both Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). For clean intermittent catheterization users with recurrent infection, oral antimicrobial prophylaxis may be offered after shared discussion of resistance risk (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C), and bladder instillations may be offered (Expert Opinion). Patients may be told that cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to reduce infection rates (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). For oral-treatment-refractory NLUTD, onabotulinumtoxinA should be recommended in spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade A) and may be offered for other neurological conditions (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) to improve storage, incontinence, and quality of life. Before botulinum toxin treatment in spontaneous voiders, urinary retention and possible intermittent catheterization must be discussed (Clinical Principle).

document_sections.heading: Surgical Treatment
document_sections.content: Selected men may be offered sphincterotomy for emptying, with mandatory counseling about its high failure risk and possible further intervention. Urethral bulking agents may be offered for stress incontinence, with counseling that benefit is modest and cure uncommon (both Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Selected patients with stress incontinence and acceptable storage parameters should be offered slings (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C) and may be offered artificial urinary sphincter (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). After discussing risks, benefits, and alternatives, bladder neck closure with another drainage method may be offered for selected refractory stress incontinence (Expert Opinion). Posterior tibial nerve stimulation may be offered to selected spontaneous voiders with urgency, frequency, or urgency incontinence; sacral neuromodulation may be offered to selected patients with these symptoms, but should not be offered to patients with spinal cord injury or spina bifida (each Conditional Recommendation or, for the restriction, Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Selected patients refractory to or intolerant of less invasive treatments for detrusor overactivity or poor compliance may be offered augmentation cystoplasty. Continent catheterizable channels may facilitate catheterization, with or without augmentation. Selected patients may be offered ileovesicostomy after counseling about risks, alternatives, and the high likelihood of additional treatment or surgery (each Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Urinary diversion should be offered if other options fail or are unsuitable to improve long-term quality of life (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Other potential therapies should be treated as investigational, with corresponding patient counseling (Expert Opinion).

document_sections.heading: Follow-up and post treatment
document_sections.content: After treatment, patients whose storage or voiding dysfunction threatens the upper tracts should undergo repeat urodynamics at an appropriate interval; those with persistent hazardous storage abnormalities should be offered further treatment (Expert Opinion). Following lower tract reconstruction using bowel, annual follow-up should include a focused history and examination, symptom assessment, basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging (Expert Opinion). Urodynamics may assess sphincterotomy outcomes (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Gross hematuria or recurrent symptomatic infection after bowel-based reconstruction warrants cystoscopy (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C).

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: NLUTD affects storage, emptying, sphincter relaxation, or continence and may cause incontinence, retention requiring CIC, or both. Non-neurogenic LUTS may coexist, and manifestations can evolve; diabetes-related dysfunction may progress from no symptoms to OAB-type symptoms and subsequently incomplete emptying with possible overflow incontinence. Neurological lesions may be suprapontine, suprasacral spinal, sacral, or peripheral. Brain and brainstem causes include tumors, PD, normal pressure hydrocephalus, CVA, and traumatic injury. In the United States approximately 795,000 people experience CVA annually, with 28-79% reporting UI afterward. MS and SCI are prominent spinal causes: estimated United States MS prevalence in 2010 was 288 to 309 per 100,000, equivalent to 523,437 to 727,344 cases; studies suggest LUTS in up to 50-90% of people with MS, and up to 65% of respondents in a 2005 survey described moderate to severe urinary symptoms. Approximately 17,700 SCI cases arise annually; 247,000 to 358,000 people were living with SCI in the United States as of 2018, and over 80% use a catheter after injury. Peripheral causes include diabetes and surgical nerve injury. In 2018, an estimated 34.2 million Americans, or 10.5% of the population, had diabetes; up to 80% of people with diabetes develop some lower urinary tract complication during life. NLUTD substantially affects QoL. Renal failure, previously a leading cause of death after SCI because of inadequate bladder management, has become less common with improved attention to storage pressure. Preventing upper tract damage is a major aim; recurrent UTI and AD are also addressed. Sexual dysfunction, male infertility, bowel dysfunction, and pediatric NLUTD are outside the guideline’s scope. Initial assessment and surveillance depend on neurological cause and severity. Possible tools include diaries, questionnaires such as NBSS and Qualiveen, PVR, uroflow, UDS, renal US, and cystoscopy; not everyone needs every test. Subsequent low-, medium-, or high-risk classification guides surveillance. Treatment choices should incorporate symptoms, urodynamics when relevant, cognition, dexterity, disease course, mobility, bowel management, and support, using shared decisions to optimize bladder-related QoL.

document_sections.heading: Literature Search Strategy
document_sections.content: MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library systematic-review databases were searched in October 2017 and again in February 2021 for newer reviews. Where reviews were missing or incomplete, PubMed (MEDLINE) and Embase were searched using prespecified PICO elements and relevant control articles. Primary-study coverage ran from January 2001 through October 2017, with a February 2021 update.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection Criteria and Process
document_sections.content: After duplicate removal, abstracts were screened for relevance and eligible designs. Randomized controlled, observational, and case-control studies could enter the evidence base. Studies of any size could be included, but statements were informed by studies enrolling at least 30 patients where those data existed. Case series, letters, editorials, laboratory or animal studies, and non-English publications were excluded in advance. Eligible full texts were assessed against PICO criteria; Figure 1 depicts the selection sequence. From 20,496 deduplicated citations, 17,460 were excluded after title and abstract review and 3,036 underwent full-text review. Of those, 2,852 were excluded: 1,443 were irrelevant, 79 had only an abstract, 938 were narrative reviews, 62 lacked relevant outcomes, 28 were already represented in an included systematic review, and 302 had samples smaller than 30 patients. The qualitative synthesis comprised 184 studies.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction
document_sections.content: The methodologist extracted information from studies that passed full-text assessment.

document_sections.heading: Quality Assessment Individual Study Quality and Potential for Bias
document_sections.content: All retained studies underwent quality assessment. Low-quality studies remained eligible, with relevant methodological limitations and strengths discussed. Overall quality combined design-specific risk-of-bias assessments with study design, comparison type, statistical power, and funding information. AMSTAR assessed systematic reviews, the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool randomized studies, and ROBINS-I observational studies.

document_sections.heading: Certainty of Evidence by GRADE
document_sections.content: GRADE assessed aggregate certainty for the outcomes informing each statement, considering bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias; a large effect or relevant confounding could support upgrading. Its certainty categories are high, moderate, low, and very low. AUA maps high certainty to evidence category A, moderate to B, and low or very low to C. Table 1 displays these definitions.

document_sections.heading: AUA Nomenclature: Linking Statement Type to Evidence Strength
document_sections.content: The AUA statement framework relates evidence strength and certainty to expected benefit, harm, and the Panel’s judgment. Strong Recommendations direct action for substantial net benefit or harm; Moderate Recommendations direct action for moderate net benefit or harm. Conditional Recommendations are non-directive when benefit and harm are balanced, comparable, or uncertain. Each may have evidence grade A, B, or C. With A evidence, future research is unlikely to change confidence; better evidence could change confidence with B and is likely to do so with C. For Conditional Recommendations, individual circumstances guide choices, and grade C permits similarly reasonable alternatives. Evidence gaps are addressed through Clinical Principles, reflecting broadly agreed care, or Expert Opinions, reflecting panel consensus grounded in professional judgment; a modified Delphi process resolves differences when needed. Table 2 sets out the framework.

document_sections.heading: Results Search for Existing Systematic Reviews
document_sections.content: The search identified 45 potentially relevant systematic reviews; 25 were selected for the evidence base. Where reviews shared primary studies and outcomes, the most complete was retained, and 20 overlapping reviews were excluded. The document also refers subsequently to 24 included systematic reviews.

document_sections.heading: Search for Primary Literature
document_sections.content: Primary studies addressed outcomes absent from included systematic reviews. The primary search was not narrowed after review selection; overlapping study outcomes were removed or not extracted twice to avoid overstating effects.

document_sections.heading: Literature Search Results
document_sections.content: The primary search found 20,496 unique citations and led to full-text assessment of 3,036 studies. Irrelevance to PICO criteria accounted for n=1,443 exclusions. Ultimately 184 primary studies entered the evidence base.

document_sections.heading: Guideline Statements
document_sections.content: The detailed statements explain how initial risk classification determines evaluation and subsequent surveillance.

document_sections.heading: Initial Evaluation of the Patient with NLUTD
document_sections.content: Initial assessment begins with a low-risk or unknown-risk designation; additional investigations establish the full risk category when the risk is unknown.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT ONE
document_sections.content: At presentation, classify NLUTD as low-risk or unknown-risk, requiring further assessment in the latter case (Clinical Principle). Risk classification is central to preventing later upper tract injury and must account for differences among and within neurological diagnoses. Suprapontine lesions commonly produce DO with coordinated voiding and low PVR, suggesting low risk, although elevated PVR after CVA or with cerebral palsy and pseudodyssynergia can imply moderate risk. Lesions below the spinal cord often have low storage pressures, but impaired contraction, elevated PVR, or later compliance loss can change risk. Suprasacral spinal lesions, including SCI, MS, and transverse myelitis, carry risk of DO and DESD; they remain unknown-risk until UDS, upper tract imaging, and renal function assessment clarify findings. These examinations identify such concerns as hydronephrosis, renal scarring, poor compliance, DO, and DESD. Table 3 displays the risk categories and assigns a patient to the highest category met.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWO
document_sections.content: Every patient with NLUTD should initially receive a detailed history, physical examination, and UA (Clinical Principle). Neurological disease does not reliably predict all urinary findings; cognitive, sensory, or motor impairments can complicate assessment and justify additional testing. History should characterize neurological onset, severity, progression, recovery potential, disability, and shunt status; bladder-emptying method; LUTS and incontinence; catheter characteristics; sexual, reproductive, and bowel function; skin condition; AD and its triggers; previous renal studies and urinary or related treatment, effectiveness, and complications; stones and UTIs; mobility, hand function, support, treatment goals, coexisting GU disease, other medical or surgical history, medications, allergies including latex, and smoking, alcohol, or other drug use. Examination should assess cognition, mobility and arm function, abdomen and flanks, pelvic or genital structures, rectum and prostate when appropriate, skin, and directed neurological function, including relevant reflexes and pelvic floor or anal sphincter activity. Validated tools such as OAB-q or NBSS may document baseline symptoms and later change. UA can identify hematuria, pyuria, glucosuria, proteinuria, or other findings; interpretation depends on symptoms, underlying disease, and catheter use, and an abnormal dipstick may require microscopy. Initial findings determine whether imaging or multichannel UDS is needed.

document_sections.heading: Table 3: NLUTD Risk Stratification
document_sections.content: The table compares renal function, PVR in voiding patients, urinary tract imaging, and urodynamic findings across Low-Risk, Moderate-Risk, and High-Risk NLUTD. Patients enter the highest stratum for which they satisfy any listed criterion.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THREE
document_sections.content: Measure PVR initially in patients who void spontaneously (Clinical Principle). PVR is urine remaining after voiding; elevation can indicate DU, BOO, or both and, if persistent, may accompany LUTS, UTI, stones, or upper tract deterioration. A low result does not exclude a hazardous, poorly compliant low-capacity bladder, with or without VUR. No universal elevated-PVR threshold exists for NLUTD; greater than 300 cc has been suggested for non-neurogenic chronic retention but is not a defined NLUTD cutoff. A potentially consequential elevation generally merits multichannel UDS and treatment when indicated. Measurement options include a bladder scanner, real-time US, and urethral catheterization. Body habitus, previous surgery, ascites, pelvic cysts, and prolapse may reduce ultrasound accuracy; catheterization is most accurate but most invasive. Rapid diuresis or inability to void in the examination environment can falsely elevate a single result, so confirm suspected abnormal elevation at another visit. PVR may subsequently be checked periodically or after management changes; inability to void on demand can prevent a valid measurement.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FOUR
document_sections.content: A voiding or catheterization diary, pad test, and non-invasive uroflow are optional initial investigations (Expert Opinion), selected when they aid diagnosis, prognosis, or decisions. Diaries record voiding or catheterization times and volumes, leakage, and potentially intake and urgency; they may reveal polyuria, relevant fluid consumption, functional bladder volume, and treatment response. Patients unable to recall intake or output accurately should complete a diary. NLUTD-specific normative and effectiveness data are sparse. A non-neurogenic diary duration of 1-7 days has been suggested; one NLUTD study found 3-day records reliable for most measures. Shorter records of 1-3 days favor completion, whereas 4-7 days provide more information but impose greater burden; the International Consultation on Incontinence suggests at least 3 days for NLUTD. Pad testing can objectively confirm or quantify leakage, including short provocative or 24-hour protocols; qualitative dye testing can establish whether leakage is present. NLUTD-specific evidence about optimal pad testing is limited. Uroflow may reveal voiding-phase dysfunction only in spontaneous voiders. NLUTD has no established normal uroflow values; low flow cannot distinguish obstruction from DU, and normal flow does not rule out another important abnormality.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIVE
document_sections.content: Do not routinely obtain initial upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, or multichannel UDS for low-risk NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Four observational studies supported the statement; their urodynamic evidence had very serious bias risk without further downgrading. A low-risk presentation typically combines a neurological diagnosis with little potential for serious GU complications, such as PD, CVA, dementia, or normal pressure hydrocephalus, with stable LUTS and no elevated PVR or UTI history. Suprapontine lesions commonly show DO, sometimes DU, but generally retain compliance, coordinated emptying, and low storage pressure; routine advanced testing is unlikely to yield actionable findings absent another concern. Elevated PVR, recurrent UTI, or unstable symptoms instead indicate unknown risk and require appropriate investigation. Reserve UDS when it could change diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment, including suspected additional obstruction.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT SIX
document_sections.content: Obtain upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, and multichannel UDS initially in unknown-risk NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies informed the recommendation and had very serious aggregate bias risk without other downgrading. Suprasacral spinal disease, stones, elevated PVR, recurrent UTI, or changing symptoms can prevent classification using history, examination, PVR, and UA alone. UDS assesses storage pressures, DLPP when relevant, and other abnormalities that can inform prognosis and treatment; neurological history and examination alone may not predict these results. No universally accepted abnormal-compliance cutoff exists, although less than 12.5 ml/cmH2O has been suggested. Sustained intravesical pressure exceeding 40 ml/cmH2O is associated with greater upper tract deterioration risk; the precise hazardous pressure is unclear. VUR, infection, and functional capacity also influence risk, making concurrent upper tract functional and imaging assessment necessary.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT SEVEN
document_sections.content: Following an acute neurological event causing NLUTD, defer risk stratification until neurological stabilization (Clinical Principle). Early brain or spinal findings may change over days, weeks, months, or up to 1-2 years, so evaluation timing should be discussed with the patient. Spinal shock can follow partial or complete SCI, producing absent reflex activity, flaccid paralysis, detrusor areflexia, and preserved sphincter tone. It commonly resolves in approximately 3-6 months but can persist for 1-2 years. Early UDS does not reliably predict later function and may be postponed. Acute brain injury can likewise cause transient detrusor areflexia, with different urodynamic findings weeks or months after recovery. Premature classification can therefore misrepresent long-term risk.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT EIGHT
document_sections.content: Do not perform cystoscopy routinely during initial NLUTD assessment (Clinical Principle). The diagnosis alone is not an indication for this invasive, potentially uncomfortable and morbid investigation. Initial cystoscopy can be appropriate for otherwise unexplained hematuria or pyuria, suspected urethral stricture or false passage, stones, or known or suspected bladder cancer. Without a specific indication, incidental findings such as trabeculation generally do not change diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment.

document_sections.heading: Autonomic Dysreflexia
document_sections.content: AD is an emergency primarily associated with SCI at T6 or above, although some individuals injured at T7 or T8 may also be susceptible. During urological procedures, bladder distension or other stimuli below the lesion may provoke sympathetic overactivity and hypertension, with headache, visual symptoms, flushing, sweating, nasal congestion, and reflex bradycardia. Bladder distension associated with retention, catheter obstruction, or procedures accounts for up to 85% of episodes; fecal impaction is another important trigger. Teams caring for susceptible patients should recognize AD and have treatment accessible.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT NINE
document_sections.content: Patients at risk of AD must be monitored hemodynamically during UDS or cystoscopy (Clinical Principle). Monitoring should be continuous, procedures should involve staff trained to recognize and manage AD, and pharmacological treatment should be readily available.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TEN
document_sections.content: If AD develops during UDS or cystoscopy, stop the procedure, drain the bladder immediately, and continue hemodynamic monitoring (Clinical Principle). Removal of the trigger and drainage are first-line measures, often followed by prompt improvement. Sit the patient upright, loosen restrictive clothing or devices, and check blood pressure at least every five minutes until baseline vital signs return. Consider medication if these measures do not improve hemodynamics.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT ELEVEN
document_sections.content: Start pharmacological management and/or escalate care when AD persists after bladder drainage (Clinical Principle). Persistent symptoms with systolic pressure greater than 150 mm Hg and/or 20 mm Hg above baseline indicate inadequate control. Topical 2% nitroglycerine paste, 1 to 2 inches applied above the spinal lesion, can lower pressure and be removed to reduce later hypotension. Immediate-release sublingual nifedipine, 10 mg capsules, is an alternative, but evidence from well-controlled AD-treatment trials is lacking and precipitous, less easily reversible hypotension requires caution. If treatment fails, a closely monitored setting and intravenous sodium nitroprusside may be appropriate. Terazosin has also been used; prazosin at 3 mg twice a day for 2 weeks has been reported to lessen AD episode severity and duration in cervical or high thoracic SCI.

document_sections.heading: Surveillance of the patient with NLUTD
document_sections.content: Surveillance intensity follows risk category, while new symptoms or complications may call for assessment outside scheduled visits.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWELVE
document_sections.content: Clinicians must explain which NLUTD signs and symptoms merit further assessment (Clinical Principle). Patients may have atypical manifestations between visits. Report new or worsening AD or UI, more frequent or febrile UTIs, flank pain, hematuria even during catheterization, and new catheter-passage difficulty. These findings may signal worsening bladder function, stones, upper tract changes, malignancy, or urethral stricture; investigations depend on clinical context and risk. Gross hematuria was reported as the presenting symptom in 32% of bladder cancer cases among patients with NLUTD. In one comparison, significant US findings requiring intervention occurred in 20 of 21 symptomatic SCI patients; among 87 asymptomatic patients receiving surveillance US, 63 examinations were normal and 24 showed insignificant findings not requiring intervention. Coordination with rehabilitation providers can help identify relevant changes.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTEEN
document_sections.content: For stable low-risk NLUTD, do not obtain surveillance upper tract imaging, renal function assessment, or multichannel UDS (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review and two observational studies informed this recommendation; observational urodynamic evidence had very serious bias risk. Low-risk patients typically have low-risk neurological disease, low PVR with spontaneous voiding, and no recurrent UTI or other urological complication. Routine advanced surveillance has little expected utility, but new symptoms or complications warrant reassessment. A post-stroke UDS study of 106 patients, comprising 84 incontinent and 22 continent patients, found no dangerous compliance, storage-pressure, or DSD findings. Appropriate low-risk patients may instead receive expectant follow-up through primary care, with education about indications for reassessment.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FOURTEEN
document_sections.content: Stable moderate-risk NLUTD warrants an annual focused history, examination, symptom assessment, and renal function assessment, with upper tract imaging every 1-2 years (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two systematic reviews and seven observational studies informed the statement; aggregate bias risk was very serious. This category includes patients requiring CIC or indwelling drainage, or with elevated PVR, but without dangerous UDS findings. Annual encounters can identify complications, catheter difficulties, and treatment response. Serum creatinine is convenient but may be misleadingly low with reduced muscle mass; a meaningful rise from baseline deserves assessment even within the normal range. A 24-hour creatinine clearance is more sensitive but burdensome; Cystatin C is less influenced by muscle mass, although cost limits use. Renal US every 1-2 years assesses asymptomatic stones and other findings; existing equivalent interval imaging may suffice. Reported recurrent renal stone rates in long-term SCI studies were 34-64%, and bladder stone recurrence reached 23%, supporting lifelong vigilance. Nuclear renal scanning is more useful for suspected obstruction or deteriorating function than as a substitute for US because it detects stones poorly. The optimal US frequency is uncertain. In one series, 48 SCI patients using CIC with initially safe UDS were followed for a mean of 6.8 years using annual US: 6% developed mild/moderate hydronephrosis and 13% renal calculi, without severe hydronephrosis or new scarring or thinning. Another US study included 1005 SCI patients, 313 with tetraplegia and 692 with paraplegia, examined a mean 32.5 +/- 49.2 months after injury: renal stones occurred in 6%, hydronephrosis in 5.5%, renal atrophy in 1.2%, and bladder trabeculation in 35.1%. Clinicians may extend imaging to every two years for reliably help-seeking patients stable over longer periods and should consider travel burden when arranging tests.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTEEN
document_sections.content: Stable high-risk NLUTD warrants annual focused history, examination, symptom and renal function assessment, annual upper tract imaging, and multichannel UDS with or without fluoroscopy, repeated when clinically indicated (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Three systematic reviews and two observational studies informed the statement, with very serious aggregate bias risk. High-risk features include poor compliance, VUR, elevated storage pressure, hydronephrosis, parenchymal loss, extensive stones, or unstable renal function. At least annual clinical assessment and imaging are needed because complications and silent deterioration may develop. A study of 116 SCI patients, mainly using reflex triggering or bladder expression, found moderate renal dysfunction in 58% and severe dysfunction in 29% after 45 years; upper tract dilatation and renal or ureteral stones requiring treatment were important risk factors. Repeat-UDS timing should be individualized: prior safe bladder measurements with controlled symptoms may lower its yield, whereas previously dangerous storage measurements or persistent symptoms increase its relevance. A review of 28 studies covering 1368 patients found insufficient evidence to establish UDS timing; the test may alter care despite absent symptoms but entails cost, travel, and risks including UTI, AD, and urethral complications. Following effective treatment and reassessment, a patient may move from high- to moderate-risk and should then follow the new category.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT SIXTEEN
document_sections.content: Reassess and repeat risk stratification when a low-risk patient develops new urinary signs or symptoms, AD, UTI, stones, or deterioration in upper tract findings or renal function (Clinical Principle). Low-risk status may have been assigned initially from benign clinical features or after reassuring imaging, renal assessment, and UDS in a formerly unknown-risk patient. It does not imply zero future risk. New problems may reflect NLUTD or unrelated disease such as BPH or SUI; subsequent follow-up should match any revised risk category.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT SEVENTEEN
document_sections.content: Multichannel UDS may be performed for moderate- or high-risk patients whose symptoms change, complications arise, or upper tract or renal function worsens (Clinical Principle). Evidence for routine testing during stability is mixed, whereas indication-driven UDS often identifies reduced compliance, raised storage pressure, VUR, or worsening DO that changes bladder management or risk category.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT EIGHTEEN
document_sections.content: Perform cystoscopy for NLUTD accompanied by hematuria, recurrent UTI, or suspected anatomical abnormality such as a stricture or false passage (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). A systematic review supporting the statement had serious bias risk. Painless visible hematuria also requires upper tract imaging, such as CT urogram or renal US. A review of 15 studies involving 103,397 SCI patients associated visible hematuria with bladder cancer; SCI-associated cancer risk is particularly notable after 20 years of disease, and indwelling catheter use carries higher squamous cell carcinoma risk than CIC. Catheter irritation cannot be assumed to explain bleeding without evaluation. Cystoscopy can detect calculi, benign lesions, strictures, false passages, foreign bodies, or diverticula. Difficult catheter passage may also call for technique or catheter changes; a retrograde urethrogram can diagnose a strongly suspected male urethral stricture.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT NINETEEN
document_sections.content: Do not perform screening or surveillance cystoscopy solely for NLUTD (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). Evidence shared with STATEMENT TWENTY comprises two systematic reviews and four observational studies with serious bias risk. Although SCI increases bladder cancer risk, the reported overall risk is 0.3%, including catheter users. Screening cystoscopy and cytology have performed poorly; in studies screening 614 patients, predominantly long-term catheter users, only one cancer was found, while benign lesions prompted biopsies and further investigations. Advanced symptomatic cancers have also arisen between annual examinations. Benefit in reducing morbidity or mortality has not been established; this is not a claim that benefit was disproven. In a review of 15 studies involving 332 patients with bladder cancer, gross hematuria was the presenting symptom in 31.6%. In 92 patients assessed by routine cystoscopy at least ten years after augmentation, screening identified no tumor; the sole malignancy was diagnosed after subsequent visible hematuria. A prior non-muscle invasive bladder cancer remains an exception: surveillance follows its pathological risk category irrespective of NLUTD.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY
document_sections.content: Do not perform screening or surveillance cystoscopy solely because a patient with NLUTD has a chronic indwelling catheter (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). The evidence and rationale are shared with STATEMENT NINETEEN: catheter-associated cancer concerns do not establish that routine cystoscopy improves outcomes, and investigation of incidental inflammatory lesions can cause harm. Clinically indicated cystoscopy and surveillance for a separate history of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer are distinct from routine NLUTD screening.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-ONE
document_sections.content: Periodically examine an indwelling catheter and its urethral or suprapubic entry site in NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Three observational studies informed this statement; evidence had very serious bias risk and was downgraded for indirectness. Urethral catheters can cause erosion, pressure necrosis, penile injury, or progressive female urethral and bladder-outlet dilation. Reduced sensation, impaired cognition, larger catheters, and prolonged sitting increase vulnerability; urethral erosion has been reported in up to 23% of men with NLUTD using a urethral catheter. Proper fixation reduces but does not eliminate risk. Increasing catheter or balloon size to address leakage can worsen female urethral damage; the cause should instead be investigated. Regular examination allows early consideration of a suprapubic tube. Suprapubic catheters avoid urethral damage but may erode through the abdominal wall if poorly secured; peristomal granulation tissue can bleed or impede exchanges and may be treated with topical silver nitrate.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-TWO
document_sections.content: For indwelling-catheter users at risk of upper or lower tract calculi, including those with SCI, recurrent UTI, immobilization, or hypercalcuria, perform urinary tract imaging every 1-2 years (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Four observational studies informed the recommendation, with very serious bias risk and further indirectness. Catheters can promote bacteriuria, infection, biofilm, and crystal formation; encrustation remaining after exchanges may seed stones. Bladder stone prevalence reported in catheter users ranges from 8% to 41%, and upper tract stones occur in 6-32%. Stones may grow without symptoms in patients with altered sensation or no spontaneous voiding. Renal and bladder US can assess both sites; cystoscopy does not evaluate the upper tract and KUB is less sensitive for bladder stones than US. Every patient with an indwelling catheter also requires surveillance appropriate to their moderate- or high-risk category.

document_sections.heading: Urinary Tract Infection
document_sections.content: This section addresses urine testing, asymptomatic bacteriuria, diagnosis and evaluation of UTI, and prevention of recurrent infection in patients with NLUTD.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-THREE
document_sections.content: Do not obtain screening or surveillance urine tests, including cultures, in asymptomatic NLUTD patients (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Three observational studies informed this statement; their aggregate risk of bias was very serious, without further downgrading. In the study by Tornic et al., 317 asymptomatic patients had cultures immediately before UDS: 61% had bacterial growth, but 18% developed symptomatic UTI over one year, and overall symptomatic UTI incidence was less than one per year. Bacterial colonization therefore did not commonly progress to symptomatic infection. Avoiding routine cultures also reduces unnecessary antibiotic exposure and the selection of resistant organisms. The IDSA 2019 guidance strongly advises against screening asymptomatic people with SCI or long-term indwelling catheters.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-FOUR
document_sections.content: Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Four observational studies supported this statement, with very serious risk of bias and no additional limitations. Unnecessary antibiotics contribute to resistance. In catheter-free SCI patients, bacteriuria recurs early after treatment and involves more resistant strains; among SCI patients using intermittent catheterization, treatment does not change subsequent asymptomatic bacteriuria or UTI rates. Exceptions are pregnancy and procedures expected to disrupt the urothelium or manipulate the upper tract. Preoperative treatment in a heavily contaminated field aims to prevent postoperative sepsis or UTI; perioperative antimicrobial treatment or prophylaxis is best practice for contaminated or clean-contaminated procedures. IDSA 2019 suggests obtaining a culture before endoscopic urologic procedures and giving a targeted short course rather than empirical treatment. A SUFU policy recommends a single oral dose of trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole for NLUTD patients undergoing UDS.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-FIVE
document_sections.content: Obtain UA and urine culture when signs or symptoms suggest UTI in NLUTD (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Five observational studies informed the recommendation; risk of bias was very serious, and evidence about symptom-based prediction was further downgraded for inconsistency. Altered sensation, neurological diagnosis and severity, and bladder-management method can change the presentation. Possible findings include fever, new incontinence or catheter leakage, increased spasticity, malaise, lethargy, cloudy or malodorous urine, back or bladder pain, dysuria, and AD; MS patients may also show apparent relapse. No symptom set alone has adequate sensitivity and specificity across NLUTD. Culture supports organism-directed treatment. In Linsenmayer and Oakley's series of 147 consecutive SCI patients (101 male; 106 at T6 or higher), UTI required new clinical findings, >104 CFU/mL and >10 WBC/hpf. Symptoms predicted UTI in 61% (n=90), but not in 39% (n=57); bladder-management method did not affect this ability. In Massa et al.'s study of 51 SCI patients (34 male, 26 at T6 or higher), negative self-assessment had a predictive value of 82.8%, compared with 32.6% for positive or uncertain self-assessment. Urinary leukocytes had sensitivity of 82.8% and negative predictive value of 93.8%; cloudy urine had positive predictive value of 61.3% and sensitivity of 65.5%. Fever and AD had specificity of 99% but sensitivity of 6.9% and 0%, respectively. Alavinia et al. found the greatest sensitivity with malodorous urine and the greatest specificity with new incontinence; cloudy urine had positive predictive value of 71%, rising to 78% when accompanied by malodor. Applicability of that study of 55 subacute inpatients with SCI to all NLUTD patients is uncertain. Ronco et al. examined 381 symptomatic episodes in 209 men with SCI and 277 asymptomatic episodes in 205 men. No individual finding established UTI. Among symptomatic episodes, cloudy and/or malodorous urine occurred in 51.4%, new UI in 51.2%, fatigue in 41.7%, and fever in 30.7%. Those findings did not correlate with higher colony counts or urinary WBC when symptomatic and asymptomatic episodes were compared; the authors speculated that fever could have other infectious causes. AD and other nonspecific symptoms also have non-UTI causes. An earlier consensus used >102 CFU/mL for CIC and >104 CFU/mL for condom catheters. IDSA 2010 CAUTI criteria require compatible symptoms, no other identified infectious source, and >103 CFU/mL; IDSA does not use pyuria alone to decide antibiotic treatment, while absent pyuria should prompt consideration of another cause. In one rehabilitation-center review of 93 SCI patients, multidrug resistance affected 48% of strains from asymptomatic bacteriuria and 66.6% from symptomatic UTI. Weekly cultures in 52 SCI patients changed in an average of 60% of those with indwelling catheters and 36% using CIC. Clark and Welk found 55.8% organism concordance among 81 patients with at least two positive cultures; concordance fell significantly with each 30-day interval (p=0.02). Susceptibility concordance was ciprofloxacin: 77.3%; nitrofurantoin: 78.5%; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: 75% and did not decline with time. Previous cultures can inform empirical selection while a new UA and culture are pending.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-SIX
document_sections.content: Order upper tract imaging for febrile UTI in NLUTD if antibiotic treatment does not produce an appropriate response, or if a moderate- or high-risk patient is overdue for routine upper tract imaging, irrespective of treatment response (Clinical Principle). Fever warrants particular concern because altered sensation may conceal flank or abdominal pain and structural or functional abnormalities can make infection complicated. Persistent fever despite appropriate treatment may indicate hydronephrosis, pyonephrosis, renal abscess, or stones. Obtain UA and culture and give appropriately selected, culture-specific antibiotics; when suspicion is high, begin empirical treatment and adjust it if culture requires. A recent culture may guide the initial choice. US or CT can evaluate nonresponders for upper tract abnormalities. Imaging remains due every one to two years for moderate-risk patients and annually for high-risk patients, even when antibiotics work.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-SEVEN
document_sections.content: When UTI is suspected in an NLUTD patient with an indwelling catheter, change the catheter, plug it until urine accumulates, and then collect a culture specimen; do not sample extension tubing or the collection bag (Clinical Principle). Biofilm on an older catheter can distort culture findings. IDSA guidance supports culture from a newly inserted catheter rather than a drainage bag, although much of the supporting research involved older chronically catheterized patients rather than NLUTD specifically. Bergqvist et al. examined 50 paired specimens from 43 men: 13 men (26%) had used a catheter for ten days or less, 13 men (26%) for 11-30 days, and 24 men (48%) for > 30 days. Fourteen paired specimens were negative by both methods, whereas bacteriuria results disagreed in 12 of 36 specimens. Their suggested suprapubic aspiration is not this Panel's recommendation. Grahn et al. studied 20 nursing-home residents (n=2 male, n=18 female) catheterized for >6 months, comparing an unchanged catheter of at least 30 days with a new catheter clamped for 30 minutes. Isolates differed for 22 of 41 strains in 17 of 20 patients. Counts <105 CFU/mL occurred in 7 of 45 old-catheter strains and 16 of 45 bladder strains (p<0.05); the old-catheter count exceeded the corresponding bladder count at least tenfold on 17 occasions. At the >105 CFU/mL threshold, old-catheter samples had sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 43%. Tenney et al. compared paired samples from 62 women (>60 years): 12 had used a catheter for 1-3 months, 26 for 4-12 months, and 24 for >one year. Older catheters yielded 246 versus 157 bacterial species (p<0.001) and a tenfold higher mean bacterial concentration (p<0.001). Total duration of catheter-based management did not affect results, but an individual catheter left for >3 weeks was more likely to yield >105 bacteria (p<0.05).

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-EIGHT
document_sections.content: Evaluate both upper and lower urinary tracts with imaging and cystoscopy when NLUTD patients experience recurrent UTIs (Clinical Principle). Imaging assesses the upper tract; initial contrast studies are unnecessary, and the risks of diagnostic ureteroscopy outweigh its benefit here. Cystoscopy is needed to inspect the lower tract. A separate guideline defines recurrent uncomplicated UTI in women as two acute bacterial cystitis episodes within six months or three within one year, but no clear NLUTD-specific definition exists. The Panel intentionally leaves that determination to clinical judgment.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT TWENTY-NINE
document_sections.content: If upper- and lower-tract assessment is unrevealing in NLUTD with recurrent UTI, clinicians may undertake UDS (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Supporting studies had very serious risk of bias and additional indirectness. Estimated recurrent UTI frequency is 2.5 episodes of infection per patient per year. In Manack et al.'s review of 48,327 patients with >1 neurogenic bladder-specific diagnosis, 38.6% experienced UTI during one year: 36.4% lower and 2.2% upper tract. Proposed contributors include catheter management, altered flora or bladder defenses, ischemia, elevated PVR, VUR, and disturbed hydrokinetics; some functional abnormalities can be identified by UDS. Lapides proposed reduced bladder perfusion as a risk factor. In two studies after successful onabotulinumtoxinA injection, Gamé et al. reported symptomatic UTI decreasing from 1.75 to 0.2 during a 6-month period in 30 patients, and Wefer et al. reported prevalence declining from 68% to 28% in 213 patients. Improvement was also reported after sacral deafferentation and augmentation. UDS can identify elevated PVR and VUR, both implicated in UTI risk. A proposed effect of DSD on turbulent flow and urinary stasis remains theoretical. UDS may also clarify LUTS attributed to repeated infection when testing does not establish a true infection.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY
document_sections.content: Do not prescribe daily antibiotics to prevent UTI in NLUTD patients managing the bladder with an indwelling catheter (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). A systematic review of fifteen studies informed the statement and had serious risk of bias. Antibiotics may postpone or reduce bacteriuria and UTI in chronically catheterized patients, but resistance is a major concern. Morton et al. reviewed 15 studies of spinal cord dysfunction: eight acute SCI studies, defined as <90 days post-injury, and seven involving non-acute SCI, defined as >90 days post-injury, or other chronic spinal cord disorders. Most involved CIC, but some included indwelling catheters. Prophylaxis did not significantly reduce symptomatic infections and was associated with approximately a two-fold increase in resistant bacteria.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-ONE
document_sections.content: Do not use daily antibiotic prophylaxis for NLUTD patients using CIC who do not have recurrent UTI (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). Evidence comprised two systematic reviews, one RCT and two observational studies, with serious aggregate risk of bias and no other downgrading. Morton et al.'s review of 15 studies published between 1980 and 1995 found a statistically significant bacteriuria reduction in acute SCI (<90 days; p<0.5) and a result approaching significance in non-acute SCI (p=0.06), but no significant decrease in symptomatic UTI and an approximate 2-fold rise in bacterial resistance; most participants used CIC, although some had indwelling catheters. A 2012 review of three crossover trials and one parallel-group trial found conflicting UTI results; one trial found fewer infections in controls, another in prophylaxis recipients, and another found fewer afebrile but not febrile infections. Differences in populations, including pediatric participants, and UTI definitions limited conclusions; its authors found insufficient evidence to recommend the practice. Whether patients with recurrent UTI benefit is a separate question. In Fisher et al.'s study of 404 CIC users without NLUTD, once-daily prophylaxis for 12 months yielded 1.3 cases/person-year of symptomatic antibiotic-treated UTI versus 2.6 cases/person-year in controls (p<0.0001), but resistance was higher: nitrofurantoin, 24% versus 9% (p=.038); trimethoprim, 67% versus 33% (p=0.0003); and co-trimoxazole, 53% versus 24% (p=.002). Those findings illustrate the infection–resistance trade-off rather than establishing benefit for NLUTD without recurrent UTI.

document_sections.heading: Non-Surgical Treatment
document_sections.content: The following sections address pelvic floor treatment, oral and intravesical medication, bladder-emptying methods, prevention of recurrent UTI, and botulinum toxin therapy.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-TWO
document_sections.content: Clinicians may recommend pelvic floor muscle training to appropriately selected NLUTD patients, especially those with MS or CVA, to improve urinary symptoms and QoL (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Evidence included two systematic reviews, one RCT and one observational study; aggregate bias risk was serious, with further downgrading for inconsistent QoL results. Behavioral studies generally had ≤20 participants per group, nonstandardized interventions and varied populations. Exercise generally improved pelvic muscle strength and endurance, with possible LUTS and QoL benefit and minimal adverse effects; most evidence involved MS or CVA. In an MS observational study (n = 37), a 9-week program with EMG biofeedback significantly improved frequency, incontinence, a 24-hour pad test, QoL and endurance; effects persisted at 24 weeks. In a female post-CVA trial, control n=17 received gait training, stretching and urinary education, whereas n=18 additionally received pelvic floor training for 6 weeks; the exercise group had significantly better vaginal pressure, LUTS and QoL. In a male post-CVA trial, standard rehabilitation (n=15) was compared with rehabilitation plus pelvic floor training and bladder education (n=16) for 12 weeks. Muscle function, strength and QoL improved significantly more with training, while frequency and urgency-incontinence episodes improved similarly in both groups; muscle gains persisted for an additional six months. A comparable female trial contrasted standard rehabilitation (n=14) with added training and education (n=12) over 12 weeks: daytime frequency, 24-hour pad test, strength and endurance improved significantly more with intervention, but SF-36 and IIQ QoL scores were comparable. A post-CVA systematic voiding program (n=124) produced no between-group difference in incontinence at six- and 12-weeks compared with facilitator support (n=125). In an SB trial, three months of usual care (n=27) was compared with intensive education, bladder and behavioral measures, exercises, and catheter care (n=27); the active group improved significantly on AUASI, UDI6, IIQ7 and WFIS, with improvement in some QoL subscales. Two reviews found no definitive evidence favoring any individual pelvic floor intervention. A third concluded that behavioral therapy improved MS-related QoL and incontinence but inappropriately pooled dissimilar trials. Given the low associated risks, the Panel supports offering pelvic floor physiotherapy to suitable patients.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-THREE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may use antimuscarinics, beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists, or both to improve NLUTD bladder-storage measures (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Four systematic reviews, five RCTs and eight observational studies informed this statement; bias risk was serious and evidence was further downgraded for inconsistency and imprecision. Antimuscarinics generally increase MCC and voided or catheterized volume and reduce detrusor pressure; urgency and incontinence may improve. No individual drug has demonstrated superiority. Dry mouth is the commonest reported adverse effect at recommended doses. Evidence linking long-term anticholinergic use with cognitive impairment or dementia conflicts and has low certainty; discuss that possible risk and treatment benefit through shared decision-making. Agents less likely to cross the blood-brain barrier may suit selected patients. Alpha-blocker plus antimuscarinic combinations may improve symptoms with relatively minor AEs. Evidence for beta-3 agonists is emerging and less robust. Of 21 included studies, six used randomized or crossover designs; half of those trials probably had adequate statistical power, but most had high or unclear bias risk and relatively brief treatment. There is insufficient high-quality, condition-specific, long-term medication evidence. A review of 30 studies reported an antimuscarinic dose relationship and, for several agents, a 30-40% reduction in MDP with a 30-40% increase in MCC; higher flexible doses appeared more effective without reduced tolerability. It found more dry mouth with oxybutynin IR than with trospium, tolterodine or propiverine, and generally more AEs with drug combinations. Its limitations included short follow-up, small studies and limited continence and QoL assessment. A randomized-trial meta-analysis found versus placebo improved MCC (WMD = 49.49 ml; 95% CI: 15.38-84.2; p<0.05), RV (WMD = 49.92 ml; 95% CI: 20.0-79.8 ml; p<0.05), patient-reported improvement or cure (RR=2.8; 95% CI: 1.64 – 4.8, p<0.05), and MDP (WMD = 38.30; 95% CI -53.17 to -23.43; p<0.05). It found no drug superior to another; dry mouth was more frequent (RR = 4.23; 95% CI: 1.85-9.67, p<0.05), while other AE rates were similar. Another review found standardized assessment tools were seldom used and called for standardized UDS, terminology, diaries and validated SCI symptom measures. The Panel regards concomitant beta-3 agonist and antimuscarinic treatment as reasonable after discussing benefits and risks, while noting that its review found no contemporary studies providing substantial direct safety and efficacy data for that combination.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-FOUR
document_sections.content: Clinicians may recommend alpha-blockers to improve voiding measures in spontaneously voiding NLUTD patients (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two RCTs and one observational study informed this recommendation. Bias risk was serious, with further downgrading for imprecision. Across studied causes, alpha-blockers may improve maximum flow and IPSS and reduce PVR; AEs were usually minor, except for the high discontinuation associated with phenoxybenzamine.

document_sections.heading: SCI patients
document_sections.content: In SCI, alpha-blockers can reduce PVR and MUP and increase MCC and voided volume, generally with minor AEs. Antimuscarinics can improve MCC, RV, voided volume and compliance while decreasing MDP, incontinence and 24-hour frequency, but may raise PVR. mirabegron may improve MCC and compliance and reduce detrusor pressure, 24-hour frequency and incontinence with few reported AEs.

document_sections.heading: Alpha-blockers
document_sections.content: A tamsulosin RCT assigned SCI patients to placebo (n = 92), 0.4 mg (n = 88) or 0.8 mg (n = 83) for one month; 134 of the original 263 completed a one-year open-label extension. Randomized-phase MUP changes were -12.2 and – 9.6 cm H20 with 0.4 and 0.8 mg versus -6.5 cm H2O with placebo; between-group differences were not statistically significant. Mean MUP change of -18.0 cm H20 differed significantly from baseline. Voided volume rose significantly by 28.2 ml with 0.8 mg. With 0.4 mg, incontinence frequency and pad use improved from baseline. Open-label QoL improved significantly, and 71% reported improvement: 44% slight and 27% substantial. Dizziness, abnormal ejaculation and fatigue were the most frequent AEs. Randomized-phase AE discontinuation was 4.4% with placebo versus 2.3 and 2.5% with active treatment; during extension it was 9.6%. The authors considered longer-term tamsulosin tolerable and beneficial for SCI bladder storage and emptying. Perkash administered terazosin up to 5 mg daily for approximately 10 days to 28 men with SCI: 50% reported better voiding, but UDS showed improvement in 42%; three stopped because of syncope, lethargy or rash. In another SCI study, 22 patients received 5 mg terazosin for one month. Mean pressure declined significantly by 36 cm H2O and MCC increased significantly by 125 mL. AD resolved in three of four affected patients; four reported complete continence. Ten continued treatment with maintained benefit at a mean of 7.75 months, while five withdrew because of AEs including syncope and peripheral edema.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: In an SCI DO trial, trospium 20 mg twice daily (n = 29) versus placebo (n = 32) for three weeks significantly increased MCC by 138.1 mL and compliance by 12.2 mL/cm H2O and reduced MDP by 37.8 cm H2O. Nausea, dry mouth and constipation were minor and reported more often with placebo, although AE reporting was unclear. In 35 SCI patients with NDO, solifenacin 10 mg for 13 months significantly increased capacity by 30 mL and RV by 62.5 mL, decreased MDP by 7.0 cm H2O, and improved compliance by 25.0 mL cm H2O; eight stopped for inadequate effect and two for intolerable AEs. In ten patients with NDO receiving controlled-release oxybutynin 10 mg to 30 mg daily for 3 months, everyone selected a final dose greater than 10 mg and four took 30 mg per day. MCC increased from 274 to 380 mL, 24-hour frequency fell from 12 to 8 voids, weekly incontinence from 13 to 6 episodes, and PVR increased significantly from 26 to 51 mL; no serious AE was reported.

document_sections.heading: Drug combinations
document_sections.content: A six-month trial in 21 SCI, 3 SB, 2 MS and 1 viral encephalomyelitis patients compared oxybutynin + trospium (n=8), oxybutynin + tolterodine (n=8), and tolterodine + trospium (n=11) after previous single-agent and double-dose failure. All three groups improved significantly and comparably in incontinence, capacity, RV and compliance. Two patients in different groups withdrew for intolerable dry mouth or blurred vision; five others reported similar mild-to-moderate effects. A one-month comparison of oxybutynin, trospium and their combination included 156 incontinent and 75 continent SCI patients. MCC rose and IDC fell significantly, but most patients did not become fully continent, and NDO remained poorly controlled in approximately one-third of initially continent patients. AEs were not assessed systematically; dry mouth occurred in 30 of 97 dual-treatment recipients.

document_sections.heading: Beta 3 adrenergic receptor agonist
document_sections.content: An observational study gave mirabegron to 15 SCI patients with NDO, beginning at 25 mg daily and increasing to 50 mg after two weeks, with 7 weeks of follow-up. Significant changes included 24-hour frequency from 8.1 to 6.4, incontinence episodes from 2.9 to 1.3, MCC from 365 to 419 mL, compliance from 28 to 54 mL/cm H2O, and storage detrusor pressure from 45.8 to 30 cm H2O. Few AEs were reported, including worse incontinence and constipation. Systematic reviews also reported clinical improvement with beta-3 adrenergic receptor agonists.

document_sections.heading: MS patients
document_sections.content: Antimuscarinics in MS may increase MCC and voided volume and reduce frequency, nocturia, incontinence, urgency episodes and urgency intensity; reported AEs are generally minor.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: Gajewski et al. compared oxybutynin 15 mg daily (n = 19) with propantheline 45 mg daily (n = 15) for seven weeks in MS. MCC rose by 144 mL versus 35 mL, respectively, with significantly greater improvement on oxybutynin. Frequency, nocturia, urgency and urgency incontinence improved significantly with oxybutynin; subjective improvement was 67% versus 36%. Most patients had mild-to-moderate AEs, and approximately one-quarter in each group withdrew for severe AEs. In another MS study, 30 patients received solifenacin 5 – 10 mg daily for two months. Frequency, daily pad use and urgency intensity decreased significantly, while voided volume increased; 20 continued treatment after completion and two withdrew for AEs.

document_sections.heading: Parkinson’s Disease patients
document_sections.content: In PD, solifenacin was associated with less 24-hour frequency, nocturia and incontinence, with minor AEs; doxazosin improved maximum flow and self-reported urinary symptoms, with mild AEs.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: An RCT assigned PD patients to placebo (n=13) or solifenacin 5-10 mg daily (n=10) for three months, followed by an eight-week active-treatment extension. Frequency over 24 hours improved significantly during randomized solifenacin treatment but not with placebo; incontinence and nocturia declined significantly during extension. AEs affected a minority and were mild.

document_sections.heading: Alpha blockers
document_sections.content: In a three-month observational PD study, 33 patients received doxazosin ER 4 mg daily. Maximum flow improved significantly from 9.3 to 11.2 mL/sec, as did QoL. Transient mild dizziness was most common and caused one discontinuation. Patients scoring <70 on the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale were more likely to improve clinically.

document_sections.heading: Patients with various causes of NLUTD
document_sections.content: Across different NLUTD causes, antimuscarinics can improve MCC, RV and catheterized volume and reduce MDP, leak point pressure, incontinence, frequency and nocturia; fewer urgency episodes and better QoL were also reported, generally with minor AEs. Alpha blockers may raise maximum flow, lower PVR and improve IPSS, although phenoxybenzamine had discontinuation of 25%.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: The SONIC randomized trial followed SCI or MS patients for one month on placebo (n = 44), oxybutynin IR 15 mg daily (n = 47), solifenacin 5 mg daily (n =50), or solifenacin 10 mg daily (n = 53). MCC increased significantly with every active regimen versus placebo, most with oxybutynin IR (165.4 mL) and solifenacin 10 mg (134.2 mL). All active groups also improved RV, MDP, DLPP and incontinence episodes significantly; several QoL measures favored solifenacin. Dry mouth and UTI were the commonest mild AEs, and three patients stopped because of side effects. A two-week crossover trial of 14 patients found tolterodine 4 mg daily increased catheterized volume and reduced incontinence significantly versus placebo. During an open-label phase allowing tolterodine 4-12 mg or oxybutynin 10-15 mg, efficacy was similar; dry mouth was worse with generally higher selected oxybutynin doses, while tolterodine 4 mg and placebo produced similar severity. An observational study of tolterodine extended-release 4 mg daily in 39 patients for three months found significant improvements in first-sensation capacity, compliance, MCC, RV, 24-hour frequency, urgency, incontinence and voided volume. Mild AEs, including dry mouth or constipation, occurred in 9%.

document_sections.heading: Alpha blockers
document_sections.content: An observational study administered phenoxybenzamine 15 to 30 mg daily to 43 patients. Fewer than half remained on treatment at six months. PVR generally decreased among the 21 continuing patients. One-quarter discontinued because of AEs such as severe orthostatic hypotension or tachycardia; six developed incontinence, and all male patients experienced ejaculatory failure.

document_sections.heading: Intravesical administration of oxybutynin
document_sections.content: Small but reasonably followed studies suggest chronic intravesical oxybutynin improves capacity and compliance, lowers MDP and incontinence, and may cause fewer systemic AEs than oral administration. In 25 SCI patients refractory to oral therapy, adding intravesical oxybutynin 15 mg three times daily to oral oxybutynin 5 mg four times daily, reduced if necessary, increased capacity significantly from 349 mL to 420 mL and decreased MDP from 54 to 26.5 cm H20 at six months. Patients with MDP <40 cm H20 increased from four to 21. AD resolved in three of five affected patients and incontinence improved in 11 of 15; UTI and dry mouth were most common, without AE-related withdrawal. In an 18-person SCI study using sequential one-day instillations of oxybutynin, propantheline and capsaicin without washout, oxybutynin produced no significant objective or subjective change; dry mouth and thirst were most frequent. Its one-day exposure limits usefulness. A randomized one-month comparison across varied NLUTD causes assigned 17 patients to oral oxybutynin 5 mg three times daily and 18 to intravesical 0.1% solution three times daily. MCC rose significantly by 18.1 mL orally versus 116.6 mL intravesically; other urodynamic and continence improvements were similar. AEs occurred in 82.4% versus 55.6%, respectively, with significantly fewer visual, gastrointestinal, nervous-system and skin events intravesically; 15 of 18 continued intravesical therapy with maintained efficacy for one year. In another mixed-cause study of 14 patients, intravesical oxybutynin 5 mg three times daily for nine months increased MCC significantly from 132 to 284 mL and compliance from 2.0 to 5.5; mean daily catheterizations fell from 16 to eight, incontinence resolved in 80% of affected patients, and no AEs were reported. No relevant systematic review of intravesical oxybutynin was found; other intravesical agents were not included. The Panel advocates this route for selected patients already performing CIC.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-FIVE
document_sections.content: Recommend intermittent rather than indwelling catheterization for bladder emptying in NLUTD (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Evidence included four systematic reviews, three RCTs and 33 observational studies; aggregate bias risk was serious and evidence was downgraded for inconsistency, with confounding also noted. Despite small samples, inconsistent outcome definitions, incomplete follow-up and disproportionate SCI data, the Panel favors intermittent catheterization because of the risks and complications of indwelling devices, while recognizing that intermittent catheterization is sometimes infeasible. Hydrophilic catheters may reduce UTI and urethral trauma, particularly in SCI. Across catheter methods, UTI appears to favor CIC, especially during longer follow-up, although definitions and follow-up differ. Suprapubic catheters generally have more bladder stones than CIC or urethral indwelling catheters. QoL tends to be best with self-catheterization and worst with indwelling devices or caregiver-dependent intermittent catheterization; some patients nevertheless prefer an indwelling device or surgery.

document_sections.heading: Hydrophilic and non-hydrophilic catheters.
document_sections.content: A 2007 review of four parallel trials could not pool symptomatic UTI findings because of differences in catheter types, clean versus sterile technique, reuse and UTI definition; wide confidence intervals crossed no difference and prior recurrent-UTI status was unspecified. A 2017 review found nine studies and pooled six RCTs. Versus single-use catheters, four pooled studies favored hydrophilic models (RR=0.84; 95% CI: 0.75-0.94; p=0.003). Versus single- or multiple-use catheters, six studies also favored them (RR=0.84; 95% CI: 0.750.94; p=0.003). Variable UTI definitions, substantial dropout and unspecified prior recurrence limited interpretation. In a six-month traumatic SCI trial beginning less than three months after injury, hydrophilic (n=108) versus uncoated (n=116) catheters delayed UTI and the first symptomatic infection requiring antibiotics significantly; dropout was 58% and 40%, respectively, following changes in management. In a 12-month RCT, hydrophilic (n=31) versus uncoated (n=31) catheters produced less hematuria and UTI, though groups differed at baseline. A retrospective follow-up four years after SCI rehabilitation found CIC users declining from 104 at discharge to 60, of whom 28 used hydrophilic and 32 uncoated devices. UTI frequency was not significantly different (p=0.499); raw rates were unavailable and most patients had no culture.

document_sections.heading: Clean versus sterile technique.
document_sections.content: Moore et al. randomized recently injured patients with tetraplegia to clean (n = 16) or sterile (n = 20) intermittent catheterization for six weeks. Symptomatic UTI occurred in 37% versus 45%, respectively. The authors concluded that the less costly and less time-consuming clean method did not increase UTI risk.

document_sections.heading: Time-dependent versus volume dependent intermittent catheterization
document_sections.content: Polliack et al. randomized patients to time-dependent (n = 11) or portable-ultrasound-guided volume-dependent (n = 13) catheterization for approximately three weeks. The volume-guided group catheterized significantly fewer times daily and had no UTI, versus three affected patients in the timed group.

document_sections.heading: Catheter length
document_sections.content: Preferred catheter length depended on gender, without clear clinical outcome differences. Patients rated compact models better for disposal, discretion, insertion, storage, transport and control.

document_sections.heading: Pre-lubricated vs. patient-applied lubrication
document_sections.content: In a seven-week comparison involving 18 patients, UTI occurred in 22.2% with patient-applied lubrication versus 7.4% with pre-lubrication; asymptomatic bacteriuria was 33.3% versus 14.8%, and mean urethral cell counts were 15.1 versus 6.3. Patients found pre-lubricated devices easier to handle, insert and remove, and more comfortable.

document_sections.heading: Intermittent versus indwelling catheter
document_sections.content: Turi et al. randomized patients to CIC (n = 40) or an indwelling urethral catheter (n = 40), without a stated follow-up duration. Pyelonephritis, epididymo-orchitis and urosepsis occurred in 5%, 2.5% and 0% with CIC, versus 25%, 7% and 5% with indwelling catheters.

document_sections.heading: Adverse events across catheter types
document_sections.content: Observational studies involved varied NLUTD causes, catheter methods, event definitions and follow-up, limiting reliable comparisons of specific devices. Even with these limitations, the Panel favored intermittent over any indwelling catheter.

document_sections.heading: Urinary tract infection
document_sections.content: Infection morbidity substantially influences bladder-management choices.
