Pooled proportions across intermittent, urethral indwelling and suprapubic catheterization favor CIC, particularly with longer follow-up, but inconsistent UTI definitions and widely varying early rates limit inference. A database study of n = 1104 with mean symptom duration of 20.3 years found bladder management, botulinum toxin injections and prophylaxis significantly predicted UTI. Annual symptomatic UTI and recurrent UTI were 83.3% and 50.0% with transurethral indwelling catheters, versus 29.6% and 9.9% with voluntary voiding; the associated odds were 10-fold and 4fold greater. Corresponding UTI and recurrence rates were 58.3% and 17.5% with suprapubic catheters, 70.5% and 31.2% with intermittent catheterization, and 61.5% and 24.8% with reflex voiding. Rates were 76.8% and 36.2% after botulinum toxin injections versus 59.0% and 23.0% without injections. With prophylaxis comprising antibiotics or other substances, rates were 72.2.% and 32.2%, versus 55.3% and 20.5% without it; these are observational associations.

document_sections.heading: Bladder calculi
document_sections.content: Combined data associate longer follow-up with more lower-tract stones through 10-12 years; evidence beyond that interval is too sparse for conclusions. Suprapubic catheter users generally have higher bladder-stone rates than intermittent or urethral indwelling catheter users. The association between upper-tract stones and follow-up duration is less clear.

document_sections.heading: QoL
document_sections.content: Across heterogeneous standardized and subjective assessments, spontaneous voiding usually produced the highest QoL scores, and intermittent catheterization was generally favored over indwelling methods. One large prospective analysis suggested that some patients prefer indwelling catheters or surgery to particular forms of intermittent catheterization. Dependence on another person to perform intermittent catheterization was consistently associated with dissatisfaction.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-SIX
document_sections.content: For suitably selected NLUTD patients requiring a chronic indwelling catheter, recommend suprapubic rather than urethral catheterization (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Four observational studies had very serious bias risk, with additional inconsistency and indirectness; small samples, variable follow-up and conflicting AE rates limit certainty. No systematic review specifically examined suprapubic catheter surgery. In 219 patients followed a mean of 50 months after insertion, 72% were satisfied and 89% preferred the device to their former urethral catheter. Intraoperative complications occurred in 10% (anesthesia 1.8%, bowel injury 2.3%, malposition 2.7%); 30-day complications occurred in 19% (UTI with sepsis 4.6%, site infection 3.65%, bleeding 1.82%, malfunction 2.28%). During follow-up, 43.5% needed intervention for an AE, including UTI in 21.1% and site infection in 15.4%. Image-guided placement in 585 patients and exchange in 439 yielded technical success of 99.6% and 92.3%, respectively; initial-placement clinical success for retention was 98.1%. Initial versus exchange AE rates were malposition 0.34% versus 0, minor bleeding 3.3% versus 1.8%, leakage 1.9% versus 1.1%, and pain 0.86% versus 0.68%. One initial-placement bowel injury required surgery (0.17% versus 0). A separate 29-patient series followed for 38.2 months found 90-day complications in 52%, including site infection 21%, urethral incontinence 17%, fistula 21%, UTI with sepsis 37%, and malfunction 24%. Subsequent intervention rates across studies ranged from 5.9% to 34%. In six women with complete catheter-related urethral destruction who received a suprapubic catheter and transvaginal bladder-neck closure, all were continent without upper-tract deterioration at 21 months. More extensive diversion may be preferable in principle but can be impracticable after prior abdominal surgery.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-SEVEN
document_sections.content: For NLUTD patients performing CIC who have recurrent UTI, clinicians may offer oral antimicrobial prophylaxis to lower UTI frequency after shared decision-making that addresses increased antibiotic-resistance risk (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review, two RCTs and three observational studies informed the statement; bias risk was serious and evidence was downgraded for inconsistency. Definitions of recurrence, culture thresholds and study protocols differed, and benefit evidence is limited. An older meta-analysis of 15 studies (7 acute and 8 non-acute phases) found no evidence supporting regular antimicrobials to reduce UTI. In acute injury within 90 days, predominantly nitrofurantoin and methenamine trials found significantly less bacteriuria, with a similar trend outside the acute phase; resistant isolates approximately doubled with antibiotics, but not with methenamine. Those trials predated the guideline review's literature cutoff. Two observational WOCA studies (n=38 and n=50), followed for 2 years, alternated single weekly antibiotics according to prior cultures: amoxicillin (3000 mg), cefixime (400 mg), fosfomycin-trometamol (6000 mg), nitrofurantoin (300 mg), or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (320–1600 mg). Symptomatic UTI/patient-year fell from 9.4 ± 5.34 to 1.84 ± 2.814 (p< 0.01) and from 9.45 ± 6.40 to 1.57 ± 2.12 (p<0.001), respectively. Febrile UTI/patient-year fell from 0.75 to 0.31 (p= 0.04) and from 5.25 ± 7.29 to 0.18 ± 0.66 (p<0.001). Hospitalizations and antibiotic-use days also declined without observed emergence of multidrug resistance. A United Kingdom open-label randomized trial included n=404 CIC users, of whom 39% had NLUTD (n=80 prophylaxis; n=79 no prophylaxis). Daily options were nitrofurantoin 50 mg, trimethoprim 100 mg or cephalexin 250 mg. During 12 months, symptomatic antibiotic-treated UTI incidence was 1.3 cases per person-year (95% CI 1.1–1.6) with prophylaxis versus 2.6 cases per person-year (2.3–2.9) without it: a 48% reduction (IRR=0.52; 95% CI 0.44–0.61; p<0.0001). Median episode counts were 1 (range 0-2) versus 2 (range 1–4). Culture-confirmed incidence was 0.74 cases per person-year (95% CI 0.58–0.94) versus 1.5 cases per person-year (1.3–1.8), a 51% reduction (IRR=0.49 (0.39–0.60). Resistance to each prophylactic antibiotic increased. A large database study also associated prophylaxis with more recurrent UTI, underscoring uncertainty and the need to weigh harms.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-EIGHT
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer bladder instillations to NLUTD patients using CIC who have recurrent UTI to lower infection frequency (Expert Opinion). Evidence is insufficient to establish any single instillation strategy because studies are few, heterogeneous and of limited quality. One irrigation RCT and one gentamicin observational study had very serious aggregate risk of bias.

document_sections.heading: Self-Intermittent Catheterization
document_sections.content: A retrospective before-and-after study of n=22 self-catheterizing NLUTD patients found that gentamicin instillation was followed by fewer symptomatic UTIs (median 4 versus 1 episodes; p<0.004), fewer UTI-treatment courses (median 3.5 versus 1; p<0.01), and less oral antibiotic use. The regimen placed 30–60 mL (14.4–28.8 mg) into the bladder after the final catheterization until the next one. Resistance did not rise during short follow-up and AEs were uncommon and self-limited. With no long-term data, resistance, adverse effects and optimal duration remain concerns. The procedure also takes time and commitment; individualized shared decision-making is encouraged.

document_sections.heading: Indwelling Urethral or Suprapubic Catheter
document_sections.content: Waites et al. randomized chronically catheterized NLUTD patients with asymptomatic bacteriuria to twice-daily irrigation for 8 weeks using saline (n = 30), 0.25% acetic acid (n = 30), or neomycin-polymyxin GU solution containing 40 mg/mL neomycin sulfate and 200,000 units/mL polymyxin B (n = 29). Each 30 mL instillation stayed in the bladder for 20 minutes. Bacterial burden, pyuria and inflammation did not differ significantly between groups.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT THIRTY-NINE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may explain to NLUTD patients with recurrent UTI using different catheter methods that cranberry extract has not been demonstrated to reduce UTI rates (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade B). The evidence base cited for the statement comprised two RCTs and one observational study with serious bias risk and no further downgrading. A wider review described five randomized trials, with n=37–305 and mostly 6 - 12 months of follow-up; all but one failed to show fewer UTIs despite differences in population, product and dose. In Gallien et al.'s MS trial, cranberry supplying 36 mg proanthocyanidins per day (n = 82) versus placebo (n = 89) for one year did not significantly alter time to first symptomatic UTI (Hazard Ratio = 0.99; 95% CI 0.5 to 1.60; p>0.05). CIC was used by 33.9%; at least one UTI occurred in 41.2% with cranberry and 40.0% with placebo, with mean counts among affected patients of 2.3 and 2.2, respectively. In an SCI trial, concentrated cranberry 2 g (n = 26) versus placebo (n = 22) for six months yielded symptomatic UTI in 38.5% versus 36.4%, without a significant difference. A four-arm SCI trial using cranberry 1600 mg, methenamine 2 g, their combination or placebo found no significant difference in six-month UTI-free survival, which ranged from 53.5% to 56%. In 37 SCI patients with indwelling catheters, 1200 mg cranberry versus placebo for one month did not significantly change bacterial or WBC counts. In a crossover SCI study of 57 patients, cranberry extract 1000 mg versus placebo for six months was associated with 7 versus 21 UTIs, 13% versus 34% experiencing at least one UTI, and annualized incidence of 0.3 versus 0.9. Its authors reported greatest benefit at glomerular filtration rate >75 ml/min, but no washout period and heterogeneous bladder methods limit this positive finding.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY
document_sections.content: Recommend onabotulinumtoxinA to NLUTD patients with SCI or MS whose condition is refractory to oral drugs, to improve bladder storage, decrease incontinence and improve QoL (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade A). Three systematic reviews, ten RCTs and three observational studies supported the statement, without serious bias or evidence downgrading. Placebo-controlled trials and reviews support both first and repeated intradetrusor injections for NDO. A single treatment improves MCC, MDP, UI and generally QoL; repeated treatment generally restores benefit without apparent efficacy loss. No efficacy difference was identified between 200 U and 300 U, although retention and initiation of CIC increase with dose. Common AEs include UTI and retention, sometimes requiring CIC in previously non-catheterizing patients.

document_sections.heading: Efficacy of Initial Injection
document_sections.content: Two meta-analyses pooled placebo-controlled SCI or SCI-and-MS trials, primarily using 200 U or 300 U onabotulinumtoxinA injected into the detrusor while sparing the trigone; UI frequency and MDP at first IDC fell, and MCC improved. Yuan et al. reported a reduction of -1.41 UI episodes (95% CI -1.70 to -1.12, p<0.05). Mean daily changes from baseline were -1.38 (95% CI: -1.83 to 0.94) with 200 U and -1.42 (95% CI: -1.81 to -1.04) with 300 U; dose-dependent difference was not apparent (p=0.974). Pooled MDP at first IDC decreased by 32.98 (95% CI: -37.33 to -28.62) versus placebo; subgroup changes were -32.71 cm H2O (95% CI: -39.32 to -26.10) with 200 U and -31.85 cm H2O (95% CI: -38.08 to -25.62) with 300 U. MCC increased versus placebo by 135.5 mL (95% CI: 118.2 to 152.8 mL; p<0.05); results by dose were 200U: 140.38; 95% CI: 114.43–166.34 and 300 U: 136.56; 95% CI: 110.91–162.21. Li et al.'s analysis of 17 SCI studies found versus placebo better UI episodes (MD: -12.45; 95% CI: -19.90 to -5.00; p=0.001), volume at IDC (MD: 163.42 mL; 95% CI: 96.41–230.43 ml; p<0.00001), and MCC (MD: 134.75 mL; 95% CI: 105.06–164.44 ml; p<0.00001). Its comparisons between 200 U and 300 U reported no significant clinical or urodynamic efficacy difference, including UI (MD: -1.27; 95% CI: -6.82 to 4.27; p=0.65), MCC (MD: -2.32 ml; 95% CI: -36.19 to 31.56 ml; p<0.89), absence of IDC (MD: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.53–1.12; p=0.18), PVR (MD: -79.85 ml; 95% CI: -120.41 to 39.29 ml; p=0.0001), and compliance (MD: 3.10 mL/cmH20; 95% CI: -7.47 to 13.67 ml/cmH20; p<0.57), as characterized by the document. In one RCT of non-catheterized MS patients given 100 U or placebo, week 6 UI change was −3.3 versus −1.1 episodes/day (p<0.001), and complete UI reduction occurred in 53.0% versus 10.3% (p < 0.001). Urgency changed by -4.3 versus -1.6 episodes/day (p< 0.001), micturition by -2.5 versus -0.8 episodes/day (p < 0.001), and voided volume by 27.8 versus 5.1 mL (p < 0.001). MCC rose by 127.2 mL (95% CI: 91.8 to 162.5 mL; p<0.001), and MDP at first IDC declined by – 19.6 cm H2O (95% CI: -35.1 to -4.0 cm H20). Increased capacity, better compliance and fewer IDC are relevant to protecting the upper tracts.

document_sections.heading: Efficacy of Initial Injection: Quality of Life Measures
document_sections.content: UI affects health-related QoL, while physiological endpoints do not necessarily capture patients' goals or satisfaction. Trials used I-QOL, modified OAB-PSTQ and PGA. Despite different instruments, all RCTs assessing patient-reported outcomes found significantly better QoL with onabotulinumtoxinA than placebo. In the DIGNITY trials, 200 U and 300 U improved these measures at weeks 6 and 12 without a clinically relevant difference between doses. Chartier-Kastler et al. found significantly more patients reaching or progressing toward their goals with either dose than with placebo; MS versus SCI did not alter overall goal attainment, and newly required CIC did not reduce treatment satisfaction. In non-catheterizing MS patients given 100 U, Tullman et al. found I-QOL improvement >3 times its minimally important difference at week 6, maintained through week 12 (p < 0.001, both time points).

document_sections.heading: Efficacy of Initial Injection: Adverse Events
document_sections.content: Balance clinical benefit against UTI, retention and possible new CIC. Yuan et al.'s six-RCT meta-analysis associated botulinum toxin A with UTI (OR = 1.68; 95% CI 1.20 to 2.35; p<0.05) and retention (OR = 6.80; 95% CI 3.46 to 13.35; p<0.05). Li et al. also found significantly more symptomatic UTI, retention, hematuria and AD with onabotulinumtoxinA than placebo. UTI definitions and bladder methods varied, but UTI was the most common AE in all RCTs, ranging from 21 – 70%. Among non-catheterizing MS patients, Tullman et al. reported UTI in 25.8% with treatment versus 6.4% with placebo and symptomatic UTI in 13.6% versus 1.3%. In that trial, retention led to CIC in 15.2% after 100 U versus 2.6% after placebo, for median durations of 64.0 and 2.0 days. In pooled DIGNITY MS data, initiation of CIC for retention was 31.4% with 200 U and 47.1% with 300 U versus 4.5% with placebo; nearly half continued for ≤ 36 weeks and the remainder for ≥ 36 weeks. Among patients newly requiring CIC, satisfaction remained high with 200 U but not with 300 U relative to those not requiring CIC. Post-treatment muscle weakness ranged from 0 – 13.4% with onabotulinumtoxinA and 0 – 14.29% with placebo, was generally transient and resolved without added treatment. Annualized MS exacerbation rates were 0.19, 0.36 and 0.20 in Cruz et al. and 0.22, 0.14 and 0.37 in Ginsberg et al. for placebo, 200 U and 300 U, respectively. Neurological AEs remain possible.

document_sections.heading: Efficacy of Repeated Injections
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis of 18 observational studies, mainly involving SCI and MS, assessed repeated toxin injections. onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U – 300 U was used in 13 studies, abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U – 1000 U in four, and both in one. Reported numbers of repeat injections and mean injection intervals ranged from 3 - 9 months and 8.3 14.9 months, respectively. Pooled MCC, RV and compliance increased and MDP decreased from baseline. First versus last injection results were not significantly different (Standard Mean Difference < 0.2): MCC 149.8 mL to 155.3 mL; MDP -23.5 and -26.8 cm H2O; RV 104.3 mL and 129.3 mL; compliance 18.2 and 18.4 mL/cm H2O. UTI, retention and hematuria predominated. Heterogeneous designs, agents and doses, selection bias and limited study quality constrain inference. Three RCTs followed repeated onabotulinumtoxinA for 12 months to 4 years and reported sustained clinical, UDS and QoL improvement. A DIGNITY extension of n=396 over 4 years reported six treatment cycles, with some patients receiving up to thirteen. Despite nearly 40% dropout, discontinuation for ineffectiveness was n=8; 2.0% and for AEs n=12; 3.0%. Daily UI reductions ranged -3.2 - -4.1 and voided-volume gains 133.2 – 156.1 mL. Treatment lasted <6 months in 22%, ≥ 6-12 months in 52% and >12 months in 26%; no new safety signal emerged.

document_sections.heading: Injection Location
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis of 2 small RCTs examined 55 SCI patients given onabotulinumtoxinA 300 U into detrusor versus submucosa. Both groups improved catheterization frequency, UI, catheterized volume, MCC, RV, filling MDP and compliance at 3 months. The document describes no significant between-group clinical or UDS difference, reporting UI episodes (MD: -1.21; 95% CI: -5.30 to 2.88; p=0.56), functional capacity (MD: -54.26; 95% CI: -81.91 to -26.61; p=0.0001), VFIDC (MD: -37.69; 95% CI: -83.60 to 8.22; p<0.00001), and Pdet (MD: -7.99; 95% CI: -21.98 to 6.00; p=0.26). The document's nonsignificance characterization conflicts with some reported p values. Small samples, short duration and unclear bias risk limit interpretation.

document_sections.heading: AbobotulinumtoxinA
document_sections.content:
Evidence for abobotulinumtoxinA remains limited by study quantity, quality and follow-up; preliminary outcomes resemble those of onabotulinumtoxinA, but larger, longer placebo-controlled multicenter trials with standardized populations, doses, injection methods and outcomes are needed. Two identified placebo-controlled RCTs had low bias risk. Ehren et al. randomized mixed-cause UI patients to placebo (n=14) or abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U (n=17), with 6-month follow-up: active treatment significantly improved UI, MCC, MDP and Qualiveen QoL, with no treatment-related AEs. Denys et al. randomized 47 patients to placebo or abobotulinumtoxinA 750 U through 15 or 30 detrusor injections and followed them for 3 months. Both active groups significantly improved daily UI, MCC, MDP and RV versus placebo without an efficacy difference by injection count. UTI was most common, with rates of 14.3% in placebo 15 injections, 57.1% in placebo 30 injections, 37.5% in abobotulinumtoxinA 15 injections, and 41.2% in abobotulinumtoxinA 30 injections. Muscle weakness in three SCI patients in the active 15-injection group resolved without intervention. Another RCT compared abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U and 750 U in a mixed population for one year. Continence was complete in 56.4% versus 73.7% (p=0.056), while other clinical and UDS improvements were similar. AEs occurred in 10.3% and included hematuria or fever, pyelonephritis, fatigue with vertigo, weakness, constipation and difficulty with CIC.

A trial comparing abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U with 750 U in a mixed neurogenic population found similar clinical and urodynamic improvement over one year. Complete continence occurred in 56.4% of the 500 U group and 73.7% of the 750 U group (p=0.056). Adverse events occurred in 10.3% and included hematuria with fever, pyelonephritis, fatigue with vertigo, muscle weakness, constipation, difficulty performing CIC, and fever. For NLUTD associated with SCI or MS and unresponsive to oral medication, evidence for onabotulinumtoxinA is Grade A. Intradetrusor treatment reduced UI, increased MCC, lowered MDP, and generally improved other clinical, UDS, and QoL measures compared with placebo. Efficacy did not differ between 200 U and 300 U, although retention and the need for CIC increased with dose. Repeated injections appeared to recover the initial benefit without an apparent decline in efficacy.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-ONE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer onabotulinumtoxinA to patients with NLUTD other than SCI or MS when oral medication has failed, with the aim of improving bladder storage, reducing incontinence, and improving QoL (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two RCTs and seven observational studies informed this statement; outcome evidence had very serious bias and was further limited by indirectness and imprecision. Evidence for efficacy and adverse events outside SCI and MS is Grade C because adequately powered, high-quality trials are lacking and observational studies have small samples and varying methods. In a placebo-controlled trial of abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U, patients without MS or SCI constituted only 16% (n=5/31); the treated mixed population improved in UI, MCC, MDP, and QoL, without reported adverse events over 6 months, but the small relevant subgroup limits applicability. In a one-year comparison of abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U and 750 U, the non-MS/non-SCI subgroup represented 12.9% (n=10/77). Complete continence in the overall groups was 56.4% and 73.7%, respectively (p=0.056), with similar clinical and UDS improvement. The review found no onabotulinumtoxinA RCT in a mixed non-MS/non-SCI population. Observational reports address single injections in these other conditions, but do not resolve the uncertainty about the balance of benefit and harm.

document_sections.heading: Parkinson’s Disease
document_sections.content: Evidence for botulinum toxin A in PD consists of small, uncontrolled, short, single-center observational studies. Symptom improvement is suggested, but concomitant BOO and detrusor dysfunction raise concern about retention after injection, particularly in older men. Knupfer et al. treated 10 patients (n=4 female, n=6 male; median age: 67.9 years) with intradetrusor onobotulinumtoxinA 200 U, including the trigone. At four months, frequency, pad use, and ICIQ-based QoL improved significantly. MCC changed from 196.2 ± 88.29 mL preoperatively to 332.6 ± 135.45 mL postoperatively; mean MDP changed from 57.9 ± 33.1 cm H2O to 18 ± 16.55 cm H2O. PVR rose nonsignificantly from 61.28 ± 75.91 mL to 77.0 ± 119.78 mL without CIC. Among the four reinjected patients, mean effect duration was 9.75 ± 4.85 months. Anderson et al. followed 20 patients (n=12 male, n=8 female; median age: 71.5 years) after office injections of onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U. At three months, questionnaires indicated moderate-to-marked relief; over six months, 59% reported a 50% decrease in incontinence relative to pretreatment (p<0.02). However, 25% did not complete the 6-month endpoint. Three men had significantly increased PVR at 1-month follow-up (mean: 310 mL); none needed CIC, and two received alpha-blocking agents. Giannantoni et al. studied onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U in 8 patients (n=1 male, n=7 female; mean age: 66 years) over six months. UI, daytime frequency, nocturia, QoL, and VAS improved; MCC increased significantly throughout follow-up and IDC disappeared in 37.5%. PVR increased at 1 month, then fell markedly at three and six months. Two women (25%) had PVR of 300 mL and required CIC twice daily, for one month in one case and caregiver-assisted CIC for three months in the other. Kulaksizoglu et al. followed 16 patients (n=10 female, n=6 male; mean age: 67.2 years) for 12 months after abobotulinumtoxinA 500 U. Frequency and UI improved at three and six months; functional capacity increased significantly at every assessment and peaked by 6 - 9 months. Patient QoL and caregiver burden improved significantly up to nine months; no adverse events were reported. In a study of onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U involving four PD and two MSA patients, daytime and nighttime frequency, UI, I-QOL, MCC, volume at first IDC, and maximum IDC pressure improved at one and three months. No systemic adverse events or UTIs occurred. Both MSA patients required daily CIC and already had elevated PVR and detrusor dysfunction before treatment, suggesting greater retention risk in this group.

document_sections.heading: Central Nervous System Lesions
document_sections.content: A retrospective comparison by Jiang et al. examined onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U in 40 people with mild CNS lesions—chronic CVA (n=23), PD (n= 9), or dementia (n=8)—and 160 OAB patients without CNS lesions. At three months, both groups had similar significant improvements in UI, urgency, urgency severity, and MCC. PVR did not differ between groups; PdetQmax and Qmax did not change in the CNS group, with no significant between-group difference. Straining to void was more frequent after CVA; other adverse events were similar. Retention rates were CVA 17.4%, PD 11.1%, dementia 0%, and OAB without CNS lesion 10%. People with advanced CNS disease and poor sensory awareness may be unsuitable for botulinum toxin because impaired bladder sensation could increase retention and UTI risk. Discuss retention and bladder-management options before treatment: some patients cannot perform CIC because of cognitive or physical impairment and may require a caregiver or temporary catheter.

document_sections.heading: Spinal Dyraphism in Adults
document_sections.content: Spinal Dyraphism (SD) is described as the most common congenital cause of neurogenic bladder; 90% present with NLUTD. Lesions tend to be incomplete, with variable manifestations, and evidence for botulinum toxin in adults is sparse. Peyronnet et al. reviewed 125 adults receiving 561 intradetrusor injections over 14 years: onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U, onabotulinumtoxinA 300 U, and abobotulinumtoxinA 750 U accounted for 34.7%, 49.2%, and 16.1%, respectively. Following the first injection, urgency and UI resolved in 62.3%, and UI resolved in 73.5%. MCC, MDP, and compliance improved significantly by 6 - 8 weeks. Female gender and older age predicted initial success, whereas poor compliance was associated with lower overall success. Adverse events occurred in 3.6% of cases: UTI 2.3%, muscle weakness 0.5%, pain 0.5%, and gross hematuria 0.2%; all were mild and transient.

document_sections.heading: Other NLUTD Conditions
document_sections.content: Beyond MS, SCI, PD, CVA, and SD, no other individual NLUTD condition was uniquely studied for botulinum toxin treatment of UI. Among more than 20 mixed-condition observational studies, only two had a non-MS/non-SCI subgroup exceeding 20% of the total. Peyronnet et al. examined 211 patients receiving onabotulinumtoxinA 200 U or 300 U, or abobotulinumtoxinA 750 U. Other NLUTD accounted for 15 patients (28.3%), 11 patients (12.7%), and 18 patients (23.1%) in the respective arms. UI improved across doses; matched analysis favored onabotulinumtoxinA 300 U over abobotulinumtoxinA 750 U for UI resolution in the overall groups (94.9% versus 76.9%; p=0.02). No separate analysis was performed for the diverse other-NLUTD subgroup. Stoehrer et al. reported seven years of experience with onabotulinumtoxinA 300 U or abobotulinumtoxinA 750U in 277 patients; other conditions made up 24.1% (n=67). Studied patients had significant improvement in MCC, MDP, RV, and compliance and sustained UI improvement. Adverse events were rare (2%); two temporary cases of generalized weakness with speech and swallowing difficulty resolved spontaneously.

document_sections.heading: Patients with an Augmentation Enterocystoplasty
document_sections.content: NDO can persist after augmentation enterocystoplasty, but evidence for botulinum toxin A in this setting is sparse. A multi-institutional retrospective study (n=21) reported subjective improvement in 86%, including less urgency, frequency, and leakage between catheterizations and larger catheterized volumes. Bladder dysfunction was idiopathic in 24%; other causes were heterogeneous. Subjective improvement after 200 U and 300 U was 85% and 87%, respectively, without standardization of dose or injection frequency. The retrospective ENTEROTOX study (n=33) examined NDO after AC: 58% met its effectiveness criterion of requesting reinjection, and mean MCC increased by 23% on post-injection UDS (333 +/- 145 mL versus 426 +/- 131 mL; p=.007). Etiology, toxin, dose, and injection sites varied. Both studies reported few adverse events. Small samples, retrospective methods, and failure to isolate NLUTD limit the evidence; prospective evaluation is needed. Evidence for onabotulinumtoxinA after oral-treatment failure remains Grade A in SCI and MS, but Grade C for other NLUTD causes, including PD, CVA, and SB; clinicians may offer it while recognizing that benefit–risk balance in those other conditions is unclear.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-TWO
document_sections.content: Before choosing botulinum toxin for a patient with NLUTD who voids spontaneously, clinicians must explain the specific retention risk and possible need for intermittent catheterization (Clinical Principle). Although onabotulinumtoxinA improves UI, storage measures, and QoL in SCI- and MS-related NDO, incomplete emptying or retention can require catheterization. Across single-injection RCTs, retention ranged from 2.6 – 54% with onabotulinumtoxinA and 1.9 – 5.0% with placebo. Yuan et al. reported OR = 6.80; 95% CI: 3.46 to 13.35; p<0.05. Li et al. reported retention of 20.49% (n=150) with onobotulinumtoxinA and 3.67% (n=15; p<0.00000) with placebo. Among initially non-catheterizing MS patients in DIGNITY, retention was 31.4% with 200 U, 47.1% with 300 U, and 4.5% with placebo; nearly half needed CIC for ≤ 36 weeks and the remainder for ≥ 36 weeks. New CIC use over treatment cycles 1-3 was 29.5%, 3.4%, and 6.0%; corresponding values reported for 300 U were 43.0, 15.0, and 4.8%. In Tullman et al., CIC for retention after 100 U was needed by 15.2%, versus 2.6% with placebo, for median durations of 64.0 and 2.0 days. Populations, toxins, doses, injection sites, retention definitions, and criteria for CIC varied across studies. Counsel patients that CIC, or possibly an indwelling catheter if CIC is infeasible, may be necessary for several weeks to months. Assess physical and cognitive ability, caregiver availability, training, supplies, and social and time demands through shared decision-making.

document_sections.heading: Surgical Treatment
document_sections.content: The following statements address operative and procedural options for NLUTD, their selection criteria, limitations, and required counseling.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-THREE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer sphincterotomy to appropriately selected men with NLUTD to aid emptying, but must explain the high likelihood of failure or later treatment or surgery (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Evidence comprised one systematic review and three observational studies with very serious bias. Oral anticholinergic treatment plus CIC is the primary approach described for SCI-related DSD; an irreversible external sphincterotomy can be considered when CIC is unacceptable or impossible, particularly with reflex voiding, feasible condom-catheter use, or poor hand function. It may improve emptying, reduce UTI, and preserve urinary tract function, but requires follow-up and possibly repeated procedures. The procedure uses endoscopic resection or laser incision at 12 o’clock. In Pan et al., 84 men with spinal injury underwent sphincterotomy for DSD (n=73), recurrent UTI (n=39), or upper-tract dilation (n=11); mean follow-up was 6.35 years. Failure occurred in 57 patients (68%, median time to failure 36 months); 30 underwent another procedure for DSD (n=18), recurrent UTI (n=10), or dilation (n=2). Thirteen required no further intervention, while 17 later failed after a mean successful period of 80.2 months. One procedure definitively controlled DSD in 32%. Reviews found generally unchanged MCC but improved PVR, MDP, end-filling pressure, and DLPP. In a placebo-controlled trial of transperineal onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U for DSD in 86 MS patients, PVR reduction did not differ statistically after one month, although treated patients had larger voided volumes and lower maximum voiding pressures. A small SCI study of 13 patients comparing onabotulinumtoxinA 100 U with lidocaine found a PVR reduction of more than 50% and less AD after onabotulinumtoxinA. Chemical sphincterotomy is not recommended routinely for DSD because its efficacy is limited over time. Monitor for recurrent UTI, AD, elevated DLPP, and residual urine. DLPP above 40 cm H20 has been associated with upper-tract damage. Possible longer-term problems include condom-catheter skin injury or loss of attachment, recurrent incontinence, further procedures, and postoperative bleeding that can require transfusion.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-FOUR
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer urethral bulking agents for NLUTD-associated SUI but must explain that benefit is modest and cure uncommon (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies had very serious bias and additional imprecision. Although minimally invasive and relatively low-risk, this treatment has limited NLUTD-specific evidence, low success rates, and poor long-term outcomes. Tabibian and Ginsberg reviewed 11 men (mean age 35 years) treated with transurethral collagen; all but one had SCI, and one had SB. Outcomes were available for nine: six received one injection, one received two, and two received three. Near-complete resolution occurred in two (22.2%), at least 50% improvement in two (22.2%), moderate improvement with continued pad use in two (22.2%), and no improvement in three (33.3%). Injection number did not appear to affect outcomes; no adverse events or attributable long-term complications were reported, but sample size and follow-up were limited. Hamid et al. studied PDS injections in 14 men with SCI-related SUI (mean age 41 years; mean injury duration 9.6 years). After mean follow-up of 37.5 months, 37.5% were dry by symptoms and UDS, 21.4% improved by at least 50% on pad use, and 42.8% did not improve despite possible repeat treatment. Whether agent selection or regular CIC changes NLUTD outcomes remains unclear; collagen is no longer available.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-FIVE
document_sections.content: Clinicians should offer slings to selected patients with NLUTD and SUI when bladder storage measures are acceptable (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review and one observational study informed the statement, with very serious bias. Consider slings particularly in patients who void independently. Before an outlet procedure, use UDS where relevant NLUTD could allow worsening compliance and harmful storage pressure; marked sphincter dysfunction may require temporary bladder-neck or urethral occlusion for adequate filling. Discuss subsequent emptying difficulty and potential progression of neurologic disease. If later CIC is foreseeable, the Panel advises against synthetic slings; an occlusive sling should instead use autologous fascia or another biologic graft. In a meta-analysis of 30 SUI-surgery studies, 15 examined slings (n=286 cases): autologous fascial slings n=177, sling wraps n=63, female synthetic slings n=20, and male synthetic slings n=26. Reported sling success and failure were 58% and 22%, but definitions of success were not consistently given. Post-hoc comparison found no statistical difference between sling and AUS success; both outperformed bulking agents. Conclusions are limited by publication dates of 1990 – 2013, no RCTs, and poorly defined outcomes. Shin et al. reported similar SUI success after midurethral sling in women with versus without neurologic disease (93.7% versus 95%; p=0.440), but more new OAB symptoms in the neurologic group (21.05% versus 5.26%; p<0.001). Individual assessment must account for SUI severity, neurologic impairment and progression, and effects on postoperative voiding.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-SIX
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer an artificial urinary sphincter to selected NLUTD patients with SUI and acceptable storage parameters (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Five observational studies had very serious bias and inconsistent results. AUS can improve SUI in men and women, but counsel about emptying dysfunction and potential CIC. Perform UDS before implantation when an outlet procedure might worsen compliance and threaten the upper tract; substantial sphincter dysfunction can require temporary outlet occlusion during assessment. Confirm sufficient hand function to operate the device. NLUTD implantation differs from treatment of post-prostatectomy incontinence because safe bladder pressures require confirmation. Across eight identified AUS studies, continence improved, but heterogeneous definitions, populations, concomitant surgery, and small observational samples prevent a uniform estimate. In 51 adult men with SB (n=16) or SCI (n=35), 60% were completely and 22% moderately continent after seven years. In another study involving 75 men and 15 women (mean age 26 years), 92% were fully continent after mean follow-up of four years; other reported ranges included up to 77.7% cured and 9.8% using one or more pads daily. Among 344 women receiving bladder-neck AUS, 54 had NLUTD; complete continence was 90.74% with NLUTD versus 84.78% without it (p=0.25). Across all women, non-mechanical complications included infection 4.8%, vaginal erosion 3.2%, urethral erosion 1.9%, labia-major erosion 1.9%, and bladder erosion 1.1%; mechanical complications fell to 8.8% after a surgical modification. NLUTD predicted shorter device survival, but complication rates by neurologic status were not reported. Patients needing CIC should understand the higher erosion or infection risk and potential revision or explantation. One series reported reoperation in 28% and intermittent catheterization in 78%; another reported that 43% of successful implants needed one revision. Bladder-neck cuff placement may reduce erosion during CIC but requires particular expertise; one series reported cuff erosion of 5.9% (3 of 51 patients). AUS in adult women should be uncommon and limited to selected circumstances; the Panel regards transvaginal cuff placement as a poor choice.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-SEVEN
document_sections.content: After detailed discussion of benefits, risks, and alternatives, clinicians may offer bladder neck closure with concurrent drainage to selected NLUTD patients with refractory SUI (Expert Opinion). BNC is irreversible and may be suitable after failed reconstruction or with severe urethral injury, stricture, or urethrocutaneous fistula. Reported continence is 75 – 100%, while fistula with recurrent leakage can develop in up to 25%. Plan for safe storage pressure, especially when adding a continent catheterizable stoma; perform UDS when outlet closure might impair compliance. Continuous drainage through an SPC changes this storage-pressure concern. Marked sphincter dysfunction can necessitate temporary outlet occlusion to assess filling, especially in moderate- or high-risk NLUTD. In women, chronic urethral catheterization commonly causes severe urethral injury; BNC can accompany an SPC, continent catheterizable stoma, or ileovesicostomy. Shpall and Ginsberg studied 21 men and 18 women, including 23 with SCI, 5 with cerebral palsy, 4 with MS, 4 with myelomeningocele, and 2 with spinal tumor. Indications included fistula, incompetent urethra, stricture, and pressure ulcer. Closure fistulas developed in 6 (15%); four required another operation (3 transabdominal, 1 transvaginal), one resolved with prolonged drainage, and one was not repaired. Colli and Lloyd reported BNC plus SPC in 35 patients (SCI 71%; MS 23%; CVA 9%): complication rate was 17%, including one vesicovaginal fistula. Men generally undergo a retropubic approach, while women may undergo retropubic or transvaginal closure. A series of 11 patients with catheter-related outlet devastation achieved initial transvaginal closure in 10 of 11. In 64 women, transvaginal versus retropubic success was 85.7% versus 81.5% (p=0.74), with shorter operating time and hospital stay transvaginally; another study found more fistulas with a transvaginal approach (p=0.01). Discuss loss of male fertility and assisted reproduction before BNC. A tight fascial bladder-neck sling can preserve emergency urethral access but is infeasible with extensive urethral tissue loss.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-EIGHT
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer posterior tibial nerve stimulation to selected NLUTD patients who void spontaneously and have urgency, frequency, or urgency incontinence (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two systematic reviews and two observational studies informed the statement; benefit evidence had serious bias and inconsistency, and overlapping MS studies could exaggerate estimated effects. PTNS is approved for non-neurogenic OAB; NLUTD evidence mainly concerns MS, PD, and CVA with storage symptoms and preserved voluntary voiding. A review of seven observational MS studies reported improvements in urgency, incontinence, first-sensation volume, bladder capacity, voided volume, PVR, frequency, and nocturia. Schedules ranged from single bilateral sessions to weekly 30-minute sessions for twelve weeks or daily 20-minute sessions for 12 weeks. Among daily-treatment patients (n=70), 83.3% reported improvements in warning time (p<0.001), urgency (p=0.023), and daily voiding (p<0.01). In a longer-term MS study, 83 received twelve weekly sessions and 74 entered maintenance; 9/74 (12%) needed treatment every 4 weeks, 18/74 (24%) every 3 weeks, 44/74 (60%) every 2 weeks, and 3/74 (4%) weekly. Willingness to sustain this frequency and reimbursement below four-week intervals remain uncertain. In another MS study, 34 received weekly treatment for 12 weeks; 29 responded with voiding-parameter improvement over 50%, and 21 completed one year of tapering treatment. These 21 had significant improvements at 6, 9, and 12 months in daytime frequency, nocturia, UI, urgency, and incontinence episodes (p<0.001). PD studies suggest improvements but have small samples, short follow-up, and high dropout. In a sham-controlled study of 13 PD patients, the active TTNS arm (n=8) received 30-minutes twice weekly for five weeks. Urgency fell from baseline at ten weeks (p=0.004), and nocturia fell after five weeks (p<0.01); several other apparent UDS improvements were not statistically significant. In men after CVA, PTNS improved urgency and frequency versus leg stretching but not urge incontinence; the schedule was two sessions per week for six weeks. Two TTNS trials after CVA reported improvements in frequency, nocturia, urgency, and urge incontinence but had short follow-up and inadequate blinding. An SCI study reported better CIC volumes and incontinence, but its medication comparator and surface electrodes limit application to percutaneous PTNS. A retrospective comparison found similar improvement in neurogenic and idiopathic OAB. Better-designed RCTs are needed.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FORTY-NINE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer sacral neuromodulation to selected NLUTD patients with urgency, frequency, or urgency incontinence (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review and two observational studies informed this recommendation; benefit evidence had serious bias and inconsistency. SNM has shown possible benefit in selected patients with MS, CVA, or PD, although its original approved indications concerned OAB, urge incontinence, nonobstructive retention, and fecal incontinence. Small MS series describe moderate improvements in frequency, incontinence, emptying, PVR, or voided volumes, with generally limited device-related adverse events. Older devices were incompatible with MRI; newer MRI-conditional devices with longer battery life may broaden use. Progression or relapse of MS can reduce benefit: Chaabane et al. reported efficacy loss after relapse in three of seven implanted patients. Mixed-neurologic observational cohorts suggest improvements in UI, urgency, MCC, voided volume, and frequency; infections and device malfunction sometimes required explantation. Zhang et al. pooled NLUTD from spinal injury, spinal malformation, pelvic surgery, diabetes, and PD: 107/182 (58.8%) proceeded to generator placement. At endpoint, frequency, urgency, nocturia, daily urine volume, leakage, and residual urine improved significantly from baseline. Among fully implanted patients, 14 adverse events (13.1%) comprised six symptom recurrences, five implant-site infections, two system disconnections, and one subjective noncooperation. Pooled reporting prevents disease-specific conclusions.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY
document_sections.content: Clinicians should not offer sacral neuromodulation to NLUTD patients with SCI or SB (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies informed the statement and had very serious bias. The Panel cites marked variation in bladder dysfunction and disease course. Studies have described improvement in incontinence, recurrent infection, upper-tract protection, voided volumes in incomplete SCI with retention, and storage outcomes in OAB, but clinical circumstances varied and revisions or additional procedures were needed. Reported adverse events include operative-site infection, generator-site pain, bothersome leg sensations, and loss of efficacy.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-ONE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer augmentation cystoplasty to selected NLUTD patients with DO or poor compliance when less invasive treatment has failed or cannot be tolerated (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review and one observational study had serious bias and inconsistent outcomes. Although AC can achieve high continence and protect the upper tract, studies are few and later procedures and lifelong monitoring are often necessary. Explain potential stones, perforation, bowel dysfunction, and mucus; confirm that the patient or caregiver can perform regular CIC. A narrative review of 20 publications could not pool results because of limited, low-quality data. Across four studies including 140 patients, most reported satisfaction without standardized QoL measures. Renal function remained stable without deterioration in 247 postoperative patients, and 11 studies reported improved continence and VUR resolution in 108 of 150 renal units. Serious adverse events were uncommon, but stones, bowel dysfunction, and mucus-related problems each exceeded 10%. Larger studies suggested that concurrent ureteral reimplantation was unnecessary and an extraperitoneal approach had equivalent efficacy with faster recovery. Reported post-AC bladder cancer risk was 0.6% to 4.5%; routine cystoscopy is not recommended without an indication such as hematuria or recurrent UTI. Reid et al. compared two 10-year series totaling 126 patients: dry rates were 83% and 85%; early complications (< 3 months) were 15%, late complications (> 3 months) 17%, and no mortality was reported.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-TWO
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer continent catheterizable channels, with or without augmentation, to selected NLUTD patients to make catheterization possible or easier (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). One systematic review had serious bias. Potential candidates include those who can self-catheterize but cannot use a damaged urethra, need BNC, or prefer easier access despite preserved urethral function and hand dexterity. Discuss complications and expected outcomes before surgery; multidisciplinary assessment can help when cognition or upper-limb function is limited. A review of 11 retrospective studies involving 213 patients found that 84% could catheterize the channel and >75% had stomal continence at median follow-up of 36 months. Reoperation was required in 40%; stenosis occurred in 4-32% (median 14%). Other reasons for surgery included fistula, stones, and perforation. Mitrofanoff, Monti or Casale tubes were used in 55%, invaginated valves in 23%, and non-invaginated tubes in 21%; AC or pouch construction accompanied 78%, and 23% had simultaneous outlet surgery. In another series of 114 patients over 10 years, 45% needed concurrent outlet surgery, major complications occurred in 16%, and readmission in 21%. At median follow-up of 40 months, 42% underwent 80 additional procedures, including a channel procedure in 20%. In six women with SCI at C7 or higher, mean CIC time fell from 27 (10-40) to 7.8 minutes (1-15), and all catheterized while seated in their wheelchairs. In another cervical-SCI series, 20 of 21 continued channel catheterization: 12 independently and 8 with family or caregiver help. These findings support individualized, multidisciplinary planning rather than an assumption of independent catheterization.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-THREE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may offer ileovesicostomy to selected NLUTD patients, but must explain benefits, alternatives, risks, and the high likelihood of further treatment or surgery (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies had very serious bias. This potentially reversible, low-pressure drainage option may suit people unable to self-catheterize because of hand dysfunction, immobility, body habitus, or condom-catheter skin injury; long-term revision risk remains concerning. Across small retrospective studies, 33 to 75% required later procedures, most often stoma revision, followed by stone removal. Tan et al. studied 50 patients (21 male; 29 female) operated on during 1999 to 2003. Mean follow-up was 26.3 months (range 1 – 79 months); SCI accounted for 42% and MS for 38%. Before surgery, 88% had incontinence and 37 used indwelling catheters. Prior interventions included pubovaginal sling 65.5%, BNC 20%, suprapubic closure 20%, enterocystoplasty 12%, and fistula repair 6%. Urethral continence was 72% (n=36) at mean follow-up of 26 months (range 1-79 months); reported rates were 42% at six months, 44.8% at one year, and 22 of 32 after more than one year. Twenty-seven patients underwent 77 reoperations: ileovesicostomy revision 6, stoma revision 8, BNC 7, fistula closure 33, sling 9, bladder onabotulinumtoxinA injection 11, collagen injection 3, and wound repair 7. Reoperation correlated with total complications (p<0.001) and stomal complications (p=0.0417); all 16 patients with four or more complications required reoperation, as did 73.7% of 19 with stomal complications. Concurrent sling or BNC did not appear to increase complications. Of 27 reoperated patients, 25 experienced postoperative incontinence at some point and 13 recovered continence by last follow-up. Those authors favored BNC over sling, with attention to ostomy fit; BNC eliminates native urethral access. Ileovesicostomy may drain poorly in obesity and requires regular long-term assessment for emptying and stones. In a separate comparison for severe urethral destruction, BNC plus SPC (n=21), BNC plus ileovesicostomy (n=17), and cystectomy plus ileal conduit (n=10) had urosepsis rates of 29%, 82%, and 60%, and subsequent surgery rates of 52%, 88%, and 50%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-FOUR
document_sections.content: Clinicians should offer urinary diversion when other NLUTD options have failed or are unsuitable, to improve long-term QoL (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Six observational studies had very serious bias and inconsistent outcomes. Continent or incontinent diversion can be a last resort for end-stage bladder or urethral dysfunction, persistent fistula, or non-healing pressure ulcer. Counseling must address hand function and available home support. In one ileal-conduit series of 33 patients (19 women, 14 men; 21 SCI, 4 MS, 3 myelitis, 5 central neurologic disease), catheter- and incontinence-related problems had resolved at mean follow-up of 48 months. In 53 MS patients followed for a median of 75 months after cystectomy and conduit construction, postoperative complications occurred in 50%; most reported complications were minor (n=23 cases; Clavien grades I-II), with 6 major complications (Clavien IIIIV). Improved urinary problems and Qualiveen scores led those authors to consider it acceptable after other options fail. Among 65 patients undergoing open (n=11), laparoscopic (n=14), or robotic (n=40) cystectomy and conduit construction, mean follow-up was 29 months and the authors reported favorable overall robotic outcomes; another series of 44 MS patients described laparoscopic surgery as safe with few complications. Fewer than 100 reported cases addressed continent diversion. In 61 patients with supratrigonal cystectomy and Hartmann pouch, mean follow-up was 5.8 years, continence improved in 90%, and complications occurred in 37%, of which 83% were Clavien grade <2. Reports of Kock reservoir in 10 SCI patients and Kock reservoir or Indiana pouch also described better continence and QoL, but did not use NLUTD-specific QoL instruments. Among 282 people with chronic (>10 years) SCI, those using diversion reported the least NLUTD-related QoL impact. Delayed complications after supravesical diversion occurred at rates of 21-50%, supporting consideration of simultaneous cystectomy. In one series of 16 patients with tetraplegia, 50% later required cystectomy for bladder empyema. Another series found recurrent bladder infection and pyocystis in 48 of 93 patients (52%; 71 with NLUTD), with five subsequent cystectomies. Among 19 patients retaining the bladder after conduit construction in another series, four developed pyocystis and three required cystectomy. A Spence procedure may drain a defunctionalized bladder in women with pyocystis; concurrent supratrigonal cystectomy or cystoprostatectomy should be strongly considered in men. A six-center comparison of extracorporeal and intracorporeal robot-assisted ileal conduit in 97 NLUTD patients found no significant perioperative differences. Continuing follow-up is necessary: after median follow-up of 75 months, 11 of 53 MS patients required surgery for a late complication, while another series reported upper-tract changes in 34%.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-FIVE
document_sections.content: Other potential NLUTD treatments should be regarded as investigational, and patients should receive corresponding counseling (Expert Opinion). Nonstandard interventions should be confined to well-designed trials when development is preliminary or adequate outcome evidence is lacking. For an adjustable continence mechanism, one retrospective study reported success in 16 patients (13 male; 3 female) over 48 months, but small size and undefined outcomes limit generalization; five out of the 13 devices required removal for malfunction, erosion, or infection. Another small retrospective study reported better continence alongside erosion, migration, infection, bladder stones, and difficulty with CIC. Early SNM after acute SCI was reported in ten patients to prevent DO and incontinence and preserve capacity while improving bowel and erectile function; use to modify early NLUTD progression remains investigational, despite this report. The Xiao procedure reroutes nerves to seek voluntary bladder and bowel control after SCI or SB. An initial report found satisfactory emptying and low PVR in 67%, fewer UTIs, and resolution of overflow UI, but later findings have been inconsistent. A US pilot reported transient leg weakness in every patient and persisting incontinence in most. In a double-blind randomized SB trial, ten patients received untethering alone and ten received untethering plus Xiao; urinary control, continence, and stimulation-induced UDS contraction did not differ. The Panel therefore confines this procedure to research settings with appropriate counseling. Tissue-engineered bladder reconstruction remains investigational. Brindley SARS places electrodes on bilateral S2-S4 nerves, usually with posterior sacral rhizotomy from S2 to S5; it was described in 1982, reported in 1984, and obtained FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption approval in 1998. An initial series of 13 patients reported voluntary voiding, low PVR, and acceptable capacity. Among 21 evaluated at one year, 85.7% voided more than 200 mL, 71.4% had PVR < 50 ml, and investigators described fewer UTIs, CIC episodes, and AD events and improved bowel management. A modified Barcelona extradural technique was studied in 104 people with SCI (n=95 men; 32.7% cervical, 65.4% thoracic, 1.9% lumbar): incontinence changed from 100% to 14% (p<0.001), UTI from 91% to 15% (p<0.001), and dysreflexia from 66.3% to 5.8% (p<0.001). After implantation, 94% reached capacity greater than 400 mL and 91% achieved effective voluntary emptying with PVR less than 50 mL. Implant infection, electrode extrusion, and receiver extrusion each occurred in 1.9%. Irreversible rhizotomy, potential loss of function in incomplete injury, and procedural complexity restrict anterior-root stimulators to research or experienced specialty centers.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up and post treatment
document_sections.content: This portion sets out reassessment after treatment and lifelong monitoring after selected reconstructions.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-SIX
document_sections.content: Clinicians should repeat UDS at a suitable post-treatment interval when impaired storage or emptying places the upper tracts at risk in NLUTD (Expert Opinion). Untreated high storage pressures, particularly impaired compliance, threaten upper-tract function. Cervical or high thoracic SCI and SB may pose especially high risk, although other neurologic disorders can also cause serious harm. Repeat multichannel UDS can determine whether pressure-reducing treatment works. Options discussed include increasing CIC frequency, oral therapy, onabotulinumtoxinA, and AC; successful treatment can improve compliance and DO, and upper-tract imaging may show better drainage. Renal risk after SCI remains lifelong. The best UDS interval is inadequately studied and disputed: an interval of two years or less is considered reasonable for at-risk patients once pressures normalize, with less frequent testing possible when clinically stable. Timing should reflect neurologic condition and baseline and subsequent risk. A voiding or catheterization diary before UDS can help determine relevant filling volumes.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-SEVEN
document_sections.content: Clinicians should offer further treatment when NLUTD-related unsafe storage parameters persist despite therapy and threaten the upper tracts (Expert Opinion). Lowering storage pressure aims primarily to preserve renal function, improve upper-tract drainage, and reduce recurrent symptomatic UTI. Escalation according to invasiveness is reasonable if repeat UDS checks efficacy at appropriate intervals. If CIC at 4 hours does not prevent incontinence or repeated infections in someone with high pressure, additional treatment should not be delayed. Persistent symptoms or elevated storage pressure despite anticholinergic or beta agonist therapy may warrant onabotulinumtoxinA or AC. For failure of all therapies, constant drainage through SPC or supravesical diversion should be strongly considered.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-EIGHT
document_sections.content: Following lower urinary tract reconstruction incorporating bowel, assess NLUTD patients annually with a focused history, physical examination, symptom review, basic metabolic panel, and urinary tract imaging (Expert Opinion). Lifelong follow-up is needed because reconstruction-related complications occur. Metabolic risk depends on prior renal function, comorbidity, bowel segment, and diversion type, and is higher with continent diversion. Evaluate electrolyte and acid–base disturbances even when asymptomatic and image for upper-tract obstruction. If terminal ileum was used, monitor B12 over time and supplement when appropriate. A continent urinary stoma without AC does not carry the same augmentation-related electrolyte or acid–base risk; annual assessment without a basic metabolic panel is sufficient in that situation.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT FIFTY-NINE
document_sections.content: Clinicians may perform UDS after sphincterotomy to assess the result (Conditional Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies had very serious bias. Sphincterotomy can improve DSD-related pressure and emptying, particularly after SCI, but residual urine and unsafe pressure can recur without obvious symptoms. Postoperative multichannel UDS is recommended in the discussion to document lower storage pressure, with continued monitoring of upper- and lower-tract emptying and bladder storage pressure thereafter.

document_sections.heading: STATEMENT SIXTY
document_sections.content: Clinicians should perform cystoscopy when NLUTD patients with bowel-based lower urinary reconstruction develop gross hematuria or symptomatic recurrent UTI (Moderate Recommendation; Evidence Level: Grade C). Two observational studies had very serious bias. Routine cystoscopy in otherwise asymptomatic stable patients is unsupported, but evaluation after bowel reconstruction remains debated. In a prospective series of 92 patients undergoing scheduled cystoscopy 10 years after AC, no asymptomatic bladder cancer was detected over median follow-up of 15 years (10-33 years). Malignancy after reconstruction usually presents with symptoms such as visible blood, unexplained recurrent UTI, or suprapubic pain; in these circumstances the discussion calls for cystoscopy, urine cytology, and abdominal and pelvic computerized tomography rather than attributing findings to CIC trauma, cystitis, or pouchitis without assessment. Cancer risk after AC is uncertain: reported follow-up probability ranged from 0-5.5% and estimated incidence from 0 to 272.3 per 100,000 patients/year. Adenocarcinoma represented 51.6% of reported tumors; 50% arose at the entero-urinary junction. Mean latency was 19 years and 90% were diagnosed more than 10 years after surgery. Evidence suggesting higher risk than in the general population was considered poor. The value of urine cytology and urinary tumor markers in surveillance remains uncertain; tumors have sometimes appeared at advanced stage between scheduled examinations.

document_sections.heading: Future Directions
document_sections.content: The Panel identifies improved symptom measurement, delivery of existing therapies, neuromodulation, reconstruction, and treatment of underlying neurologic disease as areas requiring further study.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of Bladder Dysfunction: ConditionSpecific Questionnaires
document_sections.content: Symptoms and sensory experience can differ substantially between patients with and without neurologic disease. The Panel favors condition-specific lower-urinary-tract questionnaires when feasible and recommends further development and refinement of these measures for NLUTD.

document_sections.heading: Improving Current Strategies/Implementing current strategies for new indications
document_sections.content: Botulinum toxin has improved QoL in many patients with NDO who might otherwise need invasive, irreversible surgery, but repeated injections, discomfort, and cost hinder regular access. The Panel supports study of different injection and delivery methods. Peripheral and central neuromodulation remain insufficiently studied across NLUTD groups despite promising small cohorts. Further research should determine which stimulation approaches suit particular patients; implantable tibial devices and MRI-conditional sacral devices warrant evaluation. Early neuromodulation after SCI as a possible means of changing disease progression remains a research question. SARS and the Xiao procedure also need further technical and outcome study because of surgical challenges, potential functional loss, and inconsistent results. Implanted urethral valve or pump devices are being investigated to reduce dependence on CIC: one intraurethral valve pump has an FDA indication for women with detrusor underactivity but no specific NLUTD indication, and another device is being studied in men with chronic retention. Device migration, infection, encrustation, discomfort, and obstruction remain concerns.

document_sections.heading: Novel Strategies for Urinary Diversion and Augmentation
document_sections.content: Intestinal segments are versatile and available for diversion but can cause metabolic and bowel complications. Synthetic and bioengineered replacements have not yet proved successful. Although early clinical scaffold reports appeared favorable, later reports found that biodegradable scaffolds seeded with autologous smooth-muscle and urothelial cells did not improve storage pressure after augmentation and were associated with substantial postoperative morbidity. Bladder allografting with vascular connections has been feasible in cadaveric models, but whether it can produce a functional, safe urinary tract remains unknown. The Panel encourages study of non-intestinal reconstruction and refinement of tissue-engineered approaches.

document_sections.heading: Treatment of the Neurologic Condition
document_sections.content: Treating the cause of NLUTD could theoretically improve urinary and other neurologic symptoms. Stem-cell approaches have mainly been studied after acute SCI. A review identified ten human studies (5 completed, 5 ongoing); preliminary findings suggested higher MCC and compliance and lower detrusor pressure, without improvement in UI or elimination of CIC. Higher-quality studies are needed. For SUI, questions remain about stem-cell effectiveness, type, dose, placement, and applicability to NLUTD requiring CIC. High-quality trials for underactive bladder are not yet complete, and the approach has not been specifically evaluated in NLUTD. Deep brain stimulation is used for motor symptoms in PD and other disorders; a review found that subthalamic stimulation significantly increased maximum bladder capacity, while other UDS changes lacked clinical relevance. Stem-cell treatment for PD remains uncertain and would require trials. The Panel hopes that advances in treating neurologic conditions will also improve or resolve associated urinary symptoms.
